title: Reproducibility-Aware Evaluation of Hierarchical Multiple- Instance Learning for Patient-Level Thrombosis Detection from Compression Ultrasound
abstract: Abstract Background To provide a reproducibility-aware evaluation of multi-site cine multiple-instance learning (MS-CineMIL) versus a fixed 8-frame imaging baseline under patient-level five-fold cross-validation, and to examine whether the nominal ROC AUC difference reproduces after field completion and runtime environment control. The study delineates aggregation applicability boundaries rather than presupposing a stable advantage. Methods The public ThrombUS+ Dataset #1 Training Set (v1.0; 594 subjects, 2,341 DICOM cine clips) was used. Thrombosis is a per-site label, so the patient-level endpoint was defined as engineering-positive: raw Thrombosis = 1 for any record of the same SubjectID (81/594). After quality control, 2,327 cines were retained. Partitions used SubjectID isolation. Primary metric: ROC AUC; secondary: PR AUC, Brier score. Model differences were tested by 10,000-resample patient-level paired bootstrap (empirical two-sided P values; Bonferroni α = 0.0167). Results In the V1 historical frozen analysis, the ROC AUC difference of MS-CineMIL versus the fixed 8-frame baseline was + 0.0740 (95% CI 0.0043 to 0.1454, P = 0.039), failing Bonferroni correction. In the same-environment controlled comparison, the difference was − 0.0283 (95% CI − 0.1177 to 0.0608, P = 0.538) with a larger Brier error (+ 0.0374, P < 0.001). The baseline re-run yielded 0.6390; the complete model ROC AUC was 0.6419. The between-run baseline shift (0.0711) matched the nominal gain (+ 0.0740); no stable advantage emerged. Conclusions The V1 frozen difference did not pass multiple-comparison correction, was not reproduced under controlled comparison, and was accompanied by a larger Brier error. Evidence supports boundary auditing of model components, field completeness, and aggregation strategies, but not stable superiority, clinical deployment, external applicability, or novelty claims.

Thrombosis is a per-site label, so the patient-level endpoint was defined as engineering-positive: raw Thrombosis = 1 for any record of the same SubjectID (81/594). After quality control, 2,327 cines were retained. Partitions used SubjectID isolation. Primary metric: ROC AUC; secondary: PR AUC, Brier score. Model differences were tested by 10,000-resample patient-level paired bootstrap (empirical two-sided P values; Bonferroni α = 0.0167). Results In the V1 historical frozen analysis, the ROC AUC difference of MS-CineMIL versus the fixed 8-frame baseline was + 0.0740 (95% CI 0.0043 to 0.1454, P = 0.039), failing Bonferroni correction. In the same-environment controlled comparison, the difference was − 0.0283 (95% CI − 0.1177 to 0.0608, P = 0.538) with a larger Brier error (+ 0.0374, P < 0.001). The baseline re-run yielded 0.6390; the complete model ROC AUC was 0.6419. The between-run baseline shift (0.0711) matched the nominal gain (+ 0.0740); no stable advantage emerged. Conclusions The V1 frozen difference did not pass multiple-comparison correction, was not reproduced under controlled comparison, and was accompanied by a larger Brier error. Evidence supports boundary auditing of model components, field completeness, and aggregation strategies, but not stable superiority, clinical deployment, external applicability, or novelty claims.

title: Clinically Suspected Systemic Arterial Gas Embolism during Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopy: a Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background: Systemic arterial gas embolism (SAGE) is a rare but potentially catastrophic complication of robotic-assisted bronchoscopy with lung biopsy. During general anesthesia, the earliest manifestations of SAGE may be limited to transient electrocardiographic or hemodynamic abnormalities. The absence of visible intracranial gas on subsequent imaging does not exclude the diagnosis. We report a case of clinically suspected SAGE during robotic-assisted bronchoscopy in which intraoperative sentinel signs preceded delayed emergence and focal neurologic injury. Case presentation: A 78-year-old woman underwent robotic-assisted bronchoscopy under general anesthesia for biopsy of a 4.6-cm right middle lobe ground-glass opacity using transbronchial needle aspiration and cryobiopsy. Significant airway bleeding occurred after sampling. Immediately after biopsy, she developed transient tachycardia, hypertension, bradycardia, and ST-segment elevation in lead V5. Although these abnormalities resolved, she was unresponsive shortly after extubation and developed right gaze deviation, facial twitching, abnormal movements, and absent right upper-extremity withdrawal to pain. Head computed tomography showed no acute abnormality, and brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated left frontal and precentral cortical diffusion restriction without visible intracranial gas. Because SAGE was strongly suspected, she received 100% oxygen, levetiracetam, endotracheal reintubation, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy at 2.8 atmospheres absolute approximately 4 hours after bronchoscopy. High-sensitivity troponin I peaked at 5,116 ng/L and left ventricular ejection fraction improved from 45-50% to 60% the following day. She was extubated on post-procedure day 10 with persistent neurologic deficits. On post-procedure day 18, she experienced hypoxic cardiac arrest associated with bilateral pulmonary emboli and an acute aortic dissection and died the following day after transition to comfort-focused care. Conclusions: During bronchoscopic biopsies under general anesthesia, unexplained ST-segment changes, hemodynamic instability, or delayed neurologic recovery should prompt immediate consideration of SAGE, even when initial neuroimaging is negative. Administration of 100% oxygen, airway and hemodynamic support, minimization of airway pressures, and urgent consultation for hyperbaric oxygen therapy should not be delayed while awaiting radiographic confirmation.

title: Adenosquamous carcinoma of the colon with an aberrant MLH1 immunostaining pattern: a diagnostic pitfall in mismatch repair assessment
abstract: Abstract Background Adenosquamous carcinoma (ASC) is a rare histological subtype of colorectal cancer (CRC) that carries a poor prognosis and has been associated with a distinct molecular profile - higher frequency of mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR), PD-L1 overexpression, and KRAS mutations. With recent advances in CRC therapeutics, molecular characterization of rare histological subtypes has become increasingly important. Here, we report a case of colorectal ASC with a distinctive dMMR immunohistochemical profile and provide a review of the literature on this rare colorectal neoplasm. Case Presentation: We report the case of a 64-year-old woman who presented with a three-month history of worsening abdominal pain and recent-onset hematochezia. Abdominal CT revealed a large mass involving the right colon. She underwent a total pelvic exenteration. Histopathology showed a high-grade, poorly differentiated tumor with mixed glandular and squamous components, staged as pT4b pN1a. Immunohistochemistry confirmed both glandular and squamous differentiation. Mismatch repair protein analysis showed loss of PMS2 expression and a granular, dot-like MLH1 staining pattern—interpreted as loss of expression and consistent with a known clone-specific artifact—while MSH2 and MSH6 were retained, supporting a dMMR phenotype. The patient received mFLOX chemotherapy but died four months postoperatively due to disease-related complications. Discussion This case illustrates the classic clinicopathological features of ASC, alongside a dMMR immunoprofile that may carry therapeutic relevance given the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors in MSI-high colorectal tumors. The findings also underscore the importance of correctly recognizing clone-specific MLH1 staining artifacts, as misinterpretation could falsely suggest isolated PMS2 loss and trigger unnecessary germline testing for Lynch syndrome. Given the rarity of ASC and its limited molecular characterization, accurate MMR status assessment remains critical for guiding treatment decisions and avoiding diagnostic pitfalls.

title: CT-based Deep Learning Radiomics Analysis for Predicting Postoperative Pancreatic Fistula after Pancreatectomy
abstract: Abstract Background Clinically relevant postoperative pancreatic fistula (CR-POPF) is a severe complication following pancreatic surgery. However, the preoperative prediction of CR-POPF remains challenging. This study aims to develop and validate a deep learning radiomics (DLR) model that integrates imaging and clinical features for CR-POPF prediction. Methods This retrospective study included 425 patients who underwent pancreatic surgery between January 2020 and April 2024. Then, preoperative contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) images and clinical data were collected. Afterwards, the radiomics features were extracted from the CT images, and deep learning features were obtained using ResNet50. Subsequently, these features were integrated into a DLR model, and feature selection was performed via LASSO regression, yielding seven key features. Then, a clinical model was developed using univariate and multivariable logistic regression. The combined model integrated the DLR and clinical models. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA). The DeLong test was used to compare the area under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUCs). Results The overall incidence of CR-POPF was 19.76%. The DLR model, which integrated the radiomics and deep learning features, outperformed the clinical model and radiomics-only model. In the test cohort, the combined model achieved an AUC of 0.819 (95% CI: 0.732–0.906), outperforming the clinical model (AUC: 0.767) and DLR model (AUC: 0.803). The calibration and DCA confirmed the superior clinical utility of the combined model, with higher net benefits at various risk thresholds. Conclusions The combined DLR model that integrated imaging features and clinical variables demonstrated superior performance in preoperatively predicting CR-POPF. This approach provides a promising tool for personalized risk assessment in pancreatic surgery.

title: A generalized similarity metric based on Sobolev space geometry for deformable image registration in image-guided radiotherapy
abstract: Abstract Background : Deformable image registration is an essential technique in image-guided adaptive radiotherapy. It provides voxelwise estimates of the anatomical deformations from medical image volumes acquired at different time points. However, the accuracy of the estimated motion strongly depends on image contrast, presence of noise and artifacts, and the overall image quality. Purpose : This study introduces a novel similarity metric based on the geometry of Sobolev spaces. The proposed metric provides control over the contribution of high-order image features, allowing the metric to adapt to the characteristics of the images. It unifies several established similarity metrics and enables efficient numerical computation for integration into existing registration methods. Methods : The metric was integrated into a deformable image registration algorithm and evaluated on three experiments relevant for adaptive radiotherapy: thoracic and abdominal CT registration and pre- to post-operative brain MR image registration. Registration accuracy was assessed using alignment of anatomical landmarks. Results : The proposed similarity metric achieved rapid and accurate image alignment in all three scenarios. Increasing the contribution from higher-order image features improved the estimated deformation fields by a reduction of the landmark error. In particular, increased weighting of these features improved the alignment of liver vessels and the brain cavity following tumor resection. Conclusions : The proposed metric provides the flexibility to control the relative contribution of image features for deformable image registration. It unifies several established similarity metrics while maintaining computational efficiency and accuracy standards that are compatible with image-guided radiotherapy.

title: Interactive Lesion Segmentation in Whole-Body PET/CT and Longitudinal CT: The autoPET/CT-IV Challenge
abstract: Abstract Deep learning enables automated tumour segmentation in whole-body positron emission tomography and computed tomography, but robustness remains limited by heterogeneous tracer uptake, anatomical variability, and inter-center differences. We report the fourth autoPET challenge, which evaluated interactive lesion segmentation using incremental simulated user prompts and longitudinal lesion segmentation from paired baseline and follow-up scans. In the interactive task (Task 1, ~ 30,000 training and ~ 3,000 test lesions), submitted methods improved with additional user input and achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 0.74 at the final interaction step, with performance remaining robust across tracers and centers. Longitudinal segmentation (Task 2, ~ 7,500 training and ~ 4,500 test lesions) was substantially more challenging, with a best mean Dice similarity coefficient of 0.38. Here, we show that interactive segmentation can combine automated inference with iterative expert input while maintaining performance across heterogeneous imaging domains, whereas longitudinal lesion prediction remains limited by temporal and anatomical variability.

title: Halo-Femoral Traction and Staged Surgical Correction for Severe Rigid Adult Scoliosis: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background: Surgical correction of severe rigid adult spinal deformities (ASD) with Cobb angles exceeding 100° is highly challenging due to risks of neurological injury and poor spinal flexibility. Preoperative halo-femoral traction enhances spinal compliance, facilitating safer staged corrective surgery. Few cases of this procedure for curvatures approaching 150° have been reported. Case Presentation: A 24-year-old female presented with severe right thigh and knee pain secondary to a 148° rigid thoracolumbar kyphoscoliosis. Initial imaging revealed minimal flexibility (bend correction to 94°) without neural compromise. The patient underwent continuous halo-femoral traction for several weeks to improve spinal flexibility, The patient was managed via a sequential two-step protocol: initially, under anesthesia, halo and femoral pins were placed to apply continuous traction for maximizing spinal flexibility. Subsequently, the patient underwent definitive single-stage posterior spinal instrumentation and deformity correction. Intraoperative neuromonitoring was utilized throughout to ensure neurological safety. Continuous multi-modal intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM), including somatosensory-evoked potentials (SSEPs) and motor-evoked potentials (MEPs), was utilized throughout all two surgical stages. No significant or sustained changes in SSEP or MEP signals were observed during the corrective maneuvers, supporting the early detection of potential neurological compromise and guiding safe deformity correction. Conclusion: Postoperatively, the patient achieved significant correction with a final Cobb angle of approximately 50°, accompanied by marked pain relief, improved truncal balance, and enhanced functional status as measured by clinical video-based clinical observation of gait. Radiographs at 6 weeks and subsequent follow-ups demonstrated stable fusion and sustained alignment. No neurological deficits or major complications were observed. This case illustrates the feasibility of utilizing prolonged halo-femoral traction combined with a carefully planned surgical algorithm in the management of extreme rigid adult scoliosis. The technical and strategic framework provided herein may inform clinical practice guidelines and warrants further investigation in larger cohorts.

title: Assistance curve analysis: evaluating the clinical value of AI-assisted decision making
abstract: Abstract Background. Clinical AI is almost never used alone. It shows something to a doctor, and the doctor decides. Yet the measures used to judge them describe the model, not the decision. A 2025 overview of 32 performance measures for clinical AI covers five domains, and current standard metrics do not explicitly evaluate the decisions of an assisted clinician in a paired setting. Methods. We define the net benefit of assistance, ΔNB(p), as the difference in net benefit between the decisions a clinician makes with an AI available and those they make without it. We show that ΔNB depends only on cases where the clinician changed their mind, and give a closed form in four quantities: how often the AI moves the clinician each way, and how often it is right when it does. This yields a break-even rule, a number needed to consult, and an override profile. We checked the estimators by simulation and applied the method to Collab-CXR, a public study of 227 radiologists reading chest X-rays with and without a CheXpert-trained model. Results. ΔNB(p) = [r U (π U − p) + r L (p − π L )]/(1 − p). Across 27,720 paired decisions by 33 radiologists, the AI made them less accurate by 0.83 percentage points while making their decisions better. ΔNB was + 0.0022 at p = 0.05 (95% CI + 0.0007 to + 0.0038), a 7% gain on the unaided radiologist’s net benefit, or one extra net true positive per 455 decisions. The benefit was clear between thresholds of 0.02 and 0.05; above 0.05 the interval included zero, and below about 0.019 both arms were beaten by acting on every finding. The break-even threshold was 0.201. Two further designs covering 194 radiologists agreed in direction. Effects ranged from + 0.0131 for atelectasis to − 0.0024 for cardiomediastinal abnormality. Conclusions. The value of an AI is made on the decisions it changes and cannot be read off accuracy. Judging by accuracy would have rejected a tool that improved decisions. The method needs only what a paired reader study already collects, and free software is provided for R and Python.

title: Normotension as a Red Flag: A Proposed Framework for Early Recognition of Masked Preeclampsia in Couvelaire Uterus – A Case Report and a Teaching Tool
abstract: Abstract Background Couvelaire uterus (CU) is a rare, life-threatening complication of placental abruption, occurring in about 1% of cases. Preeclampsia is a major risk factor; however, its diagnosis becomes difficult when concealed hemorrhage hides typical hypertension, delaying recognition. Additionally, the critical impact of the time from symptom onset to surgical intervention on uterine preservation is not well understood in the literature. We present a case of CU with masked preeclampsia and evolving disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) to propose a new time-based framework for early recognition and surgical decision-making. Case presentation: We report a 19-year-old unbooked primigravida at 35 + 5 weeks presenting with absent fetal movements. On admission, she was normotensive (110/60 mmHg) with a relative rise in heart rate (HR: 88 bpm), severe proteinuria (1000 mg/dL), thrombocytopenia (78×10⁹/L), and a woody uterus. Coagulation revealed PT 17.7s (INR 1.42) and fibrinogen (3.38 g/L), consistent with non-overt DIC (ISTH score 2/8). Ultrasound confirmed intrauterine fetal demise. Over seven hours, labor did not progress, necessitating emergency cesarean section. Intraoperatively, a retroplacental hematoma and CU were identified, and a prophylactic B-Lynch suture was placed (estimated blood loss 1500–2000 mL). Postoperatively, rebound hypertension to 150/100 mmHg responded promptly to magnesium sulfate, confirming masked PE. She recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day four. Discussion Based on this case, we propose three educational frameworks: (1) a three-phase hemodynamic model (occult compensation, rebound surge, therapeutic stabilization) to unmask PE during hemorrhage; (2) a "window of opportunity" concept, advocating surgical intervention within 6–8 hours of symptom onset to avoid irreversible DIC (ISTH ≥ 5) and preserve the uterus; and (3) a counterfactual analysis of two similar cases, demonstrating that timely intervention is the single most modifiable factor for uterine salvage. Conclusion Normotension in PA with proteinuria is a red flag, not reassurance. Magnesium responsiveness confirms underlying PE. B-Lynch suture is effective for uterine preservation, even in resource-limited settings. Clinicians must prioritize early evacuation, especially in conflict-affected areas.

title: Gangrenous Appendico-ileal knotting causing strangulated small-bowel obstruction and shock in a patient with a virgin abdomen: a case report
abstract: Abstract Background: Appendico-ileal knotting is a rare cause of closed-loop small-bowel obstruction in which the appendix encircles the ileum and may cause strangulation and bowel ischemia. Preoperative diagnosis is difficult because the clinical presentation is nonspecific. Case presentation: A 52-year-old Ethiopian man with no prior abdominal surgery presented after 2 days of abdominal pain, distension, bilious vomiting, and obstipation. He was hypotensive, tachycardic, dehydrated, and had generalized peritonitis. Plain abdominal radiography showed features of small-bowel obstruction. Following resuscitation, antibiotics, and vasopressor support, emergency laparotomy was performed for suspected strangulated small-bowel obstruction. title: Pulsatile Tinnitus: A Multimodality Imaging Review of Etiology and Diagnostic Evaluation
abstract: Abstract Pulsatile tinnitus is a rhythmic, pulse-synchronous auditory perception that is frequently associated with an underlying vascular or structural abnormality. While tinnitus affects approximately 10–20% of adults, pulsatile tinnitus is relatively uncommon but clinically significant, with an identifiable and potentially treatable cause detected in over 70% of patients and in up to 90% in dedicated imaging cohorts. The etiologic spectrum is broad and includes vascular, structural, systemic, benign, and malignant conditions, some of which may result in serious morbidity if unrecognized. Imaging is central to diagnosis and management, with evaluation commonly performed using high-resolution temporal bone CT, CT angiography and venography, MRI with angiographic and venographic techniques, and digital subtraction angiography in selected cases. This pictorial review integrates multimodality imaging with representative case examples to provide a structured, physiology-based diagnostic approach. By emphasizing key imaging patterns across major etiologic categories, this review aims to enhance diagnostic confidence, streamline imaging workup, and facilitate recognition of actionable causes, thereby supporting timely intervention and improved patient outcomes.

title: Pericardial Effusion Presenting as Isolated Right Upper Quadrant Pain with Deranged Liver Enzymes a Diagnostic Pitfall in the Emergency Department a Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Pericardial effusion typically presents with chest pain, dyspnoea, and positional discomfort. Presentation with isolated abdominal pain in the absence of cardiopulmonary symptoms is rare and closely mimics acute hepatobiliary pathology. Recognition is critical, since unrecognised pericardial effusion may progress to life-threatening cardiac tamponade. Case Presentation A 43-year-old black African woman with virologically suppressed human immunodeficiency virus infection (HIV), ulcerative colitis, and a history of previously treated latent tuberculosis (TB) infection presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of abdominal pain radiating to the flanks and epigastrium. Right upper quadrant tenderness on examination and elevated liver enzymes upon further investigation prompted a provisional diagnosis of cholecystitis. A subsequent chest radiograph showed a globular cardiac silhouette and bedside echocardiography confirmed a large pericardial effusion. Computed tomography (CT) demonstrated an effusion with features of right cardiac impairment, hepatic congestion and pericholecystic fluid, with no evidence of acute cholecystitis. Pericardiocentesis yielded haemoserous fluid, with resolution of symptoms and improvement in liver enzymes. The effusion re-accumulated within 5 days, with right ventricular diastolic collapse and this was surgically managed. The rapid recurrence raised suspicion of a potential inflammatory aetiology; however, the definitive aetiology remains unclear. Conclusions Pericardial effusion should be considered in patients with undifferentiated abdominal pain and liver enzyme derangement, even in the absence of typical cardiac symptoms or Beck’s triad. This case highlights the potential for cardiac pathology to mimic acute hepatobiliary disease and emphasises the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis in atypical abdominal presentations.

title: Influence of CT Tube Replacement and System Parameter Update on Reconstructed CT Values and Electron Density Conversion Curves in Radiotherapy Treatment Planning Systems
abstract: Abstract Objective Large-aperture positioning CT is a core device for radiotherapy simulation, target delineation, and accurate dose calculation. Replacement of the X‑ray tube, followed by subsequent system parameter updates (including software version upgrade, reconstruction algorithm adjustment, and detector gain calibration), may alter the X-ray energy spectrum and image reconstruction characteristics, thereby inducing systematic drift of CT numbers (Hounsfield Units, HU) and disturbing the accuracy of CT-relative electron density (CT-RED) and CT-mass density (CT-MD) conversion curves in treatment planning systems (TPS). This study aimed to quantify CT number drifts in multiple tissue‑equivalent phantoms before and after tube replacement and system parameter updates using a Philips Big Bore CT 16 scanner, to evaluate the detection efficacy of conventional AAPM TG66 image quality indicators for such occult drift, to reconstruct density conversion curves for Eclipse and Tomo TPS, and to establish a standardized quality control workflow. Methods Fault records and the tube replacement process from August 2023 to January 2024 were analyzed. Tube replacement was performed on January 13, 2024, followed by standard acceptance tests including position calibration, focus correction, long‑tube conditioning, and air scan. System software was upgraded from V3.6 to V4.8 on October 18, 2024, with resetting of reconstruction filter parameters, detector gain coefficients, and air baseline. All CT value measurements, curve reconstructions, and dosimetric verifications were performed after the software upgrade, representing the combined effect of “tube replacement + system parameter update”. Image quality was tested with a Catphan504 phantom according to AAPM TG66. CT value changes in 8 standard materials (air, polystyrene, water, LDPE, PMP, acrylic, Delrin, Teflon) before and after the intervention were compared using paired t‑tests with Bonferroni correction. CT-RED curves (standard and brain‑specific) for Eclipse and a CT-MD curve for Tomo were reconstructed using a CIRS-062M phantom containing 12 tissue‑equivalent materials. Accuracy of the new curves was validated by heterogeneous phantom planar dose verification and real patient plan QA. Results All conventional image quality indicators remained within TG66 tolerances after the intervention. Systematic CT drifts were observed in 7 of the 8 materials except water (P = 0.12, not significant), with drifts ranging 10–30 HU for most materials; Teflon showed a − 63 HU drift (P < 0.001) and air a + 33 HU drift (P < 0.001). Two CT‑RED curves for Eclipse and one CT‑MD curve for Tomo were successfully constructed, all with R² > 0.99. Dosimetric verification showed 3 mm/3% Gamma passing rates for Eclipse ≥ 98.9%, mean point‑dose deviation for Tomo 0.76%, and real patient plan QA passing rates > 98% with no significant differences before vs. after intervention (P > 0.05). Conclusion CT tube replacement and subsequent system parameter updates did not impair conventional TG66 image quality indicators, but induced systematic, material‑dependent CT number drifts that cannot be detected by routine water‑phantom uniformity tests. Re‑measurement of multi‑material CT baselines and mandatory reconstruction of density conversion curves are required. A four‑level quality control process (air calibration, multi‑material CT baseline measurement, curve reconstruction, and dosimetric verification) should be enforced after tube replacement or major software upgrades.

title: Trunk Muscle Quantity, Quality, and Two-Year Recovery in Older Women After Sagittal Adult Spinal Deformity Surgery
abstract: Abstract Purpose To determine whether dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA)-derived trunk lean mass corresponds to computed tomography (CT)-based local muscle size and attenuation, and to describe 2-year recovery after surgery for sagittal adult spinal deformity (ASD). Methods This single-center cohort study included 121 women aged 60 years or older with sagittal ASD and no major coronal curve. Ninety-two had analyzable preoperative L3 CT and paired DXA data. CT cross-sectional area (CSA) represented local muscle quantity and CT attenuation represented local radiodensity. Associations between DXA trunk lean mass and five prespecified CT metrics were tested with false-discovery-rate correction. Radiographic, physical-performance, and disability outcomes were assessed preoperatively and at 2 years. Results DXA trunk lean mass correlated with psoas CSA (r = 0.49; adjusted p = 0.005) but not with multifidus CSA or attenuation of the multifidus, erector spinae, or psoas. Sagittal alignment improved substantially. Stride length, one-leg standing, stand-up performance, and Locomo-25 improved, whereas gait speed, grip strength, and two-step outcomes did not. Oswestry Disability Index and Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire scores improved in 91 matched patients. Conclusion DXA trunk lean mass and CT attenuation provide complementary rather than interchangeable information. Two-year recovery after sagittal ASD correction was clinically meaningful but domain specific. Multimodal muscle assessment may help characterize preoperative muscle phenotype, although prognostic use requires prospective validation.

title: Contour-free multi-instance learning versus conventional CT features for preoperative Ki-67 stratification in gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumors: a retrospective comparison
abstract: Abstract Background : Manual tumor contouring adds a separate preprocessing step to CT-based prediction. We therefore evaluated whether complete-series multiinstance learning (MIL) could perform preoperative Ki-67 stratification from dual-phase CT without tumor contours and provide greater discrimination than conventional CT features. Methods : This retrospective study included 61 patients. Ki-67 cutoffs of 5%, 8%, and 10% defined three cutoff-specific tasks. Patients whose reported Ki-67 interval spanned a cutoff were excluded only from the corresponding task. Twenty-one conventional variables were analyzed with two conventional models, and frozen ResNet-18 features from the complete arterial and venous phase series were analyzed separately with five MIL methods. Four prespecified equal-logit fusion combinations were evaluated. Patient-level stratified fivefold cross-validation was repeated 10 times. Assessment comprised AUROC, AUPRC, calibration assessment, decision-curve analysis, paired bootstrap comparisons with Holm correction, and a post-training attention audit. Results : The three tasks included 59, 54, and 56 patients, with 41, 26, and 15 positive cases. The highest AUROCs were 0.645 (95% CI, 0.485–0.781) at 5%, 0.646 (95% CI, 0.496–0.788) at 8%, and 0.605 (95% CI, 0.442–0.753) at 10%. The maximum AUPRCs at 5%, 8%, and 10% were 0.822, 0.637, and 0.346. Every AUROC confidence interval included 0.5, and no comparison among the prespecified individual models or between fusion and its components remained significant after Holm correction. In the attention audit, 34 of 60 tests remained significant after global Holm correction, with 21 estimates above and 13 below their prespecified references. Conclusions : Complete-series MIL was applied separately to arterial and venous CT series for cutoff-specific Ki-67 stratification and did not require tumor contour inputs. It showed no clear discrimination advantage over conventional CT features in this cohort. External validation and direct assessment of annotation burden are required before clinical use.

title: Uterine carcinosarcoma with heterologous osteosarcomatous differentiation: a case report
abstract: Abstract Background Uterine carcinosarcoma is a rare biphasic malignant tumor, and the subtype with heterologous osteosarcomatous differentiation is exceedingly uncommon, making preoperative diagnosis challenging. Case Presentation We report the case of a 72-year-old postmenopausal woman who presented with vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic nodule within the uterine cavity, containing irregular calcified foci and punctate blood flow signals. She subsequently underwent hysteroscopic resection of the lesion with removal of the intrauterine device. Postoperative histopathology and immunohistochemistry supported a diagnosis of uterine carcinosarcoma with heterologous osteosarcomatous differentiation. To exclude a primary bone tumor and to evaluate the extent of disease, bone scintigraphy and pelvic magnetic resonance imaging were performed, followed by definitive surgical traetment. The final pathological stage was FIGO IA. Adjuvant chemotherapy with nab-paclitaxel plus carboplatin was administered. No definite evidence of recurrence or metastasis was identified during 6 months of follow-up. Conclusions This case suggests that uterine carcinosarcoma with heterologous osteosarcomatous differentiation, although rare, should be included in the differential diagnosis in postmenopausal women with abnormal uterine bleeding when ultrasonography shows an intrauterine mass with irregular calcified foci and blood flow signals, and when hysteroscopic findings suggest a malignant lesion with osseous components. Definitive diagnosis still relies on pathological examination, whereas MRI and bone scintigraphy may assist in preoperative evaluation and differential diagnosis.

title: Radiation-Induced High-Grade Glioma in a Long-Term Survivor of Medulloblastoma: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Advances in multimodal therapy have significantly improved survival in medulloblastoma, but long-term survivors remain at risk of secondary malignancies. We describe a rare case of radiation-induced high-grade glioma developing after a disease-free interval of approximately seven years, and nearly nine years following initial treatment. Case Presentation A 19-year-old male with a history of classical medulloblastoma (CNS WHO grade 4) presented nine years after his initial diagnosis with worsening headaches and fatigue. His primary tumor was treated with multiple surgical resections followed by high-dose craniospinal irradiation and adjuvant chemotherapy, after which he remained under surveillance. Seven years after completing treatment, he came in with a four-week history of weight loss and fatigue. One week before admission, he developed drowsiness, followed by a 10-day history of right focal seizures and increasing right-sided weakness. On neurological examination, he was obtunded with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9/15 and showed right-sided spastic hemiparesis with impaired verbal responsiveness. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed multiple supratentorial lesions associated with extensive vasogenic edema and mild midline shift, raising concern for a secondary malignant neoplasm. A left frontal burr-hole biopsy was subsequently performed. Histopathological examination demonstrated a highly cellular glial neoplasm composed of pleomorphic, hyperchromatic tumor cells embedded within a fibrillary background. Prominent microvascular proliferation and frequent mitotic activity were identified, consistent with a high-grade infiltrating glioma. Immunohistochemical analysis showed diffuse glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) positivity, absence of IDH1 R132H expression, retained ATRX nuclear staining, and a Ki-67 proliferation index of 15–20%. Tumor cells were negative for H3K27M, and mismatch repair protein expression was preserved. Based on the histopathological and immunophenotypic findings, a diagnosis of high-grade glioma, favoring astrocytoma, NOS, CNS WHO grade 4, was established. Given the patient's previous exposure to craniospinal radiotherapy and the prolonged latency period of nine years between treatment of the primary medulloblastoma and development of the high grade glioma, the lesion was highly suggestive of radiation-induced high-grade glioma. Despite supportive management, the patient's clinical condition deteriorated rapidly, and he succumbed to the disease one month after diagnosis. Conclusion This case illustrates the development of a secondary high-grade glioma in a long-term survivor of medulloblastoma, most likely representing a radiation-induced malignancy. It highlights the critical importance of lifelong surveillance in survivors of pediatric brain tumors, as early detection of secondary central nervous system neoplasms may allow timely intervention. Despite the limited therapeutic options available for these aggressive tumors, prompt recognition remains essential to optimize patient management and outcomes.

title: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome during enfortumab vedotin therapy: a case report
abstract: Abstract Background Antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs) are widely used to treat solid malignancies. Enfortumab vedotin (EV) is an effective therapeutic option for advanced urothelial carcinoma. Although EV-associated neurotoxicity is most commonly reported as peripheral neuropathy, central nervous system complications, particularly posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), are rare. We report a case of PRES associated with EV therapy. Case presentation: A man in his 50s underwent right nephroureterectomy for urothelial carcinoma, followed by adjuvant nivolumab therapy. Subsequently, multiple liver metastases developed, and treatment with EV was initiated. One day after EV administration during the second cycle, the patient developed acute visual impairment and altered consciousness. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences revealed hyperintense lesions in the subcortical white matter, predominantly involving both occipital lobes, consistent with PRES. EV was discontinued, and conservative management was initiated. The patient's neurological symptoms improved rapidly, and follow-up MRI demonstrated complete radiological resolution of the lesions. Conclusions In patients who develop visual disturbances, altered mental status, or other central neurological symptoms after treatment with EV, PRES should be considered in the differential diagnosis in addition to brain metastases. Early diagnosis of PRES during EV therapy may prevent irreversible neurological sequelae. Prompt neuroimaging evaluation and appropriate management are essential to achieve favorable outcomes.

Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences revealed hyperintense lesions in the subcortical white matter, predominantly involving both occipital lobes, consistent with PRES. EV was discontinued, and conservative management was initiated. The patient's neurological symptoms improved rapidly, and follow-up MRI demonstrated complete radiological resolution of the lesions. Conclusions In patients who develop visual disturbances, altered mental status, or other central neurological symptoms after treatment with EV, PRES should be considered in the differential diagnosis in addition to brain metastases. Early diagnosis of PRES during EV therapy may prevent irreversible neurological sequelae. Prompt neuroimaging evaluation and appropriate management are essential to achieve favorable outcomes.

title: FundusSigns-47: Prompt-Tuned Residual Visual Verification for Multi-Label Ophthalmic Sign Recognition
abstract: Abstract Real-world fundus photographs often contain multiple co-existing ophthalmic signs, yet automated analysis is commonly framed as binary screening or single-disease classification. We introduce FundusSigns-47, an institutional multi-label dataset of 7,111 color fundus images annotated with 47 clinically observable signs. The dataset exhibits fine-grained appearance, severe long-tail imbalance, and diverse label combinations. We also propose Selective Candidate-Verified Prompt Tuning (SCVPT). A prompt-tuned SigLIP2 ViT-g model generates candidate logits, while a learned InceptionV3 residual verifier supplies complementary visual evidence through selective class-wise routing. On the fixed test set, SCVPT achieves 57.87% mean average precision, 56.15% macro-F1, 65.82% micro-F1, 92.40% macro area under the curve, and 62.56% sample-F1. Mechanistic and fusion controls indicate that residual visual verification, rather than candidate gating alone, provides the principal improvement. An independent SigLIP2 and InceptionV3 ensemble yields higher ranking metrics, whereas SCVPT yields higher macro-F1, recall, and sample-F1. These findings support residual verification as a balanced operating strategy for multi-label ophthalmic sign recognition and motivate external validation.

title: Surgical treatment of tailgut cysts: a single-center analysis of 19 cases
abstract: Abstract Purpose Tailgut cysts are rare benign lesions with inflammatory and malignant potential. However, studies evaluating treatment outcomes in larger patient cohorts remain very limited. This study presents our institutional experience with tailgut cyst management, outlining diagnostic and therapeutic challenges and key insights gained. Methods Retrospective, descriptive single-center study, including patients with tailgut cysts surgically treated from 2014 to 2025. Results This study included 19 patients (female, 78.9%; median age, 35 years). The most frequent symptoms was lower back pain (36.8%). Meanwhile, 21% of the patients were asymptomatic. All patients underwent magnetic resonance imaging, with 78.9% suspected with a tailgut cyst or benign cystic lesion preoperatively. The mean cyst diameter was 5.8 ± 3.07 cm, and 36.8% of the patients had a multilobular morphology. Posterior (Kraske) approach was used in 78.9% of patients. One patient underwent laparoscopic cyst resection, and three required rectal resection. Posterior approach associated with minimal blood loss, lower complication rates and shorter length of stay. Regarding postoperative complication, wound infections was the most common (10.6%). Three (15,8%) patients experienced recurrence. The median follow-up period was 37 months. Conclusion This study presents one of the largest single-center cohorts of resected tailgut cysts. Magnetic resonance imaging is typically sufficient for diagnosis. Multilobular cysts are associated with recurrence, often pose diagnostic challenges, and may lead to unnecessarily extensive surgical intervention, which is associated with an increased risk of complications. The dorsal approach combined with secondary wound healing proved safe and effective, yielding high patient satisfaction and low complication rates.

title: Metachronous Bilateral Primary Breast Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma: A Case Report and Literature Review
abstract: Abstract Background: Primary breast lymphoma (PBL) is a rare extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma originating from the breast parenchyma, with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) being the most common histological subtype. Metachronous bilateral involvement is exceedingly uncommon, and standardized treatment guidelines remain lacking. Herein, we report a case of metachronous bilateral primary breast DLBCL with a 15-year disease-free interval and present a comprehensive literature review. Case presentation: A 47-year-old female presented with a palpable left breast mass in February 2026. She had a history of right breast PBL diagnosed in 2011, achieving complete remission after eight cycles of CHOP. Breast ultrasound, mammography, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a BI-RADS category 4B lesion in the left breast. Core needle biopsy confirmed DLBCL with immunohistochemistry demonstrating CD20 positivity (70%–80%), Ki-67 proliferation index of approximately 90%, and negative epithelial markers. Whole-body ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT excluded systemic involvement, confirming the diagnosis of stage IE left breast PBL. The patient received a zuberitamab-containing CMOP (Hi-CMOP). After fivecycles, repeat PET/CT demonstrated complete metabolic response with the Deauville score decreasing from 5 to 1, and breast ultrasound confirmed resolution of the breast lesion. Conclusions: PBL lacks pathognomonic clinical and imaging features, and definitive diagnosis hinges on histopathological examination with immunohistochemistry. For stage IE DLBCL-type PBL, rituximab-based immunochemotherapy followed by consolidative radiotherapy represents a rational therapeutic strategy with favorable short-term outcomes. Long-term surveillance remains essential given the risk of late contralateral recurrence. Multicenter studies with larger cohorts are warranted to establish evidence-based management guidelines.

title: Correlation between Serum MMP-1/TIMP-1 Ratio and the Severity of Diabetic Retinopathy in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Abstract Background Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) is the leading cause of blindness among the working-age population. Current screening and grading primarily rely on fundus imaging, lacking serological markers that reflect early molecular pathological changes. There is an urgent need to identify biomarkers for early warning and progression assessment of DR. Purpose To investigate the correlation between serum levels of MMP-1, MMP-2, TIMP-1, and their ratios with the severity of DR in Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), providing serological references for early identification and risk assessment of DR progression. Methods and Results Sixty-four T2DM patients were enrolled and divided into three groups based on fundus findings: Non DR group (n = 31), non-proliferative DR (NPDR) group (n = 17), and proliferative DR (PDR) group (n = 16). Serum levels of MMP-1, MMP-2, and TIMP-1 were measured using ELISA, and the MMP-1/TIMP-1 and MMP-2/TIMP-1 ratios were calculated. Results showed that serum MMP-1 levels and the MMP-1/TIMP-1 ratio exhibited an increasing trend across the three groups and were significantly positively correlated with DR severity grading (r = 0.283, P = 0.023; r = 0.344, P = 0.005). No statistically significant differences were observed in MMP-2, TIMP-1 levels, or the MMP-2/TIMP-1 ratio among the groups, nor were they significantly correlated with DR severity. Conclusion Serum MMP-1 levels and the MMP-1/TIMP-1 ratio increase with the severity of DR and may serve as novel serological candidate markers for reflecting DR progression. The MMP-1/TIMP-1 ratio showed a stronger correlation than the single marker, suggesting its potential value as a comprehensive indicator of extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation and remodeling balance in assessing DR progression. Future studies with larger sample sizes and combined ocular local samples are needed for further validation.

title: ABC versus C-Rad Technology for Intrafraction Displacement and Dosimetric Impact in Breast Cancer Radiotherapy with Breath-Hold
abstract: Abstract Purpose To compare treatment time, intrafraction errors, and dosimetric effects between active breathing control (ABC) and C-Rad optical surface monitoring in postoperative breast cancer radiotherapy. Methods Thirty patients with postoperative breast cancer were enrolled, including 15 patients in the ABC group and 15 in the C-Rad group. All patients were immobilized using a KoalaRedi arm support combined with a negative-pressure vacuum cushion and received breath-hold radiotherapy. Treatment time was recorded for each fraction. Intrafraction errors in the X, Y, and Z directions were determined from cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) scans acquired immediately after treatment. The Mann–Whitney U test was used for intergroup comparisons. Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was performed to assess the relationship between treatment time and intrafraction errors. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was used to determine the optimal treatment-time threshold for predicting a Z-direction error > 2 mm. Dosimetric simulations were performed using the maximum registration error for each patient to compare the planned dose distribution with the dose distribution after introduction of the corresponding error, with particular attention to doses to the heart, lungs, and target doses. Results Median treatment time was significantly shorter in the C-Rad group than in the ABC group (7.44 [6.50–8.07] min vs. 7.99 [7.23–8.51] min, P < 0.001). No significant intergroup differences were observed in X- or Y-direction errors; however, Z-direction errors were significantly larger in the C-Rad group (0.146 [0.06–0.21] cm vs. 0.113 [0.05–0.15] cm, P < 0.001). In the C-Rad group, Z-direction error was positively correlated with treatment time (r = 0.167, P = 0.006). A treatment time > 10.93 min predicted a Z-direction error > 2 mm (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.605; sensitivity, 86.3%; and specificity, 31.9%). Dosimetric simulation based on each patient’s maximum intrafraction error showed that, in the ABC group, the maximum error resulted in a mean reduction of 2.32% in planning target volume (PTV) D95 relative to the planned value (median, − 1.13%; P = 0.002), whereas changes in heart Dmean, ipsilateral lung V20, and mean lung dose were not statistically significant (all P > 0.05). In the C-Rad group, PTV D95 decreased by a mean of 3.80% (median, − 2.90%; P = 0.006), with no significant changes in the other dosimetric parameters. Conclusion The C-Rad technique resulted in significantly shorter single-fraction treatment times than ABC (7.44 vs. 7.99 min). However, although no significant intergroup differences were observed in lateral (X) or longitudinal (Y) errors, the vertical (Z) error was significantly larger in the C-Rad group (median, 0.13 [0.06–0.21] cm vs. 0.09 [0.05–0.15] cm, P < 0.001) and increased with longer treatment times. The threshold for predicting a Z-direction error > 2 mm was 10.93 min. Under maximum intrafraction error conditions, both techniques resulted in small reductions in target coverage (PTV D95: −2.32% for ABC and − 3.80% for C-Rad), without significant changes in doses to organs at risk.

title: Functional Agent-Driven Computational Anatomy for Preoperative Siewert Classification of Adenocarcinoma of the Esophagogastric Junction Using Three-Dimensional Contrast- Enhanced CT: a retrospective multicenter diagnostic accuracy study
abstract: Abstract Background Accurate preoperative Siewert classification of adenocarcinoma of the esophagogastric junction (AEG) is critical for surgical planning, but current imaging relies on subjective estimation, leading to poor reproducibility and potential misclassification. We developed and evaluated FACET, a functional agent-driven computational anatomy framework that converts subjective spatial judgment into calibrated, traceable 3D distance measurements between the tumor midpoint and the esophagogastric junction (EGJ) interface on contrast-enhanced CT. Methods In this retrospective multi-cohort study (development n = 70; internal validation n = 61; external validation n = 45), FACET integrated automated tumor perception, anatomy-constrained structure refinement, and mucosal-surface-guided 3D path modeling to localize the tumor midpoint and EGJ interface. Siewert types were determined by calibrated geodesic distances along the path. Histopathological Siewert type served as the reference standard. Results With the calibration factor locked at k = 0.7, FACET achieved accuracies of 71.4%, 82.0%, and 73.3% in the development, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively; the corresponding AUCs were 0.721, 0.927, and 0.770. In the external validation cohort, balanced accuracy was 76.5%. The complete workflow was implemented as an interactive desktop application for three-dimensional visualization, anatomical measurement, and Siewert classification. Conclusions FACET transforms subjective imaging interpretation into reproducible 3D anatomical assessment. In the independent external cohort, it demonstrated moderate discrimination and showed potential for cross-institutional application as a traceable decision-support tool for preoperative multidisciplinary planning in AEG patients.

title: Retroperitoneal Subhepatic Appendicitis Associated with Intestinal Malrotation
abstract: Abstract Background Acute appendicitis is one of the most common surgical emergencies in children. However, atypical anatomical positions of the appendix can lead to unusual clinical presentations and diagnostic challenges. Subhepatic appendicitis is a rare entity that may mimic hepatobiliary or gastric pathology. Case Presentation: We report the case of a 10-year-old male who presented with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, anorexia, and a single episode of vomiting. Physical examination revealed right upper quadrant tenderness. Ultrasound examination confirmed retroperitoneal subhepatic acute appendicitis. A midline abdominal incision was performed, and intraoperatively the appendix was found inflamed in the subhepatic region. Appendectomy was successfully carried out. Discussion Subhepatic appendicitis is an uncommon anatomical variation that can delay diagnosis due to its atypical presentation. Imaging studies, particularly ultrasound, play a crucial role in identifying such cases. Surgical exploration remains definitive for diagnosis and treatment. Conclusion This case highlights the importance of considering anatomical variations of the appendix in pediatric patients presenting with right upper quadrant pain. Early recognition and prompt surgical intervention are essential to avoid complications.

title: Quantifying the Effect of Synthetic Colour Fundus Photograph Scaling on Foundation Models
abstract: Abstract Scaling synthetic colour fundus photographs (CFPs) offers a tunable strategy for retinal foundation-model pretraining. From 28,430 real CFPs, we generated 568,600 synthetic CFPs and compared six one-pass strategies: real-only, synthetic-only, real-plus-1×synthetic, real-plus-5×synthetic, real-plus-10×synthetic and real-plus-20×synthetic. Average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was highest in internal validation with real-plus-10×synthetic (0.906 versus 0.862 for real-only across 12 test datasets), but in external validation with real-plus-20×synthetic (0.777 versus 0.683 across eight datasets). The real-plus-1×synthetic strategy increased both averages with the lowest counted computation among real-plus-synthetic strategies. At a matched image count, synthetic-only achieved comparable average external AUROC to real-only. Generation accounted for approximately 99% of the estimated 9 × 10¹⁹ floating-point operations for generation and backbone pretraining. These findings identify complementary uses of synthetic scaling: lower-volume supplementation for a performance–computation balance and larger volumes for stronger external generalisation, with strategy selection guided by evaluation objectives and computational resources.

title: An Interpretable Multimodal Benchmarking Framework for Resource-Efficient Medical Image Classification
abstract: Abstract Purpose We proposed compact multimodal models that integrate visual and textual inputs to classify medical images based on their accuracy, latency, memory footprint, and explainability in low-resource clinical settings. Methods We conducted experiments using nine model configurations with visual backbones (EffcientNet-B0, ConvNeXt-Pico, MobileViT-XXS) and language models (DistilBERT, MiniLM, TinyBERT) on the MedPix and Wound datasets. We benchmarked them against the image-only, text-only, and BiomedCLIP mod- els through five random seeds, measuring accuracy, parameter sizes, CPU/GPU inference time, training memory usage, and attributions using Grad-CAM, integrated gradients attributions, and fusion-gate behavior. Results EffcientNet-B0 combined with MiniLM achieved best results in wound classification, attaining 96.8% accuracy for wound severity and 89.1% for wound type. In the MedPix dataset, multimodal models attained 99.0% accuracy for image modality classification and 86.0% for anatomical location. The best- performing lightweight models utilized significantly less parameters and memory compared to BiomedCLIP. Feature attributions identified critical areas in med- ical images and important text tokens in clinical text, while fusion gates redistributed importance among modalities in uncertain cases. Conclusion A combination of images and clinical text helps to enhance classification performance as compared to single modality benchmarks and BiomedCLIP, particularly in fine-grained diagnostic tasks. The feature attri- bution demonstrates that these networks capture relevant clinical information, indicating that gated and cross-attention networks are viable options to be used in clinical settings.

The feature attri- bution demonstrates that these networks capture relevant clinical information, indicating that gated and cross-attention networks are viable options to be used in clinical settings.

title: Impact of coronary artery calcification detection on cardiovascular care trajectories in patients undergoing lung cancer screening: a systematic review
abstract: Abstract Importance: Coronary artery calcification (CAC) is commonly identified on low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) performed for lung cancer screening (LCS) and is associated with increased cardiovascular (CV) risk. Although guidelines increasingly recommend reporting and incorporating CAC into CV risk stratification, whether its detection translates into downstream CV preventive care remains unclear. Objective: To systematically evaluate reporting practices and downstream clinical management following CAC detection during LDCT LCS. Evidence Review: We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Web of Science Core Collection from inception to September 23, 2026, and searched grey literature through September 20, 2026. We included original studies of adults undergoing LDCT within established or pilot LCS programs if they evaluated downstream management following CAC detection or reporting. Reviewers independently extracted data in duplicate on CAC assessment, reporting, communication, preventive pharmacotherapy, referrals, investigations, and clinical outcomes. We assessed study quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Owing to clinical and methodological heterogeneity, we synthesized findings narratively. Findings: We included twelve studies published between 2020 and 2026 from the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia, and France. Visual assessment was the predominant method for CAC identification, although reporting and communication practices varied substantially. Statin initiation (N=7) ranged from 3% to 38%, cardiology referral (N=3) from 6.9% to 44%, and cardiac stress testing (N=2) from 12.5% to 21.6%. Structured CV follow-up pathways were evaluated in five studies. Three studies found greater a CAC severity or a more explicit reporting was associated with increased statin initiation. Study quality was moderate overall, with NOS scores ranging from four to eight of nine; common limitations included absence of comparator groups and limited adjustment for confounding. Conclusions and Relevance: CAC detected during LCS was followed by variable downstream CV preventive care, and reporting alone does not consistently translate into clinical action. Greater CAC severity and more explicit reporting were associated with increased clinical action in some studies, but reporting alone did not consistently translate into preventive management. Comparative studies are needed to determine whether structured communication and follow-up pathways improve cardiovascular care and clinical outcomes.

title: Preoperative prediction and perioperative risk updating for adjacent vertebral fracture after percutaneous vertebroplasty: development and internal validation of a two-stage prediction strategy
abstract: Abstract Background Adjacent vertebral fracture (AVF) is an important complication after percutaneous vertebroplasty (PVP) for osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture (OVCF). Existing prediction models frequently combine variables obtained at different clinical time points, which may limit their applicability for preoperative risk assessment. This study aimed to develop and internally validate a strictly preoperative prediction model and to determine whether perioperative cement-distribution information provides additional prognostic value after PVP. Methods We retrospectively included 314 consecutive patients with OVCF who underwent PVP between December 2022 and December 2024 and completed at least 18 months of follow-up. The primary outcome was AVF within 18 months after PVP. Model 1 incorporated six preoperative predictors: age, target vertebral CT Hounsfield units (CT-HU), pre-existing vertebral compression fracture (VCF) count, paraspinal fat infiltration rate (FIR), preoperative sagittal imbalance, and preoperative anterior vertebral compression rate. Model 2 retained these predictors and added cement distribution pattern. Internal validation included 1,000 bootstrap resamples, 100 repetitions of stratified five-fold cross-validation, and fixed stratified 10-fold out-of-fold (OOF) prediction. Discrimination, calibration, Brier score, decision curve analysis, and incremental model performance were evaluated. LASSO and DEXA T-score analyses were performed as sensitivity analyses. Results Among 314 patients, 80 (25.5%) developed AVF within 18 months. In Model 1, older age, lower CT-HU, greater pre-existing VCF burden, higher paraspinal FIR, sagittal imbalance, and greater anterior vertebral compression were independently associated with AVF. The apparent AUC was 0.872, the bootstrap-corrected AUC was 0.857, and the 10-fold OOF AUC was 0.854. After addition of cement distribution, contiguous O-shaped and fragmented patterns were associated with higher AVF odds than bilateral H-shaped distribution. Model 2 improved overall model fit (likelihood-ratio χ²=11.99, P = 0.0025), but the increase in OOF discrimination was small (AUC 0.859; ΔAUC = 0.005, 95% CI − 0.014 to 0.025; P = 0.622). Model 1 OOF risk strata showed observed AVF rates of 6.0%, 25.8%, and 63.2% in the low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups, respectively. Adding DEXA T-score did not materially improve Model 1. Conclusions A six-predictor preoperative model integrating bone quality, previous fracture burden, paraspinal muscle degeneration, sagittal alignment, and vertebral morphology showed good internal performance for predicting 18-month AVF after PVP. Cement distribution provided additional perioperative prognostic information and improved overall model fit, but only minimally increased discrimination. These findings support a two-stage framework in which preoperative risk is estimated first and subsequently updated using procedural information. External validation is required before clinical implementation.

title: Ciliary Body Metastasis from Lung Cancer Presenting as Acute Angle- Closure Glaucoma: Two Case Reports
abstract: Abstract Background Ciliary body metastasis is an uncommon form of uveal metastasis that may present with secondary angle-closure glaucoma. Because these lesions are concealed behind the iris, diagnosis is often delayed, and the condition may be mistaken for primary acute angle-closure glaucoma. Case Presentation: We report two patients with ciliary body metastasis from lung cancer who initially presented with acute angle-closure glaucoma. Case 1, a 63-year-old woman with a known history of lung cancer receiving targeted therapy, developed acute ocular pain, visual loss, and markedly elevated intraocular pressure. Poor response to conventional antiglaucoma therapy prompted further investigation, and ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) revealed a ciliary body mass associated with angle closure. Case 2, a 66-year-old woman with a history of hemoptysis but no known history of malignancy, presented with blurred vision, ocular pain, and elevated intraocular pressure. UBM demonstrated a larger ciliary body mass involving the anterior chamber angle. Subsequent systemic evaluation revealed previously undiagnosed metastatic lung cancer. In both cases, the clinical presentation closely resembled primary acute angle-closure glaucoma; however, atypical findings and poor response to treatment prompted further investigation. Conclusion Ciliary body metastasis may initially present as an acute glaucoma attack and should be distinguished from primary acute angle-closure glaucoma. Multiple gray-white nodules on the iris surface may indicate an occult intraocular tumor. Elevated intraocular pressure can result from tumor-related angle closure and/or obstruction of the trabecular meshwork by disseminated tumor cells. UBM is valuable for detecting occult ciliary body lesions. Because conventional pressure-lowering treatment may be ineffective, incisional intraocular surgery is not recommended when an intraocular malignancy is suspected.

title: A Systematic Review and Descriptive Quantitative Synthesis of Artificial Intelligence in Cervical Cancer Screening and Diagnosis
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) has been frequently utilised in cervical cancer screening, diagnosis, lesion assessment and clinical decision support, but the evidence remains methodologically heterogeneous. This systematic review examined the application of AI in cytology, colposcopy, visual examination, histopathology, and multimodal clinical data. Also reviewed PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and IEEE Xplore to identify 4094 records. After the exclusion of 2053 duplicates and applying pre-defined eligibility criteria, 898 studies were included. Directly extractable diagnostic-performance measures were available from 60 studies. Accuracy was reported in 40 studies, sensitivity in 19, specificity in 16 and AUC in 12 studies. A total of 13 studies reported both sensitivity and specificity. There was considerable heterogeneity in populations, datasets, reference standards, diagnostic tasks, AI methods, validation procedures and performance reporting. Complete TP, FP, TN and FN data were not available across the eligible evidence base and pooled diagnostic accuracy estimation and summary receiver-operating-characteristic analysis were not possible. Therefore, the quantitative results were summarized descriptively. Evidence indicates broad application of AI approaches but also limitations in terms of comparability, external validation, reporting completeness and clinical generalizability. Future research should focus on standardized reporting, multicenter datasets, independent external validation and prospective clinical evaluation.

title: Simulation-based inverse imaging of dynamic material-interface states from radiographic surrogates and sparse projections
abstract: Abstract Fast radiography of dynamic material interfaces is blurred, sparse, and difficult to interpret in three dimensions. Restoration, state inference, and sparse-view reconstruction are often studied separately, which makes their outputs difficult to compare against known simulation labels. We address this problem with a curated Rayleigh–Taylor instability (RTI) corpus containing 101,250 interface images from 1,350 simulations, each labeled by Atwood number, acceleration, initial perturbation amplitude, and time. The simulations are sampled on a common uniform time grid, although acceleration and time are only partly independent under the normalized-time scaling of the underlying RTI problem. Controlled temporal averaging and spatial blur generate radiograph-like surrogates with known target states. On these surrogates, a fine-tuned restoration model improves mean SSIM from 0.905 to 0.962 and mean PSNR from 20.67 to 22.05 dB relative to Restormer. The same corpus supports retrieval, regression of Atwood number and time, local ambiguity diagnostics, short-horizon temporal densification, and a lifted 4D benchmark with 54 dynamic 3D sequences and 72 synthetic projections per volume. Sparse-view neural fields reach about 35 dB on held-out views in that synthetic benchmark. At sufficiently late times, some frames are best interpreted as controlled image-processing cases because finite-domain effects can influence the morphology. Within that scope, the RTI corpus provides a shared benchmark for restoration, label-space inference, ambiguity analysis, and sparse-view reconstruction.

title: Detection of the real joint interface between ultrasonically welded aluminium strands (Al-strands) and copper terminals (Cu-terminals) connections using non-destructive testing methods
abstract: Abstract The ongoing electrification of the automotive sector increases the demand for reliable and production-robust electrically conductive joints, particularly in cell interconnection, high-voltage wiring harnesses, and power electronics. Ultrasonic metal welding has become an established joining technology because it forms metallurgical solid-state bonds for material mixes without additional filler materials. At present, the quality of ultrasonically welded joints is assessed primarily by destructive mechanical testing and simple limit value control Although these destructive methods provide reliable information on weld quality, they are limited to sample-based inspection in series production and therefore permit only restricted testing intensity. Consequently, sporadically occurring defects may remain undetected. Against this background, advanced non-destructive testing methods are gaining increasing importance, as they enable the evaluation of joint quality without impairing component functionality and improve diagnostic reliability through a higher inspection frequency. This study investigates various non-destructive testing methods for ultrasonic welded joints between copper terminals and aluminum stranded conductors. The focus lies on quantifying strand compaction by computed tomography and characterizing the effective bonded area using imaging and thermal methods. The findings enable a deeper characterization of the joining zone. Building on these results, the correlation between effective joint area and resulting shear tensile strength is investigated to improve quality prediction by AI-based systems in further studies.

title: Factors Associated with Missed CT Detection of Tracheobronchial Foreign Bodies in Children
abstract: Abstract Background Tracheobronchial foreign body (TFB) represents a life-threatening pediatric emergency. Chest CT is frequently used for radiological evaluation of children with suspected TFB; nevertheless, false-negative CT interpretations occur even among bronchoscopically confirmed cases, creating diagnostic challenges in pediatric radiology. This study aimed to identify factors associated with missed CT detection of TFB. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 951 children with bronchoscopically confirmed TFB. CT detection versus missed detection was defined based on original radiology reports from routine clinical care. Data on demographics, clinical features, and concomitant imaging findings were collected. Three independent multivariable logistic regression models with different codings of concomitant imaging findings were constructed, with bootstrap internal validation. Results The missed detection rate was 8.6% (82/951). Absence of a definite aspiration history was the most robust independent factor (OR range 2.70–2.87, all P ≤ 0.001). The strongest associations were observed in children aged 3–6 years (mean OR 4.76), followed by location in the trachea, carina, or glottis (mean OR 4.19), right bronchus (OR ≈ 2.0), and age 1–3 years (mean OR 1.95). Concomitant imaging findings showed heterogeneous associations: mixed-type (OR = 4.27) and single-type findings (OR = 2.62) significantly increased risk, whereas purely obstructive/masking findings or the presence of two or more types were not. Duration of aspiration and granulation tissue were not independently associated. Conclusions Absence of a definite aspiration history, age 3–6 years or 1–3 years, and foreign body location in the trachea, carina, glottis or right bronchus are independent factors associated with missed CT detection. Mixed or solitary concomitant imaging findings also increase risk. These factors may help radiologists identify children at high risk for CT false-negative

title: Robot-Tracked Multi-View 3D Ultrasound Reconstruction for Quantitative Assessment of Simulated Abdominal Haemorrhage in a Tissue-Mimicking Phantom
abstract: Abstract Background Rapid identification and assessment of abdominal haemorrhage are important in trauma. Conventional 2D US is well established for detecting free abdominal fluid but is unsuited to directly quantifying irregular fluid collections. This study established a robot-tracked multi-view 3D US framework for quantitative reconstruction of abdominal free fluid in a tissue-mimicking phantom. Methods A Philips VL13-5 3D transducer on a Philips EPIQ 7 system was rigidly mounted to a Franka Emika Panda robot. US–robot hand–eye calibration used 64 manually aligned 3D US volumes and 13-fold held-out pose cross-validation. A phantom with a controllable reservoir designed to represent free-fluid accumulation within the Morison’s pouch imaging region was imaged at 70 mL, 100 mL, 120 mL, 150 mL, and 190 mL. Two sonographers acquired 122 overlapping 3D US volumes along a two-pass trajectory. Tracking-derived reconstructions were refined using semi-automatic rigid registration and expert verification. Free fluid was manually segmented in all source volumes, and reconstructed volumes were compared with target injected-volume references. Results Final calibration achieved an RMS point-to-point reconstruction error of 1.23 mm; pooled held-out RMS error was 1.27 mm. Tracking-derived reconstruction reproduced the acquisition geometry but retained residual inter-volume misalignment and underestimated free-fluid volume, with MAPE of 9.78%. Expert-verified refinement reduced MAPE to 0.90%, with absolute relative volumetric errors of 0.07–2.61%. Conclusion Tracking provided a spatial basis for multi-view 3D US reconstruction, but accurate inter-volume registration was required for reliable volumetric quantification. The framework provides a benchmark for automated registration, segmentation, and wide-field multi-aperture ultrasound development.

title: A PACS-Integrated Artificial Intelligence Platform for Visualizing Radiolucent Foreign Body Aspiration
abstract: Abstract Diagnosis of radiolucent foreign body aspiration (FBA) in adults is a major clinical challenge. While previous deep learning models have successfully achieved patient-level diagnostic screening, they remain fundamentally limited as "black-box" classifiers, failing to provide the precise 3D spatial coordinates required for surgical intervention. Furthermore, the extreme scarcity of labelled FBA cases forces data-starved models to overfit, hindering broader clinical deployment. To overcome this and bridge the critical gap between radiological suspicion and surgical execution, we developed AI-PACS, a self-supervised anomaly detection and 3D visualization platform. Driven by a Lean Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (LeJEPA) and a Sparse-Inferred Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg) module, the system is pre-trained on 804 unlabelled CT scans to establish a standard Gaussian manifold of "non-FBA" airway topology. This allows AI-PACS to identify FBA as high-norm statistical outliers with "pathological invariance," effectively filtering out confounding structural noise. Validated across multi-center internal (n = 268), external (n = 103), and independent (n = 70) cohorts, AI-PACS demonstrated robust generalizability with diagnostic accuracies of 75.7%–82.5%. In a head-to-head benchmark against expert radiologists, AI-PACS significantly improved detection sensitivity from 18.8% to 56.3% (P < 0.05) and reduced the average negative exclusion screening time by 75%. By shifting the paradigm from pure diagnostic classification to automated 3D anatomical localization (S1-S10 mapping), AI-PACS acts as a digital rehearsal tool that translates invisible structural outliers into actionable interventional guidance. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Bone Remodeling of Dysplasia Epiphysealis Hemimelica of the Medial Femoral Condyle in a Child: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica is a rare osteochondral proliferative lesion in children. It is uncommon when located in the medial femoral condyle, and clinically, it is prone to misdiagnosis. Here, we report a case of a 9-year-old boy who presented with right knee pain and restricted range of motion induced by trauma. Preoperative multimodal imaging, including digital radiography, computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging, revealed complex features such as articular cartilage defects, bone marrow edema, and lobulated osseous prominences, requiring differential diagnosis from osteochondritis dissecans and bone tumors. The patient underwent surgical resection of the lesion on the medial femoral condyle of the right femur, and postoperative pathology confirmed the diagnosis of DEH. A 1.5-year post-operative DR follow-up meticulously documented the entire progression of the resected region, transitioning from early bone defect to mid-term bone remodeling, and ultimately to the complete recovery of the anatomical contour in the long term. This case indicates that the integration of multimodal imaging with pathological evaluation facilitates early and precise diagnosis of DEH. For symptomatic pediatric patients with articular involvement, surgical intervention can fully leverage the self-remodeling capacity of pediatric epiphyses, thereby yielding excellent mid- to long-term clinical outcomes.
