title: GlioMIL: A Frozen-Backbone Multiple-Instance Learning Framework for Calibrated and Explainable Glioma Radiogenomics
abstract: Abstract Non-invasive prediction of glioma molecular status from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) could reduce reliance on invasive biopsy. Still, deep-learning pipelines for this task are often trained on small cohorts and rarely assessed for calibration or explainability. We present GlioMIL, a 2.5D multiple-instance-learning (MIL) framework predicting isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status, tumour grade, O 6 -methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) promoter methylation, and 1p/19q codeletion from multi-contrast MRI, representing each tumour as a bag of tumour-guided axial slices embedded by a frozen, ImageNet-pretrained backbone and aggregated via attention-based pooling feeding multi-task heads. On a publicly available glioma cohort, a controlled five-way ablation with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired significance testing shows this frozen-backbone approach matches a fully-supervised 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) baseline, and that fusing standardised clinical and radiomic features into the pooled representation significantly improves over image-only multi-task learning for IDH and grade. However, a plain classifier on clinical and radiomic features alone, with no image input, matches or significantly exceeds the fused model on these tasks, so the frozen image branch adds no predictive value beyond structured features. MGMT and 1p/19q codeletion remain close to chance across all conditions. The fusion model is label-efficient and reasonably well calibrated, but its attention weights correspond to tumour regions only at a near-chance level, cautioning against treating attention as a reliable spatial explanation. We report our evaluation protocol, including rejection of an earlier flawed ensembling scheme and a per-fold feature-normalisation correction, to support trustworthy, reproducible reporting.

title: Evaluating Transvaginal Ultrasound for Monitoring Treatment Response in Endometrial Hyperplasia: Clinical Utility of a 5-mm Endometrial Thickness Cutoff
abstract: Abstract Objectives: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of transvaginal ultrasonographic endometrial thickness (ET) in predicting histopathological response to progestin therapy in patients with medically treated endometrial hyperplasia. Methods: In this prospective observational study, patients with histologically confirmed endometrial hyperplasia receiving progestin therapy underwent transvaginal ultrasonography and repeat histopathologic evaluation at 3 and 6 months. Endometrial thickness was categorized using predefined cut-off values (≤ 5 mm, 5.5–10 mm, 10.5–15 mm, and > 15 mm). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to assess the discriminatory performance of ET in predicting histopathologic outcomes. The influence of baseline histopathology and the presence of endometrial polyps was also evaluated Results: Across both follow-up intervals, histopathological regression was observed in all ET categories. ROC analysis demonstrated poor overall discriminatory ability of ET (AUC = 0.369 at 3 months; 0.424 at 6 months). Although an ET ≤ 5 mm was associated with higher regression rates, no single cut-off value reliably predicted treatment response. The presence of endometrial polyps was associated with increased ET measurements even among patients showing histopathologic regression. Conclusion: Transvaginal ultrasonographic measurement of endometrial thickness has limited ability to predict histopathologic regression after progestin therapy and should not substitute for tissue diagnosis. However, a threshold of ≤ 5 mm may serve as a supportive indicator of favorable therapeutic response in selected patients.

title: Diagnostic Value of Peripheral Zone PSA Density for Detecting Clinically Significant Prostate Cancer in Men with Peripheral Zone MRI Lesions Running title: Peripheral Zone PSA Density in Prostate Cancer
abstract: Abstract Background Whole-gland prostate-specific antigen density (PSAD) may underestimate the diagnostic contribution of peripheral zone (PZ) tumors, as it is diluted by transition zone (TZ) volume, which expands with age independent of cancer risk. We investigated whether PZ-specific PSAD (PSAD_PZ) improves the detection of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) in men with PZ-only multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) target lesions, and evaluated the analogous TZ-specific PSAD (PSAD_TZ) in men with TZ-only targets. Methods We analyzed 651 men from the prospectively enrolled SUPER-PC registry, supplemented by a retrospectively identified non-cancer cohort, who underwent combined systematic and MRI-targeted fusion biopsy (416 with PZ-only and 235 with TZ-only mpMRI targets). Clinically significant prostate cancer was defined as International Society of Urological Pathology Grade Group 2 or greater. The diagnostic performance of PSA, whole-gland PSAD, and zone-specific PSAD was compared using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis, and optimal cut-off values were determined using the Youden index. Results In the PZ-target group, PSAD_PZ achieved a significantly higher area under the curve (AUC) than PSA (0.825 vs. 0.707, p < 0.001) and whole-gland PSAD (0.825 vs. 0.702, p < 0.001). This advantage persisted among men with Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) category 4 or higher lesions (AUC 0.842) and remained significant after multivariable adjustment. The optimal PSAD_PZ cut-off value was 0.285 ng/mL/cm³, yielding a sensitivity of 70.8% and specificity of 84.3%. PSAD_TZ did not outperform PSA or whole-gland PSAD in the TZ-target group. Conclusions PSAD_PZ improves the detection of csPCa in men with PZ-only mpMRI targets and outperforms conventional whole-gland PSAD, supporting a zone-matched normalization strategy that may help reduce unnecessary biopsies and guide treatment decisions. PSAD_TZ conferred no comparable benefit among men with TZ-only targets.

title: Multimodal Weakly Supervised Learning of Epicardial and Pericoronary Adipose Tissuefor CCTA-Based Coronary Disease Phenotype Prediction: A Methodological Feasibility Study
abstract: Abstract \textbf{Purpose:} Epicardial (EAT) and pericoronary (PAT) adipose tissue on cardiac CT angiography (CCTA) are associated with coronary artery disease (CAD), but most computational approaches analyse a single depot using hand-crafted radiomic features. We evaluated whether multimodal integration of EAT, PAT, and clinical variables adds value over single-source models, and whether specific architectural choices meaningfully affect performance, using a dataset-defined CAD phenotype based on expert plaque assessment rather than invasive angiographic confirmation. \textbf{Methods:} We developed a weakly supervised multiple instance learning (MIL) framework combining paired EAT/PAT volumes with structured clinical variables. Using the MultiD4CAD dataset (117 patients, 39 CAD-positive), we compared single-depot imaging, multimodal fusion, clinical-only models, and MIL design variants (attention aggregation, independent versus shared-weight encoders) under stratified five-fold cross-validation with three-seed ensembling and strict out-of-fold evaluation. \textbf{Results:} The full multimodal model achieved an AUC-ROC of 83.3\% (95\% CI, 74.3--91.1), significantly outperforming the clinical-only baseline (64.4\%; $\Delta$AUC = 18.9\%, 95\% CI, 7.6--30.6). No significant differences were observed across imaging configurations or architectural variants; a parameter-efficient shared-backbone configuration (11.4M parameters) matched the default dual-backbone model (22.6M parameters) and is proposed as the preferred configuration for small cardiac imaging cohorts. A simple volumetric baseline using only depot volume and attenuation statistics performed at chance level (AUC-ROC 49.1\%), indicating that the imaging models capture spatial or textural information beyond gross tissue quantity. Calibration, decision curve analysis, and post-hoc error analysis further characterised model behaviour and failure modes, including threshold-dependent metrics whose derivation from validation-fold data is disclosed as a methodological limitation. \textbf{Conclusion:} Multimodal integration of adipose tissue imaging and clinical data improved discrimination of a CCTA-defined CAD phenotype compared with clinical variables alone, while architectural complexity did not provide measurable benefit in this small cohort. These findings represent a methodological feasibility benchmark for imaging informatics pipelines rather than evidence of clinical readiness, pending external multicentre validation.

title: Diagnostic certainty and outcome reporting in sinus fungus balls with African clinical examples
abstract: Abstract Background: Paranasal sinus fungus balls must be distinguished from allergic and invasive fungal rhinosinusitis. Small clinical reports can clarify diagnosis and treatment, but their interpretation depends on pathological confirmation, anatomical location and follow-up. This review examines these issues using selected African publications within the broader clinical literature. Main body: Targeted searches of indexed records and publisher websites were completed on 29 September 2026. A critical narrative synthesis considered definitions, diagnostic certainty, operative management and outcome reporting. Selected Tunisian reports described surgically treated lesions, including isolated frontal disease; a Moroccan concha bullosa report represented a different anatomical site and a presumptive diagnosis. In a mixed Tunisian noninvasive cohort, fungus-ball labels could not be equated with uniformly documented histological confirmation. CT findings supported suspicion, while pathology and assessment of tissue invasion determined classification. Fungal culture contributed organism information but could not reliably exclude a fungus ball when negative. International surgical evidence supported effective clearance in selected patients, without establishing an Africa-specific success rate. The review proposes explicit reporting of diagnostic evidence, anatomical access, mucosal assessment and time-specific outcomes. Short conclusion: Interpretation of fungus-ball reports requires separating imaging suspicion, documented fungal material and exclusion of invasion. Regional case reports should not be pooled uncritically with mixed fungal cohorts or used to infer continental prevalence. Standardised reporting would improve both clinical communication and the value of future multicentre research.

title: Quantifying the Impact of Evaluation Design on Deep Learning–Based CT Histologic Subtyping of Non–Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Leakage-Audited Cross-Cohort Multi-Architecture Study
abstract: Abstract Background: Computed tomography (CT)-based deep-learning performance may be strongly influenced by whether correlated images from the same patient cross evaluation partitions. We quantified the effect of evaluation design on histologic subtyping of non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and assessed cross-cohort transportability. Methods: A development cohort of 311 patients comprising 7,456 region-of-interest (ROI)-bearing CT slices was evaluated using ResNet50, ConvNeXt-Tiny, ViT-B/16, and Swin-T under two otherwise matched five-fold designs: an intentionally leakage-prone slice-random design (E1) and strict patient-grouped evaluation (E3). Final development-only models were applied without fine-tuning, threshold re-optimization, or recalibration to NSCLC-Radiomics (External A; 203 patients) and NSCLC-Radiogenomics (External B; 141 patients). Patient-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was the primary endpoint. Results: Patient-level AUROC ranged from 0.9902–0.9997 under E1 and decreased to 0.7018–0.7342 under E3. Paired E1-minus-E3 AUROC differences ranged from 0.2559–0.2971, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero for all architectures. External AUROC decreased further to 0.5973–0.6298 in External A and 0.5040–0.6084 in External B. All External A AUROC confidence intervals remained above 0.50, whereas all External B intervals included 0.50. Calibration deteriorated after external transfer, and locked E3-derived thresholds produced cohort-dependent sensitivity–specificity tradeoffs. A five-epoch sensitivity analysis preserved the overall external-validation pattern. Conclusions: Evaluation structure substantially influenced apparent CT-based deep-learning performance. Patient-level independence is necessary for credible internal assessment, but independent external testing remains essential for evaluating model transportability.

title: Toward Risk-Aware Clinical Decision Support in Gastrointestinal Endoscopy: A Tunable Asymmetric Loss with Uncertainty-Guided Referral
abstract: Abstract This study presents a deep learning framework for four-class gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy risk stratification beyond conventional binary lesion detection. Im- ages from the HyperKvasir dataset were categorized into four clinically motivated risk groups: Normal, Inflammatory, Pre-malignant, and High-Risk, informed by rec- ommendations from the American College of Gastroenterology and European Soci- ety of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy. We introduce an Asymmetric Endoscopy Loss (AEL) function that enables tunable class weighting, allowing greater emphasis on High-Risk cases while balancing overall predictive performance with safety-oriented sensitivity. Three lightweight architectures (DenseNet-121, EfficientNet-B0, and DeiT-Tiny) were evaluated using AEL, with Monte Carlo Dropout for uncertainty estimation and a referral strategy that escalates Pre-malignant and High-Risk pre- dictions for further review regardless of model confidence. GradCAM was used to provide visual interpretability. DenseNet-121 achieved a macro F1-score of 0.8419 and an AUC of 0.9730. No ground-truth High-Risk images were predicted as either of the two lower-risk tiers on the internal test set, and 43.1 % of images were eligi- ble for simulated automatic clearance under the predefined referral rule. Five-fold cross-validation provided an additional assessment of performance stability, while McNemar tests quantified paired differences between architectures. These findings support further investigation of tunable risk-weighted losses, lightweight architec- tures, and uncertainty-aware referral strategies for developing interpretable and safety-oriented GI endoscopy decision-support systems.

title: CT Colonography as a Triage Examination After a Positive Fecal Immunochemical Test: A Retrospective Cohort Study in a Chilean Screening Program
abstract: Abstract Purpose: To evaluate computed tomography colonography (CTC) as a triage examination for colonoscopy within a fecal immunochemical test (FIT)-based colorectal cancer screening program in a resource-limited region of Chile. Methods: This retrospective cohort study included asymptomatic FIT-positive individuals aged 45–75 years who underwent CTC between January 2019 and November 2022. Patients with CT Colonography Reporting and Data System (C-RADS) C2–C4 findings were referred for optical colonoscopy. The primary outcome was the per-patient positive predictive value (PPV) of CTC for polyps measuring ≥ 6 mm among patients with an evaluable colonoscopy. Results: The cohort comprised 675 patients (mean age 64.0 years, SD 9.2; 443 women, 65.6%). Overall, 473 patients (70.1%) were classified as C1 and were not referred for immediate colonoscopy, 62 (9.2%) had C3–C4 findings and 71 (10.5%) had unresolved C0 examinations. Of 131 patients referred for colonoscopy, 115 (87.8%) underwent the procedure and 108 had an evaluable examination. Colonoscopy confirmed at least one polyp measuring ≥ 6 mm in 93 patients, yielding a PPV of 86.1% (95% CI 78.3–91.4). Advanced colorectal neoplasia was confirmed in 48 patients (PPV 44.4%, 95% CI 35.4–53.8). The detection rates was 42/675 (6.2%) for advanced adenoma and 6/675 (0.9%) for colorectal cancer. Conclusion: Among FIT-positive patients with CTC findings warranting colonoscopy, clinically relevant colorectal lesions were frequently confirmed. CTC may help prioritize colonoscopy in settings with limited endoscopic capacity. Further evaluation of the complete screening pathway is warranted.

title: Optimization of Prostate T2-Weighted Imaging Using AI-Assisted Compressed Sensing Combined with Deep Learning Reconstruction: A Prospective Study
abstract: Abstract Purpose: To evaluate the value of artificial intelligence-assisted compressed sensing (ACS) combined with deep learning reconstruction (DLR) in high-resolution prostate T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), with the aim of shortening scan time while improving image quality. Materials and Methods: A total of 77 patients suspected of prostate disease based on clinical findings underwent MRI examination, of whom 60 (mean age 65.0 ± 13.9 years, range 28–86 years) completed the full scanning protocol and were included in the analysis. All patients received axial T2WI sequences using three different acceleration techniques: Group A (control group), accelerated with parallel imaging (PI), NEX = 2; Group B, accelerated with ACS, NEX = 2; Group C, accelerated with ACS combined with DLR, NEX = 1.5. Objective evaluation metrics included signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), measured separately in the peripheral zone (PZ) and transition zone (TZ). Two radiologists independently assessed overall image quality, image artifacts, and diagnostic confidence using a 5-point Likert scale. Scan times were recorded and compared across groups. Results: The scanning time in Group C was reduced by 47.2% compared with Group A, from 127 s to 67 s. Compared with Groups A and B, Group C showed significantly higher PZ-SNR, TZ-SNR, and CNR values (all corrected P < 0.017; for CNR, C vs A: P < 0.001 and C vs B: P = 0.002). Group C also demonstrated significantly better subjective scores in all three categories—overall image quality, image artifacts, and diagnostic confidence—compared with Groups A and B (all corrected P < 0.017). Conclusion: The synergistic application of ACS acquisition acceleration and DLR optimization achieves substantial scan acceleration in prostate T2WI while effectively improving image quality and diagnostic confidence. This combined strategy offers a promising approach for optimizing prostate MRI workflows. originalAbstract:
Purpose: To evaluate the value of artificial intelligence-assisted compressed sensing (ACS) combined with deep learning reconstruction (DLR) in high-resolution prostate T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), with the aim of shortening scan time while improving image quality.

Materials and Methods:

A total of 77 patients suspected of prostate disease based on clinical findings underwent MRI examination, of whom 60 (mean age 65.0 ± 13.9 years, range 28–86 years) completed the full scanning protocol and were included in the analysis. All patients received axial T2WI sequences using three different acceleration techniques: Group A (control group), accelerated with parallel imaging (PI), NEX = 2; Group B, accelerated with ACS, NEX = 2; Group C, accelerated with ACS combined with DLR, NEX = 1.5. Objective evaluation metrics included signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), measured separately in the peripheral zone (PZ) and transition zone (TZ). Two radiologists independently assessed overall image quality, image artifacts, and diagnostic confidence using a 5-point Likert scale. Scan times were recorded and compared across groups.

Results:

The scanning time in Group C was reduced by 47.2% compared with Group A, from 127 s to 67 s. Compared with Groups A and B, Group C showed significantly higher PZ-SNR, TZ-SNR, and CNR values (all corrected P < 0.017; for CNR, C vs A: P < 0.001 and C vs B: P = 0.002). Group C also demonstrated significantly better subjective scores in all three categories—overall image quality, image artifacts, and diagnostic confidence—compared with Groups A and B (all corrected P < 0.017).

Conclusion:

The synergistic application of ACS acquisition acceleration and DLR optimization achieves substantial scan acceleration in prostate T2WI while effectively improving image quality and diagnostic confidence. This combined strategy offers a promising approach for optimizing prostate MRI workflows. title: Relational Explainability of Brain Tumor MRI: Linking Classification Attention to Tumor Masks
abstract: Abstract Attention-based explanations (e.g., Grad-CAM++ (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping Plus)) are commonly used in medical imaging, but their anatomical validity is rarely evaluated quantitatively. In this work we propose a novel relational explainability framework which goes beyond the conventional qualitative attention visualization by quantitatively validating the spatial correspondence between the classifier attention and the segmented tumor regions. Brain tumor segmentation is performed using DeepLabV3+ with EfficientNet-B4 encoder and tumor classification is performed using EfficientNet-B3. The Grad-CAM++ is employed to produce class-discriminative attention maps and the Exact Top-20% attention region is derived for quantitative analysis. The framework is evaluated on brain MRI datasets of gliomas, meningiomas, pituitary tumors, and non-tumor cases. The proposed method achieved a Dice coefficient of 87.5% for tumor segmentation and classification accuracy of 99.3% on the BRISC 2025 dataset. The classification accuracy on external evaluation was 93.5%. The quantitative validation of the explainability was performed by comparing the Exact Top-20% Grad-CAM++ attention region with the segmented tumor region in terms of Relational IoU, Tumor Coverage, and CAM Precision. The proposed framework achieved an overall Relational IoU of 0.0712, Tumor Coverage of 77.09%, and CAM Precision of 7.16%. These findings demonstrate class-dependent spatial alignment between classification attention and delineated tumor regions, with substantial tumor coverage but markedly lower spatial precision, underscoring the complementary rather than identical roles of discriminative attention and anatomical segmentation. The framework also identified the complementary functions of classification attention and anatomical segmentation, offering a more comprehensive understanding of the model’s behaviour. The proposed framework is an architecture-independent validation strategy providing an objective and quantitative approach to evaluate attention-based explanations, contributing to improving the transparency, interpretability and trustworthiness of artificial intelligence systems for medical image analysis.

title: Key performance indicators for organized risk stratified prostate cancer screening in Europe: first results from the PRAISE-U and EUCanScreen pilots and the Swedish organised prostate cancer testing programme
abstract: Abstract Background. Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in men in the European Union. Following the 2022 Council Recommendation to evaluate organised screening based on prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), PRAISE-U defined 21 harmonised key performance indicators (KPIs). We report their first empirical values from the five PRAISE-U pilots and, through a common survey, from EUCanScreen pilots and the Swedish organised prostate cancer testing (OPT) programme. Methods. In PRAISE-U, men aged 50–69 years at five pilot sites in Spain, Lithuania, Poland and Ireland were invited to risk-stratified screening comprising PSA testing, first-level risk stratification, MRI for intermediate or high risk and selective biopsy, with prospective capture in a central REDCap database. EUCanScreen pilots and the Swedish organised prostate cancer testing (OPT) programme reported the same KPIs through an online survey. Results. Twelve programmes reported KPI values. Across the five PRAISE-U pilots, participation ranged from 7.1% to 43.0%, PSA exceeded 3 ng/ml in 9.2–15.0%, and compliance was 76.4–96.0% for first-level risk assessment, 89.9–98.3% for MRI and 78.9–99.0% for biopsy. Detection ranged from 8 to 26 per 1,000 screened in PRAISE-U and from 4.3 to 28 across all programmes. ISUP grade 1 accounted for 20.3–81.4% of cancers, active-surveillance uptake for 14.8–100%, and mean time from PSA result to MRI for 19–114 days; external values fell broadly within the PRAISE-U ranges. Thirteen of 21 KPIs were fully reported by all five pilots, all describing the diagnostic pathway; retention and the three impact indicators were reported only by Sweden, which reported 19 of 21. Conclusions. Diagnostic-pathway KPIs were measurable under pilot conditions, whereas programme-level indicators required a defined target population or registry linkage. Sweden, the only population-based programme, reported retention and long-term impact, identifying the infrastructure needed before organised PCa screening can be monitored at scale.

title: Ethmoidal alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma with orbital extension in a young adult: A case report and literature review
abstract: Abstract Background Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is an uncommon malignant neoplasm of skeletal muscle differentiation that predominantly affects children. Sinonasal RMS is rare in adults, and the alveolar subtype tends toward aggressive local growth with regional and distant spread. Its clinical and radiologic presentation can overlap with inflammatory, infectious, and other malignant sinonasal processes, which makes diagnosis difficult. Case presentation A 28-year-old Middle Eastern man presented with a one-week history of right-sided proptosis and right eye pain, associated with diplopia and painful upward gaze but without prominent sinonasal symptoms. Computed tomography demonstrated a heterogeneous expansile mass centered in the right ethmoid and maxillary sinuses with extension through the lamina papyracea into the right orbit. Endoscopic sinus surgery with tumor debulking and biopsy demonstrated erosion of the lamina papyracea and extensive involvement of the ethmoid air cells. Histopathology showed an infiltrative malignant small round blue cell neoplasm arranged in nests and lobules separated by delicate fibrovascular stroma, with brisk mitotic activity, including seven mitotic figures per high-power field. Tumor cells showed diffuse strong nuclear expression of myogenin and MyoD1 and retained INI1. Pan-cytokeratin, CK5/6, chromogranin, synaptophysin, S100, CD99, FLI1, CD20, and CD3 were negative. Molecular testing was positive for FOXO1 rearrangement, supporting the diagnosis of alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma. Staging demonstrated no definite distant metastatic disease. Systemic chemotherapy with ifosfamide and etoposide was initiated, and the patient remains under treatment and follow-up. Conclusion Adult sinonasal alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma is rare and can be difficult to diagnose; it may present with orbital manifestations despite limited sinonasal symptoms. Its characteristic morphology, myogenic immunophenotype, and FOXO1 rearrangement help establish the diagnosis. Management requires a multidisciplinary team and careful evaluation of orbital and intracranial extension.

title: Sonographic Appearance of Congenital Cervical Teratoma: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background : Cervical teratomas account for only 3–9% of neonatal teratomas. Although usually benign, they may cause significant airway compression, necessitating prompt diagnosis and surgical intervention. Cervical teratomas are typically cystic or cystic-solid and often contain calcifications; a predominantly solid, hypervascular mass without calcification is rare and may pose a diagnostic challenge. We report such a case to highlight its atypical sonographic features and the diagnostic value of combining ultrasound with color Doppler imaging and ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA). Case presentation : A six-hour-old female neonate was transferred for respiratory distress after tracheal intubation. Physical examination revealed a firm midline cervical mass (4×3×5cm). Ultrasonography showed a predominantly solid, heterogeneously echogenic mass with irregular margins and increased vascularity. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) demonstrated mild enhancement with tracheal displacement, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed tracheal compression. Ultrasound-guided FNA yielded fibrous and cartilaginous elements, supporting the diagnosis of teratoma. The tumor was surgically resected, and histopathology confirmed a mature solid teratoma. Conclusions : Cervical teratomas may present atypically as predominantly solid, hypervascular masses without detectable calcification. In neonates with respiratory distress and a cervical mass, prompt diagnosis and surgery are imperative. Ultrasonography combined with color Doppler imaging and FNA provides valuable preoperative information for surgical decision-making.

title: OpenWell: Energy-Based Interactive Discovery for Open-World Medical Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Volumetric medical segmentation typically relies on closed-set assumptions, failing to identify or adapt to anatomical anomalies outside a fixed training vocabulary. We propose OpenWell , an energy-based framework that bridges the gap between Open-World discovery and interactive adaptation. Unlike deterministic approaches, OpenWell models anatomical classes as probabilistic energy wells on the hypersphere, using von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distributions. This formulation captures both the semantic identity and intra-class uncertainty of tissues, enabling out-of-distribution detection via a Free Energy score. Furthermore, we introduce an Instant Enrollment mechanism: triggered by a single user interaction, the system initializes a new energy well, allowing the model to adapt to previously unseen structures in real-time without gradient-based retraining. Extensive evaluations on AMOS, BTCV, MSD-Pancreas, and TotalSegmentator-MRI demonstrate that OpenWell improves Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection AUROC over closed-set and foundation models, while achieving rapid, one-shot interactive adaptation to novel classes.

title: Three-Dimensional CBCT Assessment of Buccal and Lingual/Palatal Bone Thickness Surrounding Developing Permanent Tooth Germs in Pediatric Patients
abstract: Abstract Background The anatomical relationship between developing permanent tooth germs and the surrounding cortical bone changes during growth and may be relevant to pediatric surgical and orthodontic procedures. This study aimed to evaluate buccal and lingual/palatal bone thickness surrounding developing permanent tooth germs using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) and to assess the effects of age, sex, and tooth type. Methods This retrospective cross-sectional study included CBCT images of 106 children aged 6–12 years. Bilateral permanent canines, first and second premolars, and second molars were evaluated. Buccal bone thickness (BBT) and lingual/palatal bone thickness (L/PBT) were measured on axial sections. Statistical analyses included the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, Mann–Whitney U test, paired-samples t-test, and Spearman correlation analysis (p < 0.05). Results The mean age was 9.19 ± 1.61 years. Sex-related differences were limited, and contralateral symmetry was generally maintained (p > 0.05). Significant age-related changes were observed in several regions. In the maxilla, palatal bone thickness decreased with age, with the strongest negative correlation observed for tooth 24 (rho = − 0.505, p < 0.001). In the mandible, age was negatively correlated with buccal bone thickness of teeth 33, 34, and 45, whereas positive correlations were observed for buccal bone thickness of tooth 37 and lingual bone thickness of teeth 43, 44, and 47. Conclusions Bone thickness surrounding developing permanent tooth germs varies according to tooth type, jaw region, and age. These age-related differences reflect dentoalveolar remodeling during growth, while sex has a limited influence and contralateral symmetry is generally preserved. These findings provide anatomical reference data that may support risk assessment and treatment planning during the mixed dentition period.

title: Development of a Computer Vision System for Stone Segmentation During CVAC 2.0 In-Scope Aspiration Ureteroscopy
abstract: Abstract Objective To develop and validate StoneClear, an artificial intelligence computer vision system that automatically detects and delineates residual stone fragments (RSFs) during Steerable Ureteroscopic Renal Evacuation (SURE) with the CVAC® 2.0 Aspiration System. Methods Intraoperative videos from 10 patients undergoing flexible ureteroscopy with the CVAC® 2.0 device were prospectively collected. Board-certified urologists densely annotated 1,439 stone-containing frames across diverse appearances and selected 977 stone-free frames containing background anatomy, instrumentation, or artifacts (such as urothelium, blood, bubbles, or Randall's plaques). StoneClear was trained to first determine whether a stone was present in each frame (frame-level detection) and then automatically segment the stone region at the pixel level (pixel-level boundaries). Model performance was evaluated using patient-level 5-fold cross-validation. Results Mean preoperative stone volume on CT was 10,925.36 mm³ (median: 1,641.49 mm³) and the mean postoperative residual stone volume was 170.20 mm³ (median: 0.0 mm³). We then evaluated StoneClear ’s ability to identify and localize residual stones in endoscopic video. The model correctly identified the presence or absence of stones in 92.8% of video frames. For frames containing visible stones, the model demonstrated precise pixel-level localization with a mean Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.86, a standard metric measuring spatial overlap between AI predictions and expert surgeon outlines. On frames without visible stones, StoneClear incorrectly identified stones in 13.6% of those frames (false-positive rate), substantially outperforming several existing AI models (such as standard U-Net architectures, which yielded a 78.2% false-positive rate). Conclusions StoneClear provides a robust proof-of-concept for real-time AI-assisted intraoperative visual stone assessment within the highly dynamic environment of suction-assisted ureteroscopy. By providing objective visual tracking and accurate boundary localization during the case, this framework establishes a critical foundation for intraoperative residual stone volume estimation to assist surgeons in verifying intraoperative endoscopic clearance.

title: Automated Gleason Grading and Prostate Cancer Classification from Histopathology Images: A Systematic Review of Deep Learning Models, Generalizability, Failure Modes, and Challenges in Low-Resource Settings
abstract: Abstract Background Digital pathology and deep learning have produced rapid advances in automated prostate cancer detection and Gleason grading. However, headline performance from internal benchmark datasets does not necessarily translate to reliable clinical performance across institutions, scanners, staining protocols, specimen types, or patient populations. This review synthesizes evidence on automated Gleason grading and prostate cancer classification from histopathology images, with particular emphasis on external validation, generalizability, failure modes, human–AI interaction, and deployment in low-resource settings. Methods The review was structured according to PRISMA 2020 principles. PubMed-indexed studies, publisher records, systematic reviews, and methodological guidance were examined, with emphasis on original studies of digital histopathology AI for prostate cancer and Gleason grading. Fifty key publications were selected for the evidence synthesis, supplemented conceptually by broader literature identified in prior systematic reviews. Because the evidence is heterogeneous in specimen type, endpoint, annotation strategy, architecture, and validation design, a narrative synthesis was used rather than an unverified pooled estimate. Results The evidence demonstrates that deep learning can approach or exceed the agreement of general pathologists and can achieve expert-level performance in selected external cohorts. The PANDA challenge demonstrated strong cross-continental performance using 10,616 digitized prostate biopsies, while subsequent real-world evaluations showed wider performance variation among algorithms. External validation on prostatectomy specimens has also demonstrated strong agreement for a biopsy-trained commercial model. Prospective multicenter evidence published in 2026 indicates that AI assistance can alter Gleason grading in routine practice and increase diagnostic confidence. Persistent weaknesses include domain shift, tissue and scanning artifacts, class imbalance, difficulty distinguishing adjacent Gleason patterns, limited prospective validation, dataset leakage, opaque reference standards, and underrepresentation of low-resource settings. Conclusion AI-assisted prostate histopathology has moved beyond proof-of-concept research, but clinical readiness should not be inferred from accuracy on a single dataset. Future studies should prioritize independent multicenter validation, prespecified clinical endpoints, transparent reference standards, calibration and uncertainty reporting, robustness testing, prospective workflow studies, and implementation strategies compatible with low-resource pathology laboratories.

title: Umbilical Cord Hernia is Not an Isolated Pathology: High Rate of Associated Anomalies in a Tertiary Center Cohort
abstract: Abstract Purpose This study aimed to evaluate the clinical profile of umbilical cord hernia (UCH), a defect often considered a minor variant of omphalocele, with a specific focus on the prevalence and spectrum of associated congenital anomalies. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 45 neonates with anterior abdominal wall defects treated between August 2019 and July 2024. Patients were categorized into three groups: omphalocele (n = 15), gastroschisis (n = 19), and UCH (n = 11). Demographic data, prenatal diagnosis, associated anomalies, surgical management, and outcomes were analyzed. Results In the UCH group, six patients (54.5%) had at least one major associated anomaly. Major cardiac anomalies were present in 45.5% (5/11), chromosomal anomalies in 27.3% (3/11), and genitourinary anomalies in 36.4% (4/11) of patients. title: When One View Isn’t Enough: Multimodal Cardiac Representation Fusion for Sudden Cardiac Arrest Risk
abstract: Abstract Risk of sudden cardiac arrest may be expressed differently by anatomy, mechanical function and electrical activity, while studies that contain all three modalities for the same patient are uncommon. We developed CardiacGuard-Net, a modular deep-learning framework that learns modality-specific representations from cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR), echocardiography and twelve-lead electrocardiography (ECG), then combines them for cardiac-arrest classification. The modality-specific models achieved mean Dice 0.953 for CMR segmentation, 3.8% mean absolute error for echocardiographic ejection-fraction estimation and AUC 0.938 for 24-h arrest prediction from ECG. For multimodal evaluation, 1,204 records were assembled into a matched benchmark using age band, sex, ejection-fraction band and diagnostic category because no dataset available to the study contained all three modalities for the same patients. On this benchmark, CardiacFusion-Net achieved AUC 0.947, compared with 0.920 for late fusion. Removing the ECG, CMR or echocardiographic branch reduced AUC by 0.035, 0.026 and 0.016, respectively. A single trained model also retained discrimination when modalities were withheld, with AUCs of 0.890 for ECG alone, 0.905 for MRI+echo, 0.921 for MRI + ECG and 0.931 for echo + ECG. The multimodal results are therefore best interpreted as an internal proof-of-concept benchmark of complementary information, not as patient-level clinical validation.

title: 18F-FDG PET/CT for Differentiating Reactive Lymphadenopathy, Lymphoma, and Tuberculosis in People Living with HIV
abstract: Abstract Purpose To evaluate the diagnostic contribution of 2-deoxy-2-[¹⁸F]fluoro-D-glucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography ([¹⁸F]FDG PET/CT) metabolic, volumetric, and morphological parameters in differentiating human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-related reactive lymphadenopathy (LAP), lymphoma, and tuberculosis (TB) in people living with HIV. Methods PET/CT images of 96 patients with HIV (2010–2025) with reactive LAP (n = 67), lymphoma (n = 16), or TB (n = 13) were retrospectively reviewed. Maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax), SUVmax-to-liver ratio (SURmax), metabolic tumor volume (MTV), total lesion glycolysis (TLG), nodal morphology, extranodal involvement, and maximum-intensity-projection (MIP) symmetry were compared among groups, and the association of antiretroviral therapy (ART) exposure with PET/CT parameters was assessed within the reactive LAP group. Results SUVmax and SURmax were significantly lower in reactive LAP than in lymphoma and TB (p < 0.001), with cut-offs of 16.46 (area under the curve [AUC] 0.959) and 3.83 (AUC 0.934) showing high discriminatory performance in distinguishing reactive LAP from lymphoma. MTV and TLG were higher in lymphoma and TB (p < 0.001). Symmetric MIP uptake was present in 98.5% of reactive LAP versus 56.2% of lymphoma and 46.2% of TB cases and was strongly associated with reactive LAP (p < 0.001). SUVmax, SURmax, MTV, and TLG were significantly lower in ART-experienced than ART-naïve reactive LAP patients (p < 0.001), and [¹⁸F]FDG PET/CT guided biopsy target selection in 87.8% of biopsied patients. Conclusion [¹⁸F]FDG PET/CT may aid differentiation of reactive lymphadenopathy from lymphoma and tuberculosis in people living with HIV through combined metabolic, volumetric, and morphological parameters — particularly MIP symmetry — and effectively guides biopsy planning. However, substantial overlap remains between lymphoma and tuberculosis.

title: ‘One shunt fits all?’: A comparative laboratory study of antibiotic- impregnated shunt catheters with retrospective clinical correlation
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Several antibiotic-impregnated shunt catheters are commercially available, but direct comparative data on their biochemical and physical characteristics remain limited. Previous observations from our single-centre neurosurgical unit suggested that nominally similar catheter types may be associated with different rates of otherwise unexplained abdominal pain. We therefore conducted a prospective comparative study to investigate potential biochemical and physical differences between commercially available antibiotic-impregnated shunt catheters. Methods: Ares®, Bactiseal® and XABO® catheters were compared for antibiotic content, rifampicin degradation products, elution characteristics and antimicrobial activity. Antibiotic elution was assessed during continuous saline perfusion at 20 mL/h and 37°C over 8 weeks, while antimicrobial activity against Staphylococcus epidermidis was evaluated over 60 days. Catheter dimensions, elastic modulus and surface morphology were assessed using three-dimensional computed tomography, nanoindentation and scanning electron microscopy, respectively. An exploratory retrospective quality-improvement dataset from our single-centre unit was additionally analysed to compare the frequency of otherwise unexplained abdominal pain between catheter types. Results: The three catheter systems showed product-specific differences in antibiotic content, rifampicin degradation profiles, elution characteristics, antimicrobial activity, dimensions, mechanical properties and surface morphology. XABO® most closely matched the declared antibiotic concentrations and retained the greatest proportion of intact rifampicin, while Ares® demonstrated the highest sustained clindamycin elution. All three catheters retained measurable activity against Staphylococcus epidermidis for 60 days, with XABO® showing the largest numerical inhibition zones throughout. In the 395-patient retrospective clinical analysis, otherwise unexplained abdominal pain was recorded in 90/182 patients with Ares® catheters (49.5%) compared with 12/108 patients with Bactiseal® catheters (11.1%). After adjustment for age, sex, primary diagnosis, modified Rankin Scale score and activity level, Ares® remained associated with greater odds of abdominal pain than Bactiseal® (adjusted OR 6.89, 95% CI 2.58–18.43; p<0.001). Conclusion: Commercially available antibiotic-impregnated shunt catheters showed product-specific biochemical and physical variation, while catheter type was associated with different rates of otherwise unexplained abdominal pain in a retrospective single-centre analysis. These findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish causality or clinical superiority. Prospective multicentre studies are required to determine whether catheter-specific properties translate into clinically meaningful differences and should influence individualised shunt selection.

title: Trackerless Augmented Reality Navigation for Robotic Partial Nephrectomy using Simultaneous Localization and Mapping
abstract: Abstract Purpose. To evaluate the performance of a novel trackerless surgical navigation system for partial nephrectomy using 3D laparoscopy integrated with the simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) algorithm. Materials and Methods. Patients undergoing robotic partial nephrectomy were retrospectively analyzed. From the preoperative CT/MR images, three-dimensional (3D) models of the kidney, tumor, and vasculature were generated using a deep learning-based approach. A calibrated stereo laparoscope acquired stereo video, which was processed using the SLAM algorithm to reconstruct high-fidelity 3D surface models of the kidney. This reconstruction was registered to the preoperative kidney model using anatomical landmarks and surface-based alignment. Augmented overlays of anatomy, including the tumor, were projected onto the surgical view. Accuracy was assessed using surface target registration error (STRE), landmark registration error (LRE), and localization error. A multi-institutional surgeon survey evaluated the trackerless navigation system using 10 representative cases. Results. Twenty patients undergoing robotic partial nephrectomy were analyzed. Dense 3D surface reconstruction and laparoscope calibration were successful in all cases. Mean (SD; range) STRE, LRE, and localization errors were 1.47 (0.5; 0.6–2.5) mm, 4.3 (1.6; 1.1–6.5) mm, and 2.6 (1.2; 0.7–5.2) mm, respectively. Nine surgeons highly rated the 3D and 2D overlays (3.99 and 4.41/5). Reported cognitive load was moderate (2.38), with high scores for anatomical accuracy (4.44), trust in the overlay for intraoperative decision-making (3.89), and likelihood of adoption (4.56) on a 5-point scale. Conclusions. A trackerless SLAM-based navigation system, evaluated retrospectively on recorded operative video, demonstrates the feasibility of accurate augmented visualization during partial nephrectomy.

title: 3D CT-GraphEdgeMAE: 3D CT Image Anomaly Detection Using Self-Supervised Graph Edge Mask Autoencoders
abstract: Abstract Computer tomography anomaly detection is the fastest and the most effective method of early diagnosing malignant tumor. Large scale training data, high computation, and excessive number of parameters demand abundant computing resources. We propose a new end-end 3D CT-GraphEdgeMAE to solve the 3D CT anomaly detection. We construct the graph for 3D CT to employ a standard encoder GCN to learn node feature, and crucially, propose a novel decoder which the Hadamard product and subgraph similarity are jointly used to predict the masked edges. Furthermore, we introduce a joint topology-aware contrastive-reconstruction loss function by constructing connected subgraph for two nodes of mask edge. We perform anomaly detection via graph node classification which can effectively captures both the characteristic fine-grained features and the gradual trend of lesions. Extensive experiments are conducted on the public 3D CT dateset LUNA16. Our method specifically tailored for training under small scale dateset，utilizes all 888 cases in LUNA16 and 88 case from a subset of LUNA16. On the downstream task of nodule detection, compared with MAE and other baselines, our method achieves a 30-fold reduction in training time and lowers computational cost by 68%, while attaining competitive FROC scores of 82.2% for 888 cases and 77.9% for 88 cases.

title: Operator-rated puncture performance and first-pass lesion tissue area in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: an exploratory single-center sub-analysis of endoscopic ultrasound- guided tissue acquisition
abstract: Abstract Background: Adequate tissue acquisition is important for histological assessment and ancillary testing in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). We primarily explored the association between operator-rated puncture performance and first-pass lesion tissue area during endoscopic ultrasound-guided tissue acquisition (EUS-TA) in patients with PDAC. A secondary analysis examined whether this association was observed in the overall cohort, irrespective of final diagnosis. Methods: This exploratory single-center sub-analysis used prospective data from a multicenter randomized trial of 22-gauge fine-needle biopsy needles. Endoscopists rated overall puncture performance on a five-point scale after EUS-TA. Ratings were analyzed using two post hoc dichotomizations: very easy/easy versus indeterminate/difficult/very difficult, and very easy versus all other ratings. First-pass lesion tissue area was quantified automatically on histological slides using a digital microscope with image-analysis software. Multivariable linear regression assessed associations between ratings and tissue areas in each cohort, adjusting for needle type, puncture route, operator experience, and lesion size. Firth logistic regression assessed associations between ratings and exploratory ≥ 4-mm² benchmark attainment in the PDAC cohort. Trends in tissue area across very easy, easy, and remaining ratings were assessed using the Jonckheere–Terpstra test. Comprehensive genomic profiling (CGP) suitability was summarized descriptively. Results: Of 62 patients, 48 had PDAC. In the PDAC cohort, the very easy/easy comparison yielded inconclusive adjusted associations with tissue area and benchmark attainment. A very easy rating was associated with greater tissue area (median, 5.45 vs. 1.90 mm²; adjusted difference, 1.93 mm²; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.12–3.74) and benchmark attainment (57.7% vs. 22.7%; adjusted odds ratio, 4.44; 95% CI, 1.17–21.06). Tissue area decreased with less favorable ratings (p for trend = 0.016). Two of six patients assessed for CGP were considered suitable. In the overall cohort, lesion size remained associated with tissue area, whereas adjusted associations for both rating dichotomizations were inconclusive. Tissue area decreased with less favorable ratings (p for trend = 0.034). Conclusions: In patients with PDAC, an endoscopist’s very easy rating was associated with greater first-pass lesion tissue area after adjustment for lesion size and procedural factors. Prospective pass-by-pass studies are needed to validate this exploratory association and determine its utility in EUS-TA. Trial registration: Parent trial: Japan Registry of Clinical Trials (jRCT), jRCT1042220099, registered on 25 November 2022.

title: Patient-level coronary artery disease classification from cardiac MRI using out-of-fold heart segmentation and same-slice region controls
abstract: Abstract Background Medical-image classifiers can obtain high apparent performance from correlated slices, acquisition patterns, or anatomy outside the intended target. The downloaded CAD Cardiac MRI Dataset release contained 63,425 JPEG images but only 30 independent top-level patient folders. This study evaluated whether cardiac-region representations were more informative than exact same-slice full-image and extra-cardiac controls under patient-level validation. Methods Each Directory_* folder was treated as one patient (16 Normal, 14 Sick), as confirmed by the dataset creator. The current analysis used five patient-level cross-fitted 2.5D Attention U-Nets trained from 5,097 accepted targets (3,949 heart-present and 1,148 no-heart). Every released image received an out-of-fold mask from a model that did not train on its patient. A frozen ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet-B0 encoded full-image, cardiac-ROI, and exact-complement representations. Slice embeddings were averaged first within folder-defined series and then across series for each patient. Nested patient-level cross-validation evaluated eleven representations using exact same-slice controls, a secondary cross-class matched cohort, and paired patient-bootstrap intervals. Results The expanded manual-target state caused all five segmentation folds and all five out-of-fold prediction parts to be recomputed. Out-of-fold prediction produced 63,107 final-valid masks among 63,425 images; positive-target patient-balanced Dice was 0.809, and 73.4% of accepted no-heart targets received empty masks. On exactly 50,735 attention-eligible slices, the automatic cardiac ROI achieved AUC 0.938 (95% CI 0.847-1.000), compared with 0.830 for the full image and 0.772 for the complement. Paired AUC differences were 0.107 (95% CI 0.009–0.235) versus the full image and 0.165 (0.029–0.344) versus the complement. In the matched cohort, ROI AUC was 0.942, versus 0.821 for the full image and 0.741 for the complement. On the manual-positive subset, automatic and manual ROIs achieved AUCs of 0.973 and 0.951, respectively; their paired difference did not exclude zero. Conclusions After expanded manual annotation and a complete rerun of every dependent stage, out-of-fold cardiac localization retained an advantage over exact same-slice and matched controls. Complement AUCs of 0.741–0.835 nevertheless show substantial residual predictive information outside the intended cardiac region. With only 30 patients, no external validation, JPEG rather than DICOM data, and outcome-informed matching in a secondary analysis, these findings support a methodological proof of concept rather than clinical use.

title: Lesion-specific diagnostic performance of magnetic resonance imaging compared with arthroscopy in chronic ankle pathologies with exploratory machine learning prediction
abstract: Abstract Background Understanding the diagnostic agreement between advanced imaging and arthroscopy is essential for accurate preoperative planning and tailored therapy. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic concordance between preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and direct arthroscopic examination for principal ankle pathologies and identify key predictors of arthroscopically confirmed osteochondral lesions (OLs) using machine learning (ML) predictive algorithms. Materials and Methods This retrospective study included 54 adults with chronic or recurrent ankle symptoms, who underwent preoperative imaging and subsequent ankle arthroscopy. Arthroscopy served as the reference standard. Sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, accuracy, and Cohen κ were calculated with 95% confidence intervals. Exploratory ML models predicting arthroscopically confirmed OLs were evaluated using leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV), followed by feature importance and ablation analyses. Results For OLs, MRI demonstrated 82.1% sensitivity, 80.8% specificity, 81.5% accuracy, and substantial agreement with arthroscopy (κ = 0.629). For synovitis, MRI showed 94.3% sensitivity and 100% specificity, although the specificity was based on only one arthroscopy-negative case. For loose body detection, MRI demonstrated 50.0% sensitivity and 90.5% specificity. For ligamentous injury, the sensitivity and specificity were 100% and 25.0%, respectively, with directional discordance between MRI and arthroscopy (exact McNemar P = 0.004). In the exploratory ML analysis, linear Support Vector Machine and Logistic Regression achieved LOOCV accuracies of 81.5% and 79.6%, respectively. title: Synoptic procedural reporting to improve quality indicators in systematic Staging Endobronchial Ultrasound (EBUS) in Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC): protocol for an ambispective multi-centre quality improvement study
abstract: Abstract Background: Accurate mediastinal staging by systematic staging endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) is essential for prognosticating and guiding management in curative-intent treatment in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Narrative procedural reports are often incomplete and inconsistent between clinicians, limiting assessment of procedural quality and meaningful audit. Synoptic (structured, check-list style) reporting has improved documentation completeness and procedural quality in other domains of medicine, and a recent Australian multicentre study demonstrated synoptic reporting significantly improved both report and procedural quality in staging EBUS. This ambispective, international, multicentre study aims to evaluate whether synoptic procedural reporting improves quality indicators of systematic staging EBUS, encompassing both process and outcome measures, and will assess acceptability and feasibility to proceduralists. Methods: This ambispective multicentre, single-arm interventional study will recruit approximately 15 lung cancer services with substantial EBUS procedural volume. Eligible patients will have known or suspected clinical stage IB-IIIC NSCLC undergoing systematic staging EBUS for treatment planning. Each centre will implement a mandated synoptic report requiring documentation for each of the five mediastinal lymph nodes: examination, size of node and biopsy details. Three months of staging procedures will be contributed prior to and following implementation of this reporting practice. The primary outcome is the proportion of patients with a complete staging procedure. Secondary outcomes include PET-occult lymph node metastases detection, nodes sampled, radiologically normal node sampling, inter-site variance, and proceduralist feasibility/acceptability. A sample of 590 patients (295 pre-, 295 post-intervention) provides 80% power to detect an 8% increase in complete staging. Mixed-effects logistic and Poisson regression, with random effect for centre and adjustment for pre-specified baseline case-mix covariates, will be used. Discussion: This study will provide the first international multicentre evaluation of whether synoptic reporting improves procedural completeness and clinically meaningful outcomes in systematic staging EBUS. Demonstrating improved complete staging procedures and PET-occult lymph node detection, with proceduralist acceptability, would support widespread adoption of synoptic reporting as a quality improvement tool, strengthen alignment with WABIP quality frameworks, reduce variance in care, and support more accurate multidisciplinary decision-making for NSCLC patients. Trial registration: Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ANZCTR), ACTRN12625001281482. Registered 18 November 2025. Retrospectively registered.

title: Sex differences in quantitative fundus parameters measured by artificial intelligence: a cross-sectional community study
abstract: Abstract Background Automated analysis of fundus photographs yields numerous quantitative measures, but sex differences in these measures and their modification by systemic conditions are not well characterized. We quantified these differences in a large community screening cohort. Methods This cross-sectional study included 21,844 participants contributing 32,576 eye-level records to a community health-screening program in Ganzhou, China. EVisionAI was used to quantify 49 vascular, optic disc and cup, peripapillary atrophy, and fundus tessellation density parameters from color fundus photographs. Generalized estimating equations clustered by participant estimated male-female differences in standardized parameters. Models were unadjusted, adjusted for age and age squared, and further adjusted for 20 binary systemic conditions. Sex-by-condition interactions were examined for 19 conditions; prostatic hyperplasia was assessed separately using a three-level variable. Benjamini–Hochberg correction was applied across all fundus parameters within each model for the primary comparisons and within each condition for the interaction analyses. Results Mean age was 63.6 ± 9.8 years in women and 63.9 ± 10.1 years in men. After full adjustment and FDR correction, sex differences were found in 41 of 49 parameters: 19 of 22 optic disc and cup, 8 of 11 vascular, 7 of 7 peripapillary atrophy, and 7 of 9 fundus tessellation density measures. The largest standardized differences in men were a lower disc vertical-to-horizontal ratio (β = −0.170; 95% confidence interval, − 0.196 to − 0.144) and a higher atrophy arc height-to-disc vertical diameter ratio (β = 0.166; 95% confidence interval, 0.141 to 0.192). The arteriole-to-venule ratio was also lower in men (β = −0.113; 95% confidence interval, − 0.137 to − 0.089). Estimates were generally stable across models. Twenty-three effect-modification findings remained significant after false discovery rate correction, predominantly involving prostatic hyperplasia. Conclusions Sex differences were present across most quantitative fundus parameters and changed little after adjustment for measured systemic conditions. Their relevance to screening requires validation in datasets with ocular biometry and clinical outcomes.

title: From detection to decision: radiographic predictors of clinical complications in 514 supernumerary teeth: A retrospective cross-sectional study
abstract: Abstract Background Supernumerary teeth exhibit various morphological characteristics and may lead to a range of complications. This study aimed to evaluate radiographic characteristics of supernumerary teeth in children and to determine associations with complications and treatment status. Materials and methods This study included 386 systemically healthy paediatric patients (5–15.9 years) with 514 supernumerary teeth identified on panoramic radiographs. Variables included number, location, morphology, eruption direction, eruption status, root development stage, and complications. Statistical analyses included chi-square tests, independent samples t-tests, and multivariable binary logistic and multinomial regression models. Results The mean age was 9.07 ± 2.08 years, and 70.2% of patients were male. Significant differences were observed between erupted and impacted teeth regarding morphology, eruption direction, root development stage, complications, and Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) use (p < 0.05). Morphology and root development stage were associated with complication patterns (p < 0.05). Multivariable regression analyses showed that CBCT use was associated with eruption status, dentition “stage, side distribution, and delayed eruption. Anterior maxillary localisation was strongly associated with conical and tuberculate morphologies. Midline location was associated with increased odds of both complete and partial root development (p < 0.001). Conclusion Supernumerary teeth exhibit distinct radiographic characteristics associated with clinical complications. Morphology, eruption status, and root development were associated with clinical and radiographic findings. Early radiographic evaluation is essential for individualised treatment planning.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Cervical Cancer Histopathology in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Systematic Review of Segmentation, Classification Techniques, and Barriers to Deployment
abstract: Abstract Background and Objective Cervical cancer remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), where access to pathology expertise, screening, tissue diagnosis and digital pathology infrastructure is uneven. Histopathological examination remains central to confirming cervical neoplasia, grading lesions and guiding management. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to support pathologists by automating image segmentation and classification, but evidence on clinical generalisability and deployment in SSA is fragmented. This systematic review synthesizes AI techniques for cervical histopathology segmentation and classification and examines barriers to translation into routine practice in SSA. Methods A structured systematic evidence synthesis was prepared and reported with reference to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020). Contemporary evidence was identified from PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore and Google Scholar searches and from reference chaining of relevant systematic reviews. Eligible evidence addressed cervical histopathology or closely related cervical image-analysis tasks involving segmentation, feature learning, classification, whole-slide analysis, clinical validation or deployment. The synthesis focused on 49 substantive publications spanning classical image processing, machine learning, CNNs, transfer learning, U-Net-family and other segmentation methods, attention/transformer models, whole-slide analysis, African studies and digital-pathology implementation. Results The evidence shows a transition from thresholding, clustering, watershed, active contours and handcrafted morphological/texture features toward CNN-based segmentation and classification, transfer learning, multiple-instance learning, attention models and transformer/foundation-model approaches. Early studies were frequently based on small, pre-segmented public datasets, whereas newer studies increasingly use histology images and whole-slide images. African evidence remains limited but is expanding. An Ethiopian study used 915 histopathology images and EfficientNetB0, reporting 94.5% test accuracy for cervical cancer classification. A 2026 Rwandan study used 885 patient-level H&E cervical biopsy images and reported EfficientNetB0 accuracy of 0.99 with ROC-AUC 0.99 on a held-out test set. A Ugandan study used 5,966 cervical histopathology images acquired with smartphone-assisted microscopy and DeepLabV3 + with a ResNet34 encoder for 21-feature segmentation, reporting validation mIoU of approximately 75.8% and Dice of approximately 93.1%. Conclusion AI has substantial potential to augment cervical histopathology in SSA, but reported algorithmic performance should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical readiness. The dominant evidence gaps are external validation, prospective evaluation, multi-institutional datasets, standardised staining and imaging, transparent reporting, calibration, explainability, workflow integration and implementation economics. Future research should prioritize locally representative datasets, lightweight and edge-capable models, patient-level validation, human-in-the-loop decision support and implementation studies conducted within African pathology workflows.

title: Versajet® Hydrosurgery for Primary Axillary Hyperhidrosis with Osmidrosis: First Vietnamese Case Report with Histopathology
abstract: Abstract Background Conventional minimally invasive surgical techniques for axillary hyperhidrosis (e.g., cannula-assisted suction-curettage) carry risks of subdermal vascular plexus injury and flap necrosis (10–15%) [1] . The Versajet® Hydrosurgery System, employing the Venturi effect with high-pressure saline jet and continuous suction without thermal injury, represents a potential alternative [2,3] . Case presentation : A 33-year-old Vietnamese male (BMI 33.3 kg/m²) presented with 16-year history of bilateral primary axillary hyperhidrosis with osmidrosis (onset at age 18), HDSS 3 bilaterally, wet earwax phenotype (suggesting ABCC11 G-allele), DLQI 9/30, Park-Shin grade 3, meeting 5/6 Hornberger criteria [4] . Methods Surgery was performed on 23 April 2026 under Klein tumescent anesthesia (lidocaine 480 mg + epinephrine 1:1,000,000 + 500 mL 0.9% NaCl; 100 mL/axilla infiltration). The Versajet® II with a 45°/14 mm handpiece at power 6–8 (574 bar/8,330 psi) was used, consuming 500 mL 0.9% NaCl and 15 minutes of debridement per axilla through a 5-cm incision parallel to the axillary crease. Outcomes were assessed at 1 and 3 months using HDSS, DLQI, Park-Shin, and VSS, with paired pre-/post-excision histopathology. Results Total operative time was 100 minutes with blood loss < 30 mL and no intraoperative complications. VAS pain was 3/10 on days 1–3, resolving to 0/10 by day 10. At 3 months: HDSS 3→1, DLQI 9→1, Park-Shin 3→1, VSS 4/14, Clavien-Dindo grade I, patient satisfaction 5/5. Histopathology demonstrated 68.8–75.0% apocrine gland reduction and 32.3–45.5% eccrine gland reduction with preserved hair follicle architecture. Conclusion Hydrosurgery with the Versajet® System demonstrated high technical feasibility, significant clinical efficacy, and objective histopathological evidence of selective apocrine gland reduction while preserving the subdermal vascular plexus. Larger prospective cohort studies with long-term follow-up are warranted to standardize parameters and assess recurrence.

title: Machine learning based on non-contrast chest CT radiomics for identifying hemodynamically significant coronary stenosis in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: development and external validation
abstract: Abstract Background Patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) carry a substantial, frequently under-recognized burden of coronary artery disease, yet systematic screening with coronary CT angiography (CCTA) is impractical. We developed and externally validated machine learning models based on radiomics features from routine non-contrast chest CT, combined with clinical variables and quantitative airway parameters, to identify hemodynamically significant coronary stenosis (HSCS) in patients with COPD. Methods This retrospective study enrolled 455 patients with COPD who underwent paired non-contrast chest CT and CCTA between June 2021 and December 2025 (internal cohort, randomly split 7:3 into training [n = 318] and test [n = 137] sets) and 332 patients from an independent external validation cohort. HSCS was defined as ≥ 70% luminal stenosis in at least one major epicardial coronary artery. Whole-lung radiomics features (n = 1688) were extracted with PyRadiomics; after redundancy removal and univariate filtering within the training set, a radiomics score (Rad-score) was built with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) logistic regression. Clinical and combined models were constructed with five algorithms, including logistic regression, support vector machine, k-nearest neighbors, random forest, and light gradient boosting machine. Discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC], DeLong tests), calibration (Hosmer–Lemeshow test, calibration slope), and clinical utility (decision curve analysis) were assessed, and a nomogram was constructed. Results Age, smoking, diabetes, and a lower airway surface-area-to-volume ratio were independently associated with HSCS. Seventeen radiomics features constituted the Rad-score. The logistic regression combined model achieved AUCs of 0.854 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.802–0.906) in the training set, 0.823 (0.746–0.900) in the internal test set, and 0.798 (0.746–0.851) in the external cohort, significantly outperforming the clinical model (DeLong p = 0.008 and p = 0.002, respectively), with satisfactory calibration (Hosmer–Lemeshow p = 0.749 and 0.189) and superior net benefit across threshold probabilities of approximately 0.05–0.50. Conclusions A machine learning model based on non-contrast chest CT radiomics identifies HSCS in patients with COPD with good, externally validated performance and may support opportunistic cardiovascular risk stratification without additional radiation or contrast exposure.

title: CSF1R inhibition during cranial radiotherapy reshapes the immune environment and glial dynamics
abstract: Abstract Background: Cranial radiotherapy (cRT) induces long-lasting alterations in the brain microenvironment, including changes in glial populations and loss of neurogenesis. Pharmacological depletion of microglia via colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) inhibition has been proposed as a strategy to modulate radiation-induced neuroinflammation, but its effects on other glial populations remains incompletely understood. Methods: Nine-week-old male C57BL/6JRj mice (n=60) received either a CSF1R-inhibitor supplemented diet (pexidartinib, PLX3397) or a control diet prior to and continued for 10 days after fractionated CT-guided cRT (3x10 Gy, 30 Gy). Brain tissue was assessed at multiple time-points up to six months post cRT using immunohistochemistry for markers of microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and proliferating cells. Microglial identity and repopulation dynamics were assessed using IBA1, F4/80 and the homeostatic microglial marker P2RY12, complemented by morphometric analysis. Results: Pexidartinib alone resulted in partial microglial depletion, whereas its combination with cRT led to near-complete loss of P2RY12+ homeostatic microglia at early time points. After discontinuation of the diet this was accompanied by increased IBA1+;F4/80 high ;P2RY12 neg cell densities, consistent with replacement of the microglial niche by monocyte-derived cells. Over time, these cells exhibited gradual morphological adaptation but remained largely P2RY12 neg , indicating incomplete restoration of a homeostatic microglial phenotype. Combined treatment accelerated astrocytic reactivity compared to cRT alone and did not prevent cRT-induced loss of neurogenesis or OPCs. At later time points, partial OPC recovery was observed in selected regions in the combined treatment group. Conclusion: CSF1R inhibition during cRT profoundly alters the composition and temporal dynamics of the brain’s myeloid compartment, characterized by sustained loss of homeostatic microglia and replacement by monocyte-derived cells. Under these experimental conditions, microglial depletion did not mitigate key histopathological features associated with radiation-induced brain injury and was associated with accelerated astrocytic responses. These findings highlight the importance of timing, extent of depletion, and repopulation dynamics when considering microglia-targeting strategies in the context of cranial radiotherapy.

title: Associations of initial blood gas parameters with post-cooling MRI-derived brain volumes and Rutherford injury scores in neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy: a retrospective exploratory study
abstract: Abstract Background Quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may reveal structural alterations not captured by conventional visual assessment in neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE). This study investigated associations between initial blood gas parameters and post-cooling MRI-derived brain volumes and Rutherford MRI injury scores in neonates treated with therapeutic hypothermia. Methods This retrospective exploratory study included 79 neonates with HIE. Initial pH, partial pressure of carbon dioxide, bicarbonate, base excess, and lactate were evaluated in relation to 50 absolute MRI-derived brain-volume measures and the consensus Rutherford score. Associations were assessed using Spearman correlations and separate multivariable linear regression models adjusted for gestational age at birth, postnatal age at MRI, and sex, with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. Two blinded radiologists independently assigned Rutherford scores and resolved disagreements by consensus. Secondary analyses compared neonates with pH ≤ 7.00 and pH > 7.00. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure controlled the false discovery rate within prespecified analysis families. Results Consensus Rutherford scores were available for all 79 neonates (mean, 6.91 ± 1.34; median, 7; interquartile range, 6–8; range, 4–9). Interobserver agreement was good (absolute-agreement intraclass correlation coefficient, 0.789; quadratic-weighted κ, 0.787); exact agreement occurred in 50.6% of examinations, and scores differed by no more than 1 point in 88.6%. After false-discovery-rate correction, no initial blood gas parameter was significantly associated with the consensus Rutherford score in either unadjusted or adjusted analyses. The adjusted mean score difference between the pH groups was−0.20 (95% confidence interval,−0.93 to 0.54; p = 0.597). No blood gas–volume association remained significant after correction, and no absolute or intracranial-volume-normalized measure differed significantly between the pH groups. Conclusions This exploratory cohort provided no evidence of associations between initial blood gas parameters and post-cooling Rutherford MRI injury scores or global and regional brain volumes after correction for multiple comparisons. These findings do not exclude clinically relevant associations and require confirmation in larger studies using neonatal-validated segmentation methods.

title: County-Level Radiologist Workforce Density, Cancer Mortality, and the Modeled Impact of AI-Augmented Diagnostic Capacity: A U.S. Ecological Analysis
abstract: Abstract Timely cancer diagnosis depends on adequate diagnostic imaging capacity, yet radiologist workforce availability remains unevenly distributed across U.S. counties. This study examined the association between county-level diagnostic radiologist density and age-adjusted cancer mortality across 3,073 U.S. counties using cross-sectional ecological analysis integrating provider enrollment, cancer registry, socioeconomic, and population data. In the fully adjusted model, higher log-transformed radiologist density was significantly associated with lower cancer mortality (β = −2.01 per 100,000; 95% CI: −2.82 to − 1.19; p < 0.001), with results robust to spatial autocorrelation (spatial error model β = −1.96) and twelve sensitivity analyses. Counties with zero radiologist presence (n = 1,334; population 22.6 million) were identified as having the greatest modeled mortality burden. Decision-analytic scenario modeling estimated that AI-equivalent augmentation matching the median nonzero-county density (ΔAI = 6.05 per 100,000) would correspond to a modeled annual mortality difference equivalent to approximately 887 deaths in this subgroup. The modeled association showed diminishing marginal differences, with larger estimated differentials when capacity was introduced into zero-radiologist counties than in higher-density settings. These findings suggest radiologist workforce distribution may represent a policy-relevant marker of diagnostic capacity and highlight zero-radiologist counties as targets for further evaluation of capacity-expanding interventions, including AI-equivalent approaches.
