title: Multimodal Visual Question Answering System for Survival Prognosis in PSMA-Targeted Radiopharmaceutical Therapy.
abstract: Large language models show great promise for clinical decision support but generally lack medical imaging integration. Therefore, vision-language models have been proposed, but there is little evidence on their performance, particularly compared with conventional machine learning. Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy is a well-established treatment for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), but it is still not known which patients will be good long-term responders. Therefore, this study proposes a physician-inspired visual question answering (VQA) framework that emulates the structured integration of PSMA-directed imaging and clinical data used in routine clinical assessment for overall survival prognostication. Methods: As a proof of concept, we conducted a retrospective, multicenter study across 2 academic institutions that included 110 patients with mCRPC who were treated with either [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA I&T or [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617. Our VQA approach incorporates a 3-dimensional image encoder, the domain-specific language model RadBERT, and a cross-modal transformer to process baseline and interim (after 2 cycles) PET and SPECT images, clinical data, and clinical query. The model was trained to predict 24-mo survival, and performance was compared with state-of-the-art approaches. External validation was performed with the [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 cohort. Results: The VQA model outperformed all state-of-the-art approaches while showing accuracy comparable to the query-free attention multimodal fusion model. Specifically, it achieved 81.8% accuracy (95% CI, 0.52-0.95) when integrating SPECT or PET images with prostate-specific antigen measurements. External validation of the VQA showed 71.9% accuracy (95% CI, 0.53-0.86) after few-shot fine-tuning, with further improvement over all state-of-the-art approaches in survival stratification. The VQA approach showed the closest calibration with the ground-truth survival distribution, with no significant differences observed (log-rank test, P = 0.76). Receiver operating characteristic analysis showed the highest area under the curve (0.75) among the evaluated models. Together, these findings suggest that the VQA approach demonstrated adaptability across different PSMA ligands while maintaining slightly improved yet comparable overall survival prognostic performance. Conclusion: By adopting a physician-inspired assessment workflow, the VQA framework shows advantages in integrating imaging and laboratory data for clinical decision support compared with conventional machine learning. The preliminary results indicate that VQA-based approaches warrant future evaluation for survival prognostication in patients with mCRPC who are receiving PSMA radiopharmaceutical therapy.

title: Toward a Biopsy-Free Diagnosis of Prostate Cancer: Potential of Combined 18 F-Flotufolastat PSMA PET and mpMRI.
abstract: This retrospective analysis aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of 18 F-flotufolastat PET/MRI for the detection of clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa). The primary objective of the study was to assess the proportion of patients for whom a prostate biopsy could be safely circumvented by combining the Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) from multiparametric MRI and quantitative data from PET. Methods: This study included 79 patients with suspicion of csPCa based on elevated prostate-specific antigen (>4 ng/mL) who underwent 18 F-flotufolastat PET/MRI before biopsy or surgical resection of the prostate. Analytic methods included receiver operating characteristic analysis, logistic regression, and threshold-based evaluation of PI-RADS and of SUV max Imaging findings were compared against histopathology. Results: csPCa (International Society of Urological Pathology grade group ≥ 2) was confirmed in 42 patients, whereas histopathology excluded csPCa in 37 patients. The combination of PI-RADS and SUV max resulted in an area under the curve (AUC) of 87.1%, outperforming PI-RADS alone (AUC of 75.2%) and SUV max alone (AUC of 80.7); however, differences were not statistically significant. A PI-RADS score of at least 3 and 18 F-flotufolastat PET showed comparable sensitivity (0.90 vs. 0.91) and specificity (0.42 vs. 0.32) in the detection of csPCa, when applying a low SUV max threshold (>4.5). Using a high SUV max threshold (>10.0) increased the specificity of 18 F-flotufolastat PET to 100%. Furthermore, combined PET/MRI increased the number of patients for whom csPCa can be reliably diagnosed to 28%, as well as increasing to 29% the number of patients for whom csPCa can be ruled out with a very high degree of certainty. Conclusion: This retrospective analysis suggests that prostate-specific membrane antigen PET/MRI can stratify patients with suspected prostate cancer into 3 groups: one with a very high likelihood of csPCa who may undergo definitive therapy without biopsy, one with a very low risk for csPCa who may not require biopsy, and an indeterminate group who still need biopsy. Overall, in our cohort, prostate biopsy would have been avoided in 57% of patients. Therefore, there is an urgent need for prospective studies on prostate-specific membrane antigen PET/MRI to reduce the number of unnecessary biopsies in men with suspected prostate cancer.

title: [ 68 Ga]Ga-SSO120 PET/CT Imaging in Pediatric Patients with Neuroblastoma: Biodistribution and Whole-Body Radiation Dosimetry.
abstract: The clinical standard for neuroblastoma detection is based on targeting the norepinephrine transporter with [ 123 I]MIBG, which has several challenges. Imaging the somatostatin receptor (SSTR) is a strong alternative. In contrast to standard DOTATATE, SSTR antagonist imaging with [ 68 Ga]Ga-satoreotide trizoxetan ([ 68 Ga]-SSO120) can potentially improve lesion detection as it targets both active and inactive SSTRs. We present the biodistribution and radiation exposure results of [ 68 Ga]Ga-SSO120 PET/CT imaging in pediatric patients with neuroblastoma. Methods: Patients age 3-7 y with stage 4 neuroblastoma received 2 MBq/kg of [ 68 Ga]Ga-SSO120, followed by a 60-min dynamic scan and a static PET/CT scan. SUV normalized to lean body mass (SUL max , SUL mean , SUL peak ) and time-activity curves were measured for suspected lesions and various tissue compartments. title: Theranostic Approach Using Radioiodinated Trimethoprim Targeting E. coli Dihydrofolate Reductase in Engineered Cells.
abstract: Radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) has re-emerged as a potent approach for targeting tumors, particularly for the treatment of neuroendocrine tumors and prostate cancer expressing the somatostatin and prostate-specific membrane antigen receptors, respectively. In addition to endogenously expressed proteins specific for these cancers, RPT has been explored using synthetic, engineered expression of proteins in tumor tissues. An early example of this was the use of sodium iodide symporter delivered to tumors using viral vectors, which were subsequently treated with [ 131 I]NaI. This approach is complicated by the natural uptake in human tissues that express sodium iodide symporter (e.g., the thyroid). However, given the rapid acceleration of gene and cell therapies, expansion and re-exploration of the synthetic, genetically engineered RPT paradigm is warranted. This is especially true for RPT, which can be coupled with PET companion imaging agents. Methods: Here, we developed a β-emitter radiotherapeutic probe, radioiodinated trimethoprim ([ 131 I]I-TMP), and evaluated its therapeutic potential. In addition, we developed [ 124/125 I]I-TMP radiotracers for uptake and imaging studies. The selective cytotoxicity of [ 131 I]I-TMP toward E. coli dihydrofolate reductase (eDHFR)-expressing cells was evaluated using time- and dose-dependent responses. Biodistribution was characterized in healthy mice followed by small-animal PET/CT studies using a tumor xenograft model and [ 124 I]I-TMP. Finally, the eDHFR synthetic RPT approach was applied in murine cancer models to evaluate its cytotoxicity in tumors. Results: Radioiodinated trimethoprim radiotracers ([ 131/125/124 I]I-TMP) exhibited selective uptake in eDHFR-positive tumors both in vitro and in vivo. Small-animal imaging with [ 124 I]I-TMP demonstrated specific retention in I45-eDHFR tumors with negligible background signals. A dose-dependent and time-dependent cytotoxic effect was observed selectively in eDHFR cell lines. Furthermore, targeted treatment with [ 131 I]I-TMP led to a significant reduction in tumor volume expressing eDHFR compared with wild-type tumors or untreated controls. Conclusion: This synthetic RPT approach shows promise for future applications in targeted cancer therapies and genetic medicine, particularly in the realm of theranostic strategies that integrate trimethoprim-based companion imaging and radiotherapy for the treatment of cancer.

title: End-to-End PET/CT Interpretation and Quantification with an LLM-Orchestrated AI Agent: A Real-World Pilot Study.
abstract: Although deep learning models have improved individual PET analysis, image processing, and quantification tasks, end-to-end automation from raw DICOM data to quantitative clinical reporting remains limited, particularly in heterogeneous real-world settings. Methods: As a proof-of-concept, an autonomous large language model (LLM)-orchestrated multitool agent for end-to-end PET/CT interpretation was developed. A reasoning-based, text-based LLM selected appropriate series from raw DICOM, coordinated registration and SUV conversion, invoked segmentation and detection tools, generated maximum-intensity projections, called a vision-enabled LLM for interpretation, and synthesized structured draft reports. The system was retrospectively evaluated in 170 patients undergoing baseline [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT for lung cancer staging, with clinical reports serving as the reference standard. Results: The agent successfully completed the full end-to-end workflow from raw DICOM selection to structured draft report generation without human intervention in all 170 examinations. Primary tumor detection achieved 100% sensitivity. For nodal involvement, sensitivity was 84.8% and specificity was 39.4%, whereas distant metastasis detection showed 70.2% sensitivity and 65.0% specificity. Discrepancy analysis of 58 nodal and 57 metastatic mismatch cases revealed systematic false-positive findings related to reactive or physiologic uptake and false-negative findings involving small-volume or anatomically atypical metastases. Conclusion: LLM-orchestrated PET/CT agents enabled workflow-level automation from raw DICOM to quantification and structured draft reporting under real-world conditions. Although primary tumor detection was highly reliable, nodal and metastatic assessment revealed systematic limitations, supporting a collaborative role with continued expert oversight in complex clinical scenarios.

title: Prognostic Value of a Composite Score Incorporating Baseline [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT and [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT When Screening for [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA Treatment Eligibility (PROFILE Study).
abstract: We investigated the prognostic value of baseline [ 18 F]FDG and [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617. Methods: In this multicenter retrospective study, the associations between several clinical, biologic, and radiologic parameters and overall survival (OS) were tested in a development cohort using univariable analyses, followed by the construction of a multivariable Cox model. The PROFILE prognostic score was subsequently derived from this model, internally validated, and externally validated in an independent cohort. Results: Data from 174 patients from 3 centers were used to construct the multivariable Cox model. Five independent adverse prognostic factors were identified and incorporated into the PROFILE score: an SUV max exceeding 300% of the PERCIST threshold on [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT, a "nonhigh" classification on [ 68 Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET/CT using the visual PSMA tumor-to-salivary gland ratio, a baseline hemoglobin level of 11 g/dL or less, a baseline alkaline phosphatase level of greater than 220 IU/L, and a disease duration not exceeding 100 mo. The PROFILE score stratified patients into 3 risk groups and achieved a Harrell C-index of 0.67 (95% CI, 0.62-0.72). The median OS in the low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups was 17.2, 13.0, and 8.6 mo, respectively ( P < 0.0001). These results were confirmed in 114 patients in an independent, single-center validation cohort, with median OS of 20.4, 14.3, and 8.8 mo ( P < 0.0001), respectively, and a C-index of 0.73 (95% CI, 0.68-0.78). Conclusion: The PROFILE score offers valuable prognostic information for patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer when considering the use of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 therapy.

title: Prognostic Value of <sup>68</sup>Ga-NOTA-AE105 uPAR PET/CT in Resected Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Single-Center Prospective Study.
abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer shows wide variability in outcomes after curative-intent resection. 18 F-FDG PET/CT is indispensable for staging but primarily reflects glucose metabolism rather than the invasion-related tumor biology that may contribute to recurrence. 68 Ga-NOTA-AE105 PET/CT images the urokinase-type plasminogen activator receptor (uPAR), a cell-surface mediator of local invasion and metastatic spread. We assessed whether preoperative 68 Ga-uPAR PET/CT is prognostic for postoperative recurrence. Methods: We conducted a single-center cohort study of patients with resectable lung adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma who were prospectively enrolled to undergo preoperative 68 Ga-uPAR PET/CT in addition to standard-of-care 18 F-FDG PET/CT. Primary tumor SUV mean and SUV max were measured for both tracers, and tumor tissue uPAR expression was quantified by immunohistochemistry (H-score). Postoperative recurrence was the primary endpoint and was analyzed in a competing-risks framework with death as a competing event. The primary prognostic analyses evaluated 68 Ga-uPAR SUVs, 18 F-FDG SUVs, and uPAR H-score as continuous variables using univariable cause-specific Cox models. A 1.5-y horizon was used for exploratory Youden-derived high versus low groups, for which cumulative incidence of recurrence was estimated using the Aalen-Johansen method. Trial registration number is NCT02755675 Results: Thirty-seven patients comprised the analysis cohort, of whom 14 developed recurrence during a median follow-up of 2.38 y (interquartile range, 1.97-8.20 y). Four patients died without prior recurrence. 68 Ga-uPAR uptake correlated with tumor tissue uPAR expression, whereas 18 F-FDG uptake did not. As continuous prognostic factors, higher 68 Ga-uPAR SUV max (hazard ratio, 2.16; 95% CI, 1.34-3.49; P = 0.002) and higher uPAR H-score (hazard ratio, 1.04 per unit; 95% CI, 1.01-1.08; P = 0.017) were associated with recurrence; 68 Ga-uPAR SUV mean showed borderline evidence of association ( P = 0.053), whereas 18 F-FDG uptake was not prognostic. Exploratory 1.5-y threshold analyses showed greater early recurrence in the high SUV mean and high H-score groups; the SUV max comparison did not reach statistical significance. Conclusion: Preoperative 68 Ga-uPAR PET uptake reflected tumor uPAR expression and was associated with early postoperative recurrence, whereas 18 F-FDG uptake was not prognostic in this cohort. These findings suggest that uPAR PET captures invasion-related tumor biology that is not fully reflected by glucose metabolism imaging. External validation is required.

title: Evaluating Interim Progression: First Posttherapy 177 Lu-PSMA SPECT/CT Relative to Baseline PSMA PET/CT.
abstract: Prostate Cancer Working Group 4 recommends using prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET for response assessment of patients with androgen pathway receptor modulator-resistant prostate cancer treated with 177 Lu-PSMA-617. For that purpose, the time interval between baseline PSMA PET and initiation of therapy is critical as interim disease progression may influence the performance of PET as a response assessment tool. Methods: We visually assessed the frequency of interim disease progression seen on the first posttherapy 177 Lu-PSMA-617 SPECT/CT in 87 patients with androgen pathway receptor modulator-resistant prostate cancer. The time interval between baseline PSMA PET and initiation of therapy, pretherapy prostate-specific antigen (PSA) measures, and treatment outcomes between patients with or without interim progression on SPECT/CT were also compared. Results: For the 32 patients (36.8%) with interim progression, the PET to therapy interval (88 d) was significantly greater than those without progression (42 d, P < 0.001) despite adjusting for age, Gleason grade, and PSA doubling time. A time interval between baseline PSMA PET and initiation of therapy exceeding 30 d was seen in approximately 94% of patients with interim progression. PSA response and overall survival were not impacted by interim progression. Conclusion: Baseline PSMA PET may not represent the true disease status if the first cycle of 177 Lu-PSMA-617 occurs more than 30 d after baseline PET.

title: <sup>18</sup>F-BMS-986192 PET to Predict Durable Response to Nivolumab in NSCLC: A Novel Approach Beyond PD-L1 Immunohistochemistry.
abstract: Programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunohistochemistry, the current standard biomarker for predicting response to programmed death protein 1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitors in non-small cell lung cancer, has moderate predictive value among others because of tumor heterogeneity and limited biopsy representation, whereas PD-L1 PET/CT using 18 F-BMS-986192 enables noninvasive, whole-tumor assessment of PD-L1 expression and heterogeneity, potentially improving prediction of response to immunotherapy. Methods: In this prospective multicenter biomarker exploration study, patients with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer eligible for nivolumab-based therapies underwent baseline 18 F-BMS-986192 PET/CT, 18 F-FDG PET/CT, and tumor biopsy for PD-L1 immunohistochemistry before treatment initiation. The primary endpoint was durable clinical benefit, defined as progression-free survival (PFS) of 9 mo or greater, with secondary analyses assessing associations among tracer uptake, PD-L1 expression, survival outcomes, and PET-based radiomic features. Results: Of 91 enrolled patients, 77 were included in the final analysis of 18 F-BMS-986192 PET/CT. Although PD-L1 immunohistochemistry did not differ between patients with PFS of less than 9 mo versus 9 mo or greater, PD-L1 PET uptake in lung lesions was significantly higher in patients with PFS of at least 9 mo ( P = 0.01). Using an optimal mean SUV peak cutoff of 2.4, PD-L1 PET demonstrated a high negative predictive value (94%) for durable clinical benefit, with significant associations for both PFS and overall survival, particularly in patients receiving first-line treatment. title: Head-to-Head Comparison of 18 F-SynVest-1 PET and 18 F-FDG PET in the Differentiation of Patients with Cognitive Decline.
abstract: Although 18 F-FDG PET is commonly used in the differential diagnosis of cognitive decline, synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A PET may offer a more direct assessment of synaptic integrity and address limitations associated with 18 F-FDG, such as sensitivity to sensory stimuli and glycemic variations. In this study, a head-to-head comparison of 18 F-SynVesT-1 and 18 F-FDG was performed for differentiating causes of cognitive decline in a tertiary clinical setting. Methods: Patients with cognitive decline referred for 18 F-FDG PET were recruited to undergo 18 F-SynVesT-1 PET/MRI (49 ± 26 d after 18 F-FDG PET). Diagnosis was determined by routine clinical follow-up (median, 11 mo) and classified as Alzheimer disease (AD), frontotemporal degeneration (FTD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), other neurodegenerative disorders (ONDs), or nonneurodegenerative disorders (NoNDs). Volume-wise and voxelwise semiquantitative analyses were performed using tracer-specific healthy volunteers. Diagnostic accuracy for both tracers was evaluated through logistic regression and by consensus from 3 readers. Noninferiority was defined by an area-under-the-curve margin (ΔAUC) of -0.10 within a 95% CI, using the clinical follow-up diagnosis as the gold standard. Results: Ninety-four patients were included: 44 with AD, 12 with FTD, 4 with DLB, 5 with ONDs, and 29 with NoNDs. Volume-wise and voxelwise analyses showed that, in patients with AD and DLB, reductions in the temporoparietal and precuneus/posterior cingulate were less pronounced with 18 F-SynVesT-1 PET than with 18 F-FDG PET (e.g., posterior cingulate in AD, -10% vs. -20%). In FTD, the most impacted areas showed greater variability, typically affecting the anterior temporal and frontal cortices, depending on the FTD subtype. Visual assessment showed lower sensitivity for AD with 18 F-SynVesT-1 PET than with 18 F-FDG PET (0.57 vs. 0.73) with equal specificity (0.76), whereas quantitative analysis yielded a lower area under the curve (0.71 vs. 0.81; ΔAUC, -0.10; 95% CI, -0.21 to 0.01). For FTD, 18 F-SynVesT-1 visual classification yielded similar sensitivity and specificity (0.58 and 0.90) compared with 18 F-FDG (0.50 and 0.93) but a lower quantitative area under the curve (0.64 vs. 0.76; ΔAUC, -0.12; 95% CI, -0.27 to 0.04). Conclusion: 18 F-SynVesT-1 PET enabled accurate classification of disease-specific patterns of cognitive decline. Although classification performance for FTD was similar to that of 18 F-FDG PET, the lower effect size in neocortical binding resulted in lower sensitivity for AD. Larger study samples are needed to formally evaluate tracer noninferiority in this clinical context for all subgroups.

title: A Phase 2, Open-Label, Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating Safety and Efficacy of Dose-Intensified Versus Standard Dosing Regimens of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-597 in mCRPC (OPTIMAL-PSMA).
abstract: OPTIMAL-PSMA aims to determine the safety and efficacy of a dose-intensified (intense induction followed by a maintenance period) regimen of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-597 compared with the standard-of-care regimen (every 6 wk for up to 6 doses) in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). Methods: OPTIMAL-PSMA is a phase 2, open-label, 2-arm, multicenter, randomized controlled trial of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-597, a novel prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) peptide with low nontarget organ dosimetry. A total of 120 patients with mCRPC will be enrolled and randomized 2:1 to receive either a dose-intensified regimen (arm 1) or the standard-of-care regimen (arm 2) of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-597. Eligible participants must have mCRPC with disease progression after androgen receptor pathway inhibitor therapy, have received or are not considered medically fit for docetaxel chemotherapy, and demonstrate PSMA-avid disease on PET/CT. Participants assigned to arm 1 will receive early intensified [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-597 dosing (7.5 or 8.5 GBq on the basis of an interim safety assessment) on days 1, 3, and 15 and during weeks 10, 20, and 30 (6 doses). All participants in arm 2 will receive the standard dose of 7.5 GBq of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-597 administered every 6 wk until they are no longer clinically benefiting, for a maximum of 6 doses. Clinical and laboratory safety assessments will be conducted 3 times weekly, with diagnostic CT and bone scans performed at 8 wk and then every 12 wk until radiographic progression. Translational studies incorporate serial multiple-time-point circulating tumor DNA matched with SPECT/CT dosimetry at each time point and PSMA PET at baseline and 8 wk for correlation with clinical outcomes. The primary endpoint is a 90% or greater decline in prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level. Key secondary endpoints include the safety of intensified dosing, a 50% or greater decline in PSA level, radiographic and PSA progression-free survival, and overall survival. Translational endpoints include evaluation of serial circulating tumor DNA, biologic effective dose with intensified versus standard dosing of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-597, and evaluation of serial SPECT/CT and PSMA PET/CT for treatment response. Conclusion: OPTIMAL-PSMA will determine whether a dose-intensified regimen of [ 177 Lu]Lu-PSMA-597 is safe and improves depth of response and survival outcomes compared with the standard dosing regimen. The results of this study may redefine the optimal treatment scheduling for PSMA-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy for patients with mCRPC.

title: Radiopharmaceutical Therapy with [<sup>177</sup>Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in Refractory Meningiomas: Results from the French Multicenter MELUTE Cohort.
abstract: Evidence supporting the efficacy and safety of [ 177 Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in refractory meningiomas derives mainly from small, single-center studies. The French national multicenter MELUTE study aimed to consolidate these data using a standardized regimen within a compassionate-use program approved by a national multidisciplinary tumor board. Methods: In this retrospective multicenter cohort study, patients with refractory meningiomas treated with [ 177 Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in 18 French centers between July 2022 and December 2024 were included. Treatment consisted of 7.4 GBq every 8 wk for up to 4 cycles. Clinical data (demographics, histologic World Health Organization grade [WHO], prior treatments, number of cycles, toxicity, progression, survival status as of October 1, 2025) were collected. Baseline [ 68 Ga]Ga-DOTATOC PET and brain MRI scans obtained before and after treatment were centrally reviewed. The primary endpoint was 6-mo progression-free survival (PFS) assessed using volumetric Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology Group criteria. Secondary endpoints were PFS, overall survival (OS), and safety. Results: Sixty-nine patients were included (mean age, 65.1 ± 13.2 y; 52% female): 13 WHO grade 1, 42 WHO grade 2, 8 WHO grade 3, and 6 without histology. Most had prior surgery (86%) or radiotherapy (93%); 32% received prior systemic therapy. Twelve patients (17%) did not complete 4 cycles; only one discontinuation was toxicity-related. Six-month PFS was 70% (95% CI, 58.7-80.4%). Median PFS was 14.6 mo (95% CI, 13.3-18.5 mo), and median OS was 27.6 mo (95% CI, 24.2 mo to not reached). Grade 3 adverse events, mainly lymphopenia, occurred in 16%. Meningioma WHO grade independently predicted PFS, whereas higher Karnofsky performance status and corticosteroid use were protective; worse OS was associated with higher baseline tumor growth rate and prior systemic therapy. Conclusion: MELUTE demonstrates promising efficacy and favorable safety of [ 177 Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in refractory meningiomas with limited therapeutic options.

title: Preclinical PET Imaging of Trastuzumab Deruxtecan in Tumors with Heterogeneous HER2 Expression.
abstract: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) has clinical activity in human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-low and -ultralow tumors in addition to HER2-positive tumors. However, no consistent correlation has been observed between traditional HER2 scoring criteria and response to T-DXd in HER2-low and HER2-ultralow tumors. There is a need for complementary approaches to monitor T-DXd delivery in vivo and potentially improve understanding of which tumors may benefit from T-DXd therapy. This study evaluated tumor uptake of radiolabeled T-DXd in tumors with varying HER2 protein levels using PET in treatment-naïve tumors and during T-DXd therapy. Methods: Chelator-conjugated T-DXd or trastuzumab was prepared via conventional lysine conjugation and radiolabeled with 64 Cu. The binding and in vitro cytotoxicity of the conjugates were determined in cancer cell lines. PET/CT was performed across 11 tumor models (representing 5 tumor types), including cell xenografts, patient-derived xenografts, and syngeneic models in both subcutaneous and orthotopic models. Image-based tumor uptake of the radiolabeled antibodies was quantified in all models. In the treatment studies, mice bearing CT26-hHER2 tumors that express heterogeneous HER2 with an immunohistochemistry score of 2+ levels received weekly coinjections of therapeutic T-DXd (6 mg/kg) together with imaging-dose [ 64 Cu]Cu-NOTA-T-DXd (4 mg/kg), corresponding to a total T-DXd administered dose of 10 mg/kg. Results: [ 64 Cu]Cu-NOTA-T-DXd was obtained at a radiochemical purity of at least 98%. Purified [ 64 Cu]Cu-NOTA-T-DXd bound to cells in a concentration-dependent manner and had a positive correlation between HER2 protein levels and bound T-DXd. Conjugation of T-DXd to NOTA did not affect T-DXd binding or cytotoxicity in cancer cells. [ 64 Cu]Cu-NOTA-T-DXd mean tumor uptake varied across models (7.45 ± 1.28 to 19.10 ± 2.50 %ID/mL), and the mean uptake was similar to that of the parental antibody 64 Cu-labeled trastuzumab. Preimaging doses of either trastuzumab or pertuzumab did not affect [ 64 Cu]Cu-NOTA-T-DXd uptake in tumors. There was a positive correlation between the change in [ 64 Cu]Cu-NOTA-T-DXd uptake and the change in tumor volume between weeks 1 and 2 of T-DXd treatment ( P < 0.01) in CT26.hHER2 tumors grown in immunocompetent mice. Conclusion: [ 64 Cu]Cu-NOTA-T-DXd PET detects antibody-drug accumulation in tumors with low HER2 protein levels and may provide an early imaging biomarker associated with response. These studies show the potential of using HER2-targeted imaging in preclinical models to noninvasively assess antibody-drug conjugate delivery and explore imaging-based biomarkers associated with T-DXd response.

title: Test-Retest Repeatability of [<sup>18</sup>F]FDG Uptake by Solid Tumors on PET/MRI: A Prospective, Multicenter Study Using the QIBA Protocol.
abstract: Prior oncologic PET/MRI repeatability studies have been limited by single-center designs, small cohorts, or select patient populations. Our primary aim was to estimate the test-retest repeatability of uptake metrics on [ 18 F]FDG PET/MRI studies across a variety of cancer types. A secondary aim was to assess the impact of intersession μ-map variability on repeatability. Methods: In this prospective study involving 2 institutions with different PET/MRI scanners, subjects completing standard-of-care [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT or MRI examinations were recruited to undergo 2 research [ 18 F]FDG PET/MRIs (i.e., test and retest) within a 1-9 d period per Quantitative Imaging Biomarker Alliance specifications. Enrollment required at least 1 measurable lesion (long axis ≥ 2 cm, known or expected SUV max ≥ 4.0) and no active oncologic therapy. SUV max and SUV peak were extracted from measurable lesions (1-5 per subject). At site 1, attenuation-coefficient maps (i.e., μ-maps) were inspected for substantial differences across sessions. Additionally, at site 1, the retest μ-map was coregistered to the test μ-map, and the PET attenuation-correction process was repeated for the test session based on the retest μ-map. Intersession repeatability was assessed via Bland-Altman plots, and within-subject coefficients of variation (wCVs) were calculated. Results: At site 1, 10 subjects with 11 measurable lesions were analyzed, and the wCVs for SUV max and SUV peak were 12.3% and 9.6%, respectively. At site 2, 11 subjects with 30 measurable lesions were analyzed, and the wCVs for SUV max and SUV peak were 9.5% and 8.8%, respectively. At site 1, repeating attenuation correction of the test PET data with the retest μ-map slightly improved repeatability, reducing the wCV to 10.1% for SUV max and to 9.1% for SUV peak For 8 of 11 lesions at site 1, the μ-map substitution altered the test-retest change by less than 5%, with no appreciable intersession μ-map differences or artifacts. Conclusion: The test-retest repeatability of SUV max among hypermetabolic lesions on [ 18 F]FDG PET/MRI, using data from 2 scanner models, was similar to the Quantitative Imaging Biomarker Alliance's wCV benchmark of 10%-12% for [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT. Intersession μ-map variations had minimal negative impact on repeatability.

title: β-Cell Mass and Function, Pancreatic Volume, and Fat Differences Between Short- and Long-Duration Type 1 Diabetes: A Detailed PET/CT Imaging Study.
abstract: People with recent-onset diabetes often have preserved C-peptide production, which tends to decline during the first 7 y after diagnosis and stabilizes thereafter. Whether this holds true for β-cell mass is unknown. In this pooled post hoc analysis, we aimed to investigate total β-cell mass in individuals with short- and long-duration type 1 diabetes. Methods: Data of 16 individuals with short- (<7 y) and 10 with long-duration type 1 diabetes (≥7 y) who underwent [ 68 Ga]Ga-NODAGA-exendin-4 PET/CT and mixed-meal tolerance test were used to determine total β-cell mass and function, respectively. Intrapancreatic fat deposition and pancreatic volume were derived from CT. Results: Total β-cell mass was higher in individuals with short-duration type 1 diabetes compared with those with long-duration type 1 diabetes (4.4 ± 1.8 vs. 2.8 ± 1.3 kBq/MBq, P = 0.012). Larger pancreatic volume, lower intrapancreatic fat deposition, and higher β-cell function were observed in individuals with short-duration type 1 diabetes compared with the long-duration group. Total β-cell mass positively correlated with β-cell function ( r = 0.46, P = 0.019) and pancreatic volume ( r = 0.91, P < 0.0001) and inversely correlated with body mass index ( r = -0.61, P = 0.0009). Conclusion: This study offers insights in the potential of imaging markers together with function tests to monitor disease progression and may offer valuable information for the timing to restore β-cell function or to slow down β-cell destruction.

title: B7H3-Targeted Molecular Imaging for Highly Specific Diagnosis and In Vivo Noninvasive Detection of B7H3 in Breast Cancer.
abstract: B7 homolog 3 (B7H3) is widely expressed in solid tumors, but its role in the diagnosis of breast cancer is unclear. We aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of [ 68 Ga]Ga-B7H3-BCH PET/CT in breast cancer patients. Methods: Thirty patients with diverse subtypes of breast cancer underwent both [ 68 Ga]Ga-B7H3-BCH and [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT. Immunohistochemical staining for B7H3 was performed in 25 patients. Results: B7H3 positivity was detected in 84% of samples by immunohistochemistry. [ 68 Ga]Ga-B7H3-BCH demonstrated a higher lesion detection rate compared with [ 18 F]FDG (96.8% vs. 92.4%) among 157 lesions. Median SUV max was 9.5 in strongly positive lesions; bone metastases had the highest uptake (median SUV max , 10.9). Imaging resulted in changing the stage or treatment in 8 patients. Hormone receptor-positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative lesions showed the highest B7H3 positivity (87.5%) and uptake (median SUV max , 10.5). Conclusion: [ 68 Ga]Ga-B7H3-BCH PET/CT offers high sensitivity for staging advanced breast cancer and noninvasive B7H3 screening. It may influence clinical decisions and appears to reveal subtype-specific uptake, with a tendency to favor hormone receptor-positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative disease.

title: [<sup>18</sup>F]DOPA PET Reveals Metabolically Active Transcriptomic States Associated with Clinical Outcome in Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors.
abstract: [ 18 F]fluorodihydroxyphenylalanine ([ 18 F]DOPA) uptake is dependent on amino acid transport and decarboxylation pathways, including large neutral amino acid transporter 1, encoded by SLC7A5 , which are linked to tumor aggressiveness. This study evaluated whether in vivo uptake of [ 18 F]DOPA can serve as an imaging biomarker for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (panNETs), reflecting a tumor's transcriptional status and a patient's clinical course. Methods: This retrospective single-center study was based on a transcriptomic cohort of 74 primary panNETs. A subset of 22 panNETs from patients who underwent preoperative [ 18 F]DOPA PET/CT constituted the discovery radiotranscriptomic cohort. [ 18 F]DOPA tumor uptake was quantified using SUV max and integrated with matched RNA-sequencing data. Unsupervised clustering, differential expression analysis, gene set enrichment, and tumor microenvironment deconvolution were performed to identify transcriptional programs associated with [ 18 F]DOPA uptake. The prognostic value of SLC7A5 was evaluated in the discovery cohort, the full transcriptomic cohort ( n = 74), and an independent external cohort ( n = 33). Results: Unsupervised clustering of gene expression profiles identified 2 robust molecular subtypes: cluster 1 and cluster 2. Cluster 1 showed higher [ 18 F]DOPA uptake than did cluster 2, with a median SUV max of 24.3 versus 5.9, respectively ( P = 0.030), and was associated with more advanced clinicopathologic features and shorter event-free survival. This subtype was also characterized by enrichment in extracellular matrix, stromal, vascular, and immune-related components, along with upregulation of amino acid transport and amine metabolism genes, including SLC7A5 As a mechanistic link between tracer uptake and tumor metabolism, SLC7A5 expression significantly stratified event-free survival in the discovery cohort and remained prognostic in the full cohort. Conclusion: [ 18 F]DOPA PET uptake was associated with amino acid-driven metabolic programs in panNETs, including SLC7A5 expression, and adverse clinical features. These findings suggest that [ 18 F]DOPA uptake may provide a noninvasive readout of tumor metabolic activity, although its value as an imaging biomarker requires independent validation.

title: Clinical Value of [ 68 Ga]Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT Versus [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT for Primary Staging of Gastroesophageal Adenocarcinoma: Results from a Prospective Northern European Trial.
abstract: Previous studies have demonstrated promising results for radiolabeled fibroblast activation protein inhibitor (FAPI) PET/CT in gastric cancer (GC) when compared with [18F]FDG PET/CT. In this prospective clinical trial, we assessed the impact of [68Ga]Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT compared with [18F]FDG PET/CT and contrast-enhanced CT (ceCT) on primary staging and management of Danish patients with GC and gastroesophageal junction cancer (GEJC). Methods: Between February 8, 2024, and September 26, 2025, consecutive patients with GC or GEJC who were candidates for surgical resection and perioperative chemotherapy were included in this trial. [68Ga]Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT images were deidentified and presented to the treating clinicians after the trial, at which point [68Ga]Ga-FAPI-46 PET/CT-based staging and tentative patient management were determined. Results: Twenty patients were included in the trial, including 15 (75%) with GEJC and 5 (25%) with GC; all patients were diagnosed with adenocarcinoma. For the primary tumor, [68Ga]Ga-FAPI-46 and [18F]FDG PET/CT agreed in 18 (90%) of cases, and both modalities demonstrated a detection rate of 90% (95% CI, 68%-99%). For clinical nodal staging, ceCT detected more lymph nodes than did [68Ga]Ga-FAPI-46 PET and [18F]FDG PET alone (81 vs. 53 vs. 44, respectively). [68Ga]Ga-FAPI-46 PET did not detect additional lymph nodes beyond those detected with ceCT. Despite detecting fewer lymph nodes overall, [18F]FDG PET identified 6 additional lymph nodes in 5 patients, resulting in clinical nodal upstaging in 4 cases (20%) compared with both [68Ga]Ga-FAPI-46 PET and ceCT. [68Ga]Ga-FAPI-46 PET would have led to clinical metastatic upstaging in 4 patients (20%) because of the identification of potential distant metastases (1 peritoneal and 3 liver metastases), which would have resulted in a change in recommended patient management from curative-intent to palliative treatment in 3 patients (15%). Conclusion: The primary clinical value of [68Ga]Ga-FAPI-46 PET was its ability to detect distant metastases that were negative on [18F]FDG PET and ceCT, potentially impacting patient management. There were no obvious advantages in the evaluation of primary tumor and regional lymph nodes. Although the study population is relatively small and mostly consists of patients with GEJC, this study represents the first prospective investigation of consecutive patients in a well-defined, clinical northern European setting and indicates potential future roles for [68Ga]Ga-FAPI-46 PET in GC and GEJC.

title: Impact of PSMA PET/CT Staging on Long-Term Outcomes in Patients with Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: Results of a Large Single-Center Cohort.
abstract: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET/CT has become the gold standard for staging and restaging prostate cancer, with superior diagnostic accuracy over conventional imaging and established prognostic value. However, there are limited data on whether PSMA PET/CT-improved staging accuracy is associated with improved long-term patient outcomes. This study analyzes the association between PSMA PET/CT at primary staging and overall survival (OS), biochemical recurrence (BCR), and cancer-specific survival (CSS) in a large university hospital cohort at a center where PSMA PET/CT has been clinically available for over 13 y. Methods: This retrospective single-center study included all 11,146 patients with prostate cancer diagnosed between 2013 and 2023. The final analysis cohort consisted of 6999 patients, of whom 505 (7.2%) underwent PSMA PET/CT for primary staging. We classified patients into 3 groups using D'Amico risk classification. Survival analyses were performed using Kaplan-Meier methods and adjusted Cox regression models. To control for selection bias, propensity score matching and overlap weighting were applied. Landmark analysis addressed selection and immortal time biases, and Fine-Gray models accounted for competing risk of death in a BCR analysis. Results: PSMA PET/CT was associated with a longer time to BCR (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.51; 95% CI, 0.38-0.68; P < 0.001), longer CSS (HR = 0.37; 95% CI, 0.22-0.61; P < 0.001), and longer OS (HR = 0.54; 95% CI, 0.40-0.70; P < 0.001). PSMA PET imaging was associated with particularly better outcomes in high-risk patients, especially those treated with radiotherapy. In the radiotherapy group, the HRs were 0.42 for OS, 0.42 for BCR, and 0.25 for CSS (all P < 0.001), whereas no statistically significant association was observed in patients undergoing radical prostatectomy. As the formal interaction test between PSMA PET/CT and treatment modality was not statistically significant, this differential finding should be considered exploratory. Across all 9 sensitivity analyses, HRs were consistently below 1, indicating a uniform direction of benefit. Conclusion: The association observed in this large real-world cohort supports the clinical value of PSMA PET/CT for primary staging. Findings were particularly favorable among high-risk patients undergoing radiotherapy, although this subgroup difference should be interpreted as exploratory given the nonsignificant interaction test. These results support a potential role for PSMA PET/CT in improving patient selection and detecting oligometastatic disease, enabling higher precision in treatment planning.

title: 68 Ga-Labeled Dimeric Cyclic Peptide for Nectin-4-Targeted PET Imaging: From Preclinical Evaluation to First-in-Human Imaging in Breast Cancer.
abstract: Nectin-4 is an attractive target for molecular imaging and targeted therapy because of its overexpression in multiple malignancies. We developed a nectin cell adhesion molecule 4 (nectin-4)-targeted 68 Ga-labeled dimeric cyclic peptide PET tracer, [ 68 Ga]Ga-TDN1, for noninvasive imaging of nectin-4 expression. Methods: TDN1 was generated by click chemistry to conjugate 2 nectin-4-binding bicyclic peptides and was radiolabeled with 68 Ga. Binding affinity was assessed by surface plasmon resonance. Target specificity and tumor-targeting ability were evaluated by cell uptake, blocking, small-animal PET/CT, and biodistribution studies in nectin-4-positive and nectin-4-negative tumor models. [ 68 Ga]Ga-TDN1 was further compared with [ 68 Ga]Ga-N188 in preclinical models. After preclinical evaluation, [ 68 Ga]Ga-TDN1 PET/CT was investigated in a pilot first-in-human study in 6 patients with breast cancer and directly compared with [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT. Results: TDN1 showed high affinity for nectin-4 ( K D = 1.92 × 10 -10 M). In preclinical studies, [ 68 Ga]Ga-TDN1 showed specific uptake in nectin-4-positive cells and tumors, low uptake in nectin-4-negative models, and marked reduction in uptake under blocking conditions. Compared with [ 68 Ga]Ga-N188, [ 68 Ga]Ga-TDN1 showed higher tumor uptake and longer retention across multiple nectin-4-positive xenografts. In the pilot clinical study, [ 68 Ga]Ga-TDN1 was well-tolerated and showed favorable biodistribution and dosimetry. [ 68 Ga]Ga-TDN1 PET/CT revealed imaging performance comparable to that of [ 18 F]FDG PET/CT for primary tumors and most nodal metastases and demonstrated higher uptake and improved lesion detection in bone and liver metastases in selected patients. [ 68 Ga]Ga-TDN1 was a clinically translatable nectin-4-targeted PET tracer with high affinity, favorable pharmacokinetics, and specific tumor uptake. Preclinical and pilot clinical results supported further clinical evaluation of [ 68 Ga]Ga-TDN1 for noninvasive imaging of nectin-4 expression, particularly for assessment of metastatic disease.

title: An Infant Brain MR Image Segmentation Method with Attention Mechanism, Multi-Resolution Deep Supervision and Class Weight Tuning Strategy.
abstract: Background Infant brain tissue segmentation is critical for understanding early brain development and detecting neurodevelopmental abnormalities. However, accurate segmentation remains challenging due to partial-volume effects, imaging noise, and low contrast between tissues in isointense regions. Objective This study aimed to automatically segment infant brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) images into white matter, gray matter, and cerebrospinal fluid. Material and methods In this analytical study, we addressed the challenges of infant brain tissue segmentation. We proposed a deep, lightweight dense backbone architecture incorporating transition blocks. The backbone was enhanced with a spatial-channel attention mechanism to capture global dependencies and emphasize task-relevant features, as well as multi-resolution deep supervision to mitigate vanishing gradients and reduce overfitting. Moreover, we used class weighting strategy to deal with class imbalance and low contrast between brain tissues. Results Our method attains Dice similarity scores of 91.80%, 92.07% and 94.58% for white matter, gray matter, and cerebrospinal fluid, respectively. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations show that the proposed approach accurately segments infant brain MR images and reduces errors in isointense regions. Conclusion The results demonstrate that the proposed method precisely delineates infant brain tissues and effectively overcomes common segmentation challenges.

title: Optimizing embryo transfer management in cows: Ultrasound-based pre-transfer screening and management of non-eligible recipients.
abstract: A single pre-transfer ultrasound screening cannot capture dynamic changes from estrus to ovulation. This may leads to inaccurate recipient selection and undetected reproductive abnormalities in non-eligible cows. We established a dynamic ultrasound monitoring (DUM) protocol with examinations on estrus day D0 (estrus detection), D1 (ovulation confirmation), and D6 (morphological assessment of the corpus luteum [CL]), and provided stage-specific management for non-eligible recipients. A total of 2,329 cows were randomly assigned to a control group (n = 1,165; a single ultrasonographic evaluation at the time of embryo transfer [ET]) or DUM group (n = 1,164). Before ET, first-service cows received a Presynch11/Ovsynch protocol, whereas second- and third-service cows were either observed for estrus or treated with an Ovsynch protocol based on whether or not they were observed in estrus up to pregnancy diagnosis of the previous breeding. In the control group, all non-eligible cows uniformly received Ovsynch + timed artificial insemination (AI). In the DUM group, non-eligible cows received stage-specific treatments based on ultrasound findings. In both groups, non-eligible cows were subsequently bred only via AI. The DUM group had a higher proportion of reconfirmed pregnancies per ET (43.2% vs. 37.4%). Among DUM cows, larger follicle diameter on D0 increased the proportion of reconfirmed pregnancies per ET (OR = 1.504), while severe bleeding at transfer reduced it (OR = 0.464). The non-eligible rates were similar between groups (28.9% in the control group and 28.2% in the DUM group). In the control group, the reasons for non-eligibility were predominantly absent CL (70.9%) or poor CL quality (17.2%), based on the single D7 evaluation. In the DUM group, the reasons were distributed across time points: 31.6% on D0 (presence of a large CL), and on D6, 26.7% due to no CL and 23.4% due to poor CL quality. Among non-eligible cows, the DUM group had a higher proportion of pregnancies per subsequent AI (42.9% vs. 28.5%), fewer services per pregnancy (2.53 vs. 2.82) and shorter days open (130.10 vs. 135.88). The cost per successful pregnancy in eligible recipients was $78.69 lower in the DUM group than in the control group. In conclusion, the DUM protocol improves both ET success and subsequent fertility of non-eligible recipients, offering an efficient management strategy for dairy herds.

title: Survival disparities in primary malignant spine tumors: a national analysis of academic and community hospital care.
abstract: Objective Primary malignant osseous tumors of the mobile spine are rare and require complex, multidisciplinary care. Treatment outcomes may differ between academic and community hospitals due to variations in resources, expertise, and infrastructure. This study evaluates demographics, care delivery patterns, and clinical outcomes, including both short- and long-term survival, for patients treated at academic versus community cancer programs using the National Cancer Database. Methods A retrospective analysis of a prospectively maintained database was performed. Nine hundred forty-three patients diagnosed with primary malignant osseous tumors of the mobile spine between 2004 and 2017 were identified. Patients were stratified by facility type: there were 601 patients treated at academic comprehensive cancer programs (ACADs) and 342 treated at comprehensive community cancer programs (CCCPs). Demographic, treatment, and clinical data were compared using descriptive statistics. Outcomes included inpatient length of stay, time to treatment, 30- and 90-day mortality, vital status at last contact, and overall survival. A multivariable Cox proportional hazards model assessed factors associated with overall survival. Results Patients at ACADs were significantly younger and more likely to have private insurance. The size and histopathological composition of the tumors did not differ significantly between facility types. ACAD patients experienced significantly longer inpatient stays and longer time to radiation initiation among patients receiving radiation with documented start dates. Time to chemotherapy did not significantly differ (p = 0.91). Thirty- and 90-day mortality were comparable between facility types among eligible surgical cases. At last follow-up, a significantly greater proportion of ACAD patients were alive (50.2% vs 38.3%, p < 0.001), and the median time from diagnosis to last contact or death was longer at ACADs (40.8 vs 33.2 months, p = 0.001). In the primary multivariable Cox model, treatment at an academic facility was associated with improved overall survival (hazard ratio [HR] 0.766, 95% CI 0.627-0.937; p = 0.009). In a sensitivity model adjusting for histopathology rather than grade, this association was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (CCCP vs ACAD, HR 1.19, p = 0.081). Conclusions Patients treated at academic centers had longer inpatient stays and longer time to radiation initiation, yet academic facility treatment was associated with improved overall survival in the primary multivariable model. After accounting for histopathological subtype in sensitivity analysis, the facility-type association was attenuated, suggesting survival differences reflect both tumor biology and system-level care pathways.

title: Morphological subtypes of Chiari malformation type I and clinical outcomes after posterior fossa decompression.
abstract: Objective Chiari malformation type I (CM-I) is the most common structural hindbrain defect in humans and causes debilitating headaches and other neurological symptoms frequently requiring surgery. Although patients' brains have heterogeneous shapes, diagnosis is based on a single radiographic measure with only 1 available pathology-directed treatment. The authors sought to determine whether there are distinct morphological subtypes of CM-I and to determine whether patients with different subtypes differ in clinical response to neurosurgical decompression. Methods For this cohort study, 186 adult patients with CM-I (152 females, 34 males; mean age 40.6 years) with high-resolution T1-weighted MR images were retrospectively identified from the records of 2 large-volume tertiary care centers. Cerebellar morphology was measured by nonlinearly transforming T1-weighted MRI data to a template brain to generate cerebellar deformation maps, and spectral clustering was performed to identify morphological patient subtypes. Headache freedom after posterior fossa decompression (PFD) was compared between morphological clusters using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Results Three distinct morphological subtypes of CM-I were identified: cluster A was characterized by posteroinferior cerebellar fullness and platybasia; cluster B, by midline anteroposterior compression; and cluster C, primarily by tonsillar descent. Similar clusters were generated after random partitioning of patients, and cluster assignments using partitioned data and the full data set were significantly associated (p < 0.0001). After PFD, headaches were found to recur more frequently and sooner in patients with cluster B morphology (HR 6.0, 95% CI 1.5-22.9; p = 0.01). Conclusions These analyses suggest that there are different subtypes of CM-I in patients, with distinct cerebellar shapes that respond differently to PFD, indicating that global cerebellar morphology may inform more personalized evaluation and treatment of CM-I. Future research should involve independent validation of this cluster scheme, identification of genetic and other etiological factors responsible for phenotypic heterogeneity, and optimization of treatment for patients with cluster B morphology, which was observed here to be associated with less effective surgical outcomes. Broadly, implementation of automated statistical shape analysis may represent an effective method to identify clinically meaningful subgroups of diseases characterized by structural deformations.

title: Clinical cutoffs for plasma biomarkers to identify intracranial pathology in traumatic brain injury patients with Glasgow Coma Scale scores 13 to 15: a TRACK-TBI study.
abstract: The authors sought to identify plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and ubiquitin c-terminal hydrolase-L1 (UCH-L1) cutoffs corresponding to a range of high positive predictive values (PPVs) for detecting intracranial pathology on CT and detecting pathology on MRI (when CT is negative) in patients who present to a level I trauma center for TBI evaluation with Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores of 13-15. This is a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data from the Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury (TRACK-TBI) study, which is a longitudinal, observational study of patients with TBI who presented to one of 18 US level I trauma centers within 24 hours of injury. Blood samples were collected within 24 hours. Plasma samples were analyzed for GFAP (pg/mL) and UCH-L1 (pg/mL). The CT or MRI scan was considered positive (CT+, MRI+) if there was evidence of acute intracranial pathology related to TBI. Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis (AUC) was performed to evaluate the ability of day-1 GFAP and UCH-L1 to discriminate CT+ versus CT-, and CT-/MRI+ versus CT-/MRI-. A K-fold cross-validation procedure was used to identify GFAP cutoffs for predicting CT+ among patients with GCS scores of 13-15 and for predicting MRI+ among patients with GCS scores of 13-15 and CT- subjects, based on the adjusted PPV thresholds. Among the 1718 TBI participants with GCS scores 13-15, 633 (37%) had CT+ findings. Of the 1085 CT- participants, 608 underwent MRI at 2 weeks postinjury, of whom 154 (25%) had MRI+ findings. Day-1 GFAP had an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.82 (95% CI 0.80-0.84), and UCH-L1 had an AUC of 0.60 (95% CI 0.57-0.63) for discriminating CT+ from CT-. Day-1 GFAP had an AUC of 0.76 (95% CI 0.71-0.81) while UCH-L1 had an AUC of 0.60 (95% CI 0.55-0.65) for discriminating CT-/MRI+ from CT-/MRI-. For CT+ prediction, assuming a prevalence of 0.36 (from our data) and 0.1 (from the literature), the median GFAP cutoffs to achieve an adjusted PPV of 0.9 were 2879 (95% CI 2195-4704) and 5191 (95% CI 3779-5426), respectively. title: Magnetically guided microrobot via minimally invasive percutaneous cisternal access: a first preclinical evaluation.
abstract: Objective Magnetically guided microrobots could enable minimally invasive intracranial interventions by navigating CSF spaces without traversing brain parenchyma. However, clinical translation requires in vivo validation of delivery, control, retrieval, and short-term safety under realistic workflow conditions. The aim of this study was to assess the feasibility and initial safety of percutaneous cisterna magna access, microrobot navigation, and retrieval using an image-integrated electromagnetic coil platform in a large-animal model, targeting future application to Dandy-Walker malformation cyst fenestration. Methods In this Good Laboratory Practice-compliant ovine study, 7 male sheep were allocated to an MRI-only control group (n = 1), flexion control group (n = 1), and treatment group (n = 3; percutaneous cisternal access, deployment of a 3.5 × 7-mm Parylene-C-coated bladed microrobot with a neodymium core, magnetic navigation, scripted dwell, and retrieval), with 2 animals designated as alternates. Preoperative MRI was used for planning, with intraoperative cone-beam CT fusion and biplanar fluoroscopy. The follow-up period was 28 days and included daily observation, weekly neurological examination, and analysis of hematology/chemistry, intraoperative CSF, and terminal necropsy with histopathology. Outcomes were descriptive. Results The full workflow was completed in all 3 treated animals without conversion or rescue. Cannulation succeeded on the first attempt; continuous fluoroscopic visibility and stable magnetic control were maintained; and retrieval succeeded in a single maneuver. Postoperative recovery was uneventful, with weight gain and no neurological deficits over 28 days of follow-up. Laboratory values were within reference ranges except for 1 case of transient leukocytosis (day 0) that resolved. CSF was acellular/normal. Necropsy showed localized procedure-site changes only (dural fibrosis, thin adhesions in 2 of 3 treated animals). Histology revealed focal superficial vermian gliosis ≤ 2 mm in 2 of 3 treated animals without hemorrhage, necrosis, or off-target injury, and controls were within normal limits (1 case of minimal incidental axonal change in the flexion control). Conclusions Percutaneous cisternal delivery and retrieval of an untethered microrobot were feasible and tolerated in sheep, with localized tissue responses at 28 days. These findings support further studies focused on longer follow-up, workflow optimization, and disease-specific efficacy.

title: Diagnostic performance of bedside transcranial ultrasound after decompressive craniectomy: a comparative study with cranial computed tomography.
abstract: Objective The aim of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic effectiveness and accuracy of bedside transcranial ultrasonography performed through the craniectomy in diagnosing typical post-decompressive craniectomy (DC) complications, using cranial CT as the reference standard. Methods This retrospective study analyzed 88 consecutive patients who underwent DC between January 2023 and December 2024. In each case, bedside transcraniectomy ultrasonography (BTUS) was performed prior to CT imaging, and findings from both modalities were compared. Diagnostic agreement was evaluated using Cohen's kappa coefficient. The sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value were calculated for BTUS in identifying complications, including hematomas, hygroma, hydrocephalus, abscess, edema, and midline shift. Results BTUS has high diagnostic accuracy compared with CT, with overall sensitivities ranging from 59.4% (edema) to 100% (hematomas) and specificities between 94.2% and 100%. Strong or almost perfect agreement (κ > 0.8) was observed for most complications. The rate of false negatives was lowest for space-occupying lesions and highest for diffuse pathologies, such as edema. Negative predictive values remained above 80% for all major complication types. Conclusions BTUS provides a rapid, noninvasive, and readily available tool for the initial detection and monitoring of postcraniectomy complications. While it does not entirely replace CT in complex cases, it holds significant potential as a first-line screening and monitoring modality in neurosurgical intensive care settings. Bedside ultrasonography can significantly reduce reliance on CT scans, particularly in unstable or radiation-sensitive patients. Incorporating routine BTUS into post-DC monitoring protocols could enhance patient safety, expedite diagnosis, and optimize resource utlization in neurocritical care.

title: Cryoprobe to current practice: neurosurgical legacies of Dr. Irving S. Cooper in movement disorders.
abstract: Before the advent of levodopa therapy for Parkinson's disease, surgical lesioning of the motor thalamus or globus pallidus represented the primary therapeutic intervention for Parkinson's disease and essential tremor at a time when effective medical alternatives were severely limited. In this context, Irving S. Cooper directed one of the most prolific and controversial lesioning practices of the mid-20th century, performing thousands of procedures and documenting outcomes. Through chemopallidectomy, chemothalamectomy, and later cryosurgical techniques, Cooper investigated the relationship between basal ganglia targets and motor symptoms, establishing reproducible symptom-anatomy associations for tremor and rigidity. Cooper's work introduced a systematic approach to target selection that contrasted with earlier lesioning methods. His outcomes demonstrated alleviation of tremor and rigidity when lesions were accurately placed, while highlighting risks of bilateral procedures. Most notably, the cryogenic "test-freeze" method allowed reversible intraoperative physiological inhibition, enabling assessment of clinical benefit before permanent lesions. Although many techniques were later abandoned, principles derived from Cooper's work continue to shape contemporary practice. Modern neuromodulation strategies, including deep brain stimulation and MR-guided focused ultrasound, rely on symptom-based targeting paradigms established during the lesioning era. This vignette examines how Cooper's innovations informed modern targeting strategies and standards of safety in functional neurosurgery.

title: Brain network changes in patients with glioma-related epilepsy after frontal resection.
abstract: Objective Clinical factors such as IDH status, preoperative seizures, and frontal tumor location influence the prognosis of postoperative glioma-related epilepsy (GRE), but the underlying network-level mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to identify network-based predictors of postoperative GRE. Methods The authors retrospectively analyzed 109 patients with frontal glioma (76 left sided). All patients underwent preoperative and 1-week postoperative resting-state functional MRI and diffusion tensor imaging. Changes in network characteristics, including structural-functional coupling and functional connectivity (FC), were evaluated. Using the left-sided cohort as the training set, Cox proportional hazards regression analysis was applied to identify network-based risk factors for postoperative GRE and construct a predictive model. The right-sided cohort served as a validation set. Results Patients with postoperative GRE showed reduced structural-functional coupling between the dorsal attention network (DAN) and the frontoparietal network (FPN), along with decreased FC within and between these networks. Increased DAN-FPN coupling and higher FC between the lesional-hemisphere prefrontal thalamus and the whole brain were protective against postoperative GRE. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.785 in the training cohort and 0.922 in the validation cohort (both p < 0.0001). Conclusions Altered structural-functional coupling and FC between attention-related networks are associated with postoperative GRE in frontal glioma. Enhanced DAN-FPN coupling and thalamocortical connectivity may serve as protective network markers.

title: Spatial localization patterns in MRI-negative Cushing disease: a comparative pituitary heat map analysis.
abstract: Objective MRI-negative Cushing disease is challenging to treat due to difficulty with tumor localization and lower biochemical remission rates. Surgeons primarily rely on visual and tactile feedback to identify abnormal pituitary tissue. In this study, the authors analyzed intraoperative sketches of histology-confirmed corticotroph adenomas to compare the spatial distributions of MRI-positive and MRI-negative tumors. By characterizing these distribution patterns, the authors aimed to improve the localization and surgical targeting of MRI-negative pathology. Methods The authors retrospectively reviewed patients with Cushing disease who underwent microscopic transsphenoidal resection by the late Dr. Edward H. Oldfield at the authors' institution from December 2007 to March 2017. Patients were stratified into MRI-positive and MRI-negative cohorts. A standardized pituitary sketch visualizing both coronal and sagittal planes was used for postoperative documentation. For every patient, Dr. Oldfield annotated the anatomical location of the histologically confirmed corticotroph adenoma. Image acquisition, processing, and heat map-based spatial analysis were performed to assess cumulative tumor density. Spatial differences were evaluated with cluster-based correction for multiple comparisons. Surgical outcomes were then compared between the 2 cohorts. Results A total of 153 patients with Cushing disease and histologically confirmed pituitary corticotroph adenoma (133 MRI-positive and 20 MRI-negative adenomas) were analyzed. Baseline demographic and biochemical characteristics were similar across MRI status. Both cohorts demonstrated similar anatomical presentation, with over 50% of patients presenting with corticotroph adenomas in the anterior aspect of the pituitary gland. MRI-positive tumors were more likely to localize to the lateral and dorsal aspects of the anterior pituitary (p < 0.05). In contrast, MRI-negative adenomas showed no distinct area of increased prevalence. Postoperatively, the MRI-negative cohort had higher nadir cortisol levels (2.9 vs 1.5 μg/dl, p = 0.001) and increased reoperation rates (20% vs 3.8%, p = 0.027). Remission rates were lower in MRI-negative patients but not statistically significant (75.0% vs 91.0%, p = 0.050). Conclusions MRI-negative corticotroph adenomas were less frequently localized in the lateral and dorsal aspects of the anterior pituitary compared to MRI-positive tumors, with no distinct region of increased prevalence. These findings support a unique surgical strategy that leverages the anatomical distribution of histologically confirmed adenomas to guide gland exploration and resection of hidden tumors. While these observations may provide anatomical context for surgical exploration in radiographically occult disease, operative decision-making should remain guided by intraoperative findings and individual patient anatomy.

title: Quantitative MRI to assess baseline shunt flow in patients with hydrocephalus: a noninvasive tool to aid clinical decision-making.
abstract: Objective Hydrocephalus is a common yet serious condition, and ventricular shunts are used for lifesaving CSF diversion. Existing methods for shunt evaluation provide correlative/qualitative information, leading to commonplace clinical diagnostic challenges. The aim of this study was to determine accurate and noninvasive measures of volumetric CSF flow rates through ventricular shunts using the phase-contrast (PC) sequence in routine MRI for pediatric patients with hydrocephalus. Methods The authors conducted a prospective observational cohort study of patients with ventricular shunts who underwent a clinically indicated brain MRI and the adjunct PC-MRI shunt flow sequence at a single center between January 2023 and January 2024. At the study institution, PC-MRI has been integrated as a supplementary imaging technique to quantify shunt flow alongside fast protocol MRI for shunted patients. Clinical and imaging data were collected. Data distributions and paired changes in flow measurements over time were assessed using appropriate statistical tests. Results Overall, 207 patients (107 male, mean age 11.3 years [range 8 days-27 years]) who underwent PC-MRI were included; 98% had a VP shunt. The mean CSF flow rate was 9.9 ± 8 mL/hour (range 0.5-54 mL/hour). No significant differences were noted by age, sex, etiology of hydrocephalus, valve type, time interval since shunt placement, BMI, fronto-occipital horn ratio, and frontal horn or atrial width. Repeat PC-MRI was performed in 11 patients, and there was no significant difference in flow measurements between initial and follow-up images (p = 0.83) among these patients. PC-MRI identified alterations that accurately demonstrated failure in 3 patients and avoided unnecessary surgery in a fourth patient. Conclusions Addition of PC-MRI to routine imaging examinations in patients with ventricular shunts accurately and noninvasively measured CSF shunt flow. Flow rate data can provide supplementary information regarding shunt function and serve as a baseline for future comparison assessments. These findings suggest a role for routine acquisition of patient-specific baseline shunt flow measurement in shunted pediatric patients with hydrocephalus.

title: Near real-time intraoperative assessment of pituitary neuroendocrine tumors using stimulated Raman histology during endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery: comparison with conventional histopathology.
abstract: Objective Accurate intraoperative identification of adenomatous versus normal pituitary tissue remains challenging during surgery for pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (PitNETs), as both can appear similar macroscopically. Stimulated Raman histology (SRH) is a label-free optical imaging technique that provides high-resolution digital histological images of unprocessed tissue within minutes. This study evaluated the feasibility, diagnostic accuracy, and histopathological concordance of SRH compared with conventional hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining in PitNETs. Methods Adult patients (≥ 18 years) who underwent surgery for suspected PitNET were included. Fresh tissue samples from the tumor core and, when feasible, from peritumoral regions were analyzed intraoperatively using SRH followed by standard histopathological processing. A board-certified neuropathologist, blinded to clinical data, independently compared SRH and H&E images regarding diagnostic accuracy, tissue classification (adenomatous vs nonadenomatous), and histopathological features using a semiquantitative scoring system. Results A total of 28 patients were included, yielding 66 tissue samples for final comparative analysis. SRH imaging was feasible in all cases. SRH demonstrated excellent comparability with conventional H&E in 37 samples (56.1%), good comparability in 20 (30.3%), and low comparability in 9 (13.6%). No significant difference in comparability was observed between tumor core and peritumoral tissue samples (p = 0.409). SRH accurately depicted key histopathological features, including the loss of the lobular glandular structure in adenomatous tissue and connective tissue organization in surrounding structures. Characteristic subtype features-such as Crooke cells in corticotroph PitNET or perivascular tumor cell arrangements in gonadotroph PitNET-were also identifiable. Conclusions SRH showed high feasibility for intraoperative assessment of PitNETs, generating near H&E-quality digital images within minutes. It reliably enabled distinguishing tumor from normal gland tissue and detected tumor infiltration into adjacent structures. These findings support SRH as a useful aid to intraoperative decision-making in pituitary surgery, with future AI integration likely to further improve diagnostic speed and accuracy.

No significant difference in comparability was observed between tumor core and peritumoral tissue samples (p = 0.409). SRH accurately depicted key histopathological features, including the loss of the lobular glandular structure in adenomatous tissue and connective tissue organization in surrounding structures. Characteristic subtype features-such as Crooke cells in corticotroph PitNET or perivascular tumor cell arrangements in gonadotroph PitNET-were also identifiable.

Conclusions

SRH showed high feasibility for intraoperative assessment of PitNETs, generating near H&E-quality digital images within minutes. It reliably enabled distinguishing tumor from normal gland tissue and detected tumor infiltration into adjacent structures. These findings support SRH as a useful aid to intraoperative decision-making in pituitary surgery, with future AI integration likely to further improve diagnostic speed and accuracy.

title: Transforaminal endoscopic lumbar discectomy: an economically viable option for lumbar disc herniations? A hierarchical Bayesian analysis using time-driven activity-based costing.
abstract: Objective Transforaminal endoscopic lumbar discectomy (TELD) has yet to achieve widespread adoption, in large part due to an unclear understanding of cost drivers. Therefore, using time-driven activity-based costing (TDABC), the authors sought to 1) compare risk-adjusted differences in the true costs (not charges or reimbursement) of TELD versus open and tubular microdiscectomy, and 2) identify independent predictors of cost for TELD. Methods A retrospective cohort study (2020-2024) was conducted of all cases of TELD and microdiscectomy performed at a single institution. The primary exposure was procedure: TELD, open microdiscectomy, or tubular microdiscectomy. The primary outcome was cost, calculated using TDABC. Bayesian hierarchical regression was performed to 1) estimate risk-adjusted cost differences between procedures and 2) identify independent predictors of cost for endoscopy. Covariates included age, sex, American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) class, use of navigation, disc herniation (central/paracentral, foraminal/extraforaminal, or lateral recess/subarticular), number of decompressed levels, and surgeon. Results A total of 503 patients underwent TELD (113, 22.5%) or microdiscectomy (390, 77.5%) for lumbar disc herniation. After adjusting for confounders, TELD was significantly more expensive than both open microdiscectomy (mean difference [MD] $1105, 95% Bayesian credible interval [BCI] $846-$1392) and tubular microdiscectomy (MD $1012, 95% BCI $616-$1432), driven by greater cost of consumables, particularly access/navigation kits (i.e., spinal access kits, endoscopic portals) and specialized instruments (i.e., high-speed drills, endoscopic forceps). Personnel costs did not differ significantly across procedures. Factors independently associated with greater cost for endoscopy included use of intraoperative navigation, patient ASA class, and disc herniation location. Specifically, navigation increased total cost by approximately 29% (estimate 0.258, 95% BCI 0.158-0.358; > 99.9% posterior probability). Likewise, each 1-standard deviation increase in ASA class increased cost by 4.2% (estimate 0.042, 95% BCI 0.004-0.080; 98.4% posterior probability). Compared to foraminal/extraforaminal herniations, central/paracentral herniations increased cost by 7.4% (estimate 0.071, 95% BCI 0.000-0.140; 97.6% posterior probability). Conclusions TELD was more expensive than both open and tubular microdiscectomy, largely driven by more expensive consumables. Moreover, both modifiable and nonmodifiable factors were identified as independent drivers of cost for endoscopy. Continued refinement of technique and patient selection, along with targeted vendor negotiations to reduce consumable costs, may improve both the economic viability and overall utilization of endoscopy.
