title: Confined to Kambin's prism: MRI-based segmentation and prediction of the need for superior articular process removal in transforaminal endoscopic decompression.
abstract: Objective The endoscopic transforaminal lumbar approach offers reduced tissue disruption and faster recovery compared with other open and minimally invasive approaches but is limited by the narrow and variable anatomy of the transforaminal corridor. Degenerative changes such as superior articular process (SAP) hypertrophy can block safe access, forcing the surgeon to remove part of the SAP (foraminoplasty) either by reaming or drilling. This decision is often made subjectively or discovered intraoperatively. Recent advances in MRI-based nerve segmentation may provide an objective method to predict this need preoperatively. Methods The records of 23 patients who underwent endoscopic decompression and had high-resolution (≤ 2.4 mm) preoperative lumbar MR images were reviewed. The authors segmented neural and osseous structures using commercial planning software (Brainlab) and then placed a 6-mm virtual dilator along a simulated transforaminal trajectory to assess corridor patency. Operative reports and video confirmed whether SAP reaming was performed. Pre- and postoperative patient-reported outcomes were analyzed. Results Segmentation showed an unobstructed 6-mm corridor in 22 of 23 patients (96%). The single patient with a predicted obstruction had SAP hypertrophy and required reaming. The simulation and the operative report agreed in every case. On average, patients improved significantly in every recorded clinical outcome within 2 years postoperatively. The size of the surgical corridor had a mild positive relationship to positive surgical outcomes, although not significant. The single patient with reaming had greater magnitude of clinical score improvement compared with the other patients for physical health, Oswestry Disability Index, and leg and back pain, although the difference was not significant. Conclusions MRI-based segmentation accurately identified foraminal anatomy that required foraminoplasty for access. This workflow turns a subjective intraoperative judgment into a reproducible, patient-specific geometrical assessment.

title: Sacral spinal dural arteriovenous fistula: diagnostic pitfalls and treatment challenges. Illustrative case.
abstract: Background Sacral spinal dural arteriovenous fistulas (sDAVFs) are rare and easily missed on imaging, especially when supplied by internal iliac branches. Regional vascular anatomy may complicate endovascular treatment approaches. Observations A 71-year-old man with symptoms suggestive of spinal myelopathy underwent spinal MRI, which revealed multisegment T2 cord hyperintensity from T7 to L1 without serpiginous flow voids; spinal MR angiography (MRA) findings were negative for sDAVF. On spinal digital subtraction angiography (DSA), selective internal iliac injection identified a right S1 sDAVF originating from a lateral sacral artery branch. Transarterial Onyx embolization formed a plug proximal to the fistula, resulting in failed obliteration. Subsequent microsurgical disconnection via S1 laminectomy appeared successful on intraoperative ICG angiography, but postoperative angiography revealed residual shunting. Reexploration with L5 laminectomy allowed definitive microsurgical ligation, resulting in lasting cure at the 1-year follow-up. Lessons Negative spinal MRI/MRA findings do not rule out sacral sDAVF; complete spinal DSA, including internal iliac injection, is critical if sacral sDAVF is suspected. Sacral angioarchitecture may hinder durable embolization, warranting consideration of upfront microsurgical ligation. With ligation, intraoperative ICG angiography may miss residual flow; immediate postoperative angiography should be best practice. With microsurgical ligation, broad exposures may be ideal for identifying all arterialized veins. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26220.

title: Spinal intradural arachnoid cyst in an infant with motor developmental delay showing intraoperative MEP improvement: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Spinal intradural arachnoid cysts (SIACs) are relatively rare, but they can cause neurological symptoms. The authors report a case of an infant with an SIAC presenting with motor developmental delay, highlighting the intraoperative improvement of motor evoked potentials (MEPs). Observations A 14-month-old girl presented with a lower limb motor developmental delay. Spinal MRI revealed an SIAC at the C7-T4 level, compressing the spinal cord from the dorsal side. She underwent surgical fenestration of the cyst. Intraoperatively, transcranial MEP amplitudes in the lower extremities were initially lower than those in the upper extremities. Following cyst fenestration and decompression, the MEP amplitudes increased more than 10-fold compared to the baseline and were maintained. Postoperatively, her motor functions gradually improved. By 5 months after surgery, her developmental delay had resolved, and she achieved age-appropriate motor milestones. Lessons In this pediatric case of an SIAC, surgical decompression led to a significant and immediate increase in MEP amplitudes. This physiological change was followed by an improvement in the patient's motor development, suggesting that intraoperative MEP monitoring can be a useful tool for evaluating the immediate effect of decompression in infants with an SIAC. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26285.

title: Skull infarction and chronic subdural exudates in a pediatric patient with sickle cell anemia: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Skull infarction is a rare sickle cell disease (SCD) complication. While epidural hematomas from calvarial infarction have been sporadically reported, subdural collections and sterile exudates mimicking intracranial empyema remain poorly characterized. Observations A 6-year-old boy with nonverbal autism and SCD presented with progressive periorbital swelling, fever, and extremity pain. CT raised concern for orbital cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess, and subdural empyema. MRI revealed a diffuse heterogeneous calvarial marrow signal with multifocal nonenhancement and restricted diffusion consistent with bone infarction, alongside right convexity subdural fluid and bilateral epidural and subperiosteal rim-enhancing collections demonstrating susceptibility artifacts. Emergency craniotomy and orbital exploration yielded hemosiderin-stained fluid, and necrotic bone without purulence. All operative cultures were negative. Postoperative imaging demonstrated expansion of the subdural collection to 8 mm with 6-7 mm of midline shift, managed with dexamethasone. Nine months later, the patient re-presented with recurrent subperiosteal hemorrhage without infection. Lessons Calvarial infarction in SCD can produce sterile collections that mimic infectious processes. Intraoperative findings and culture data are essential in distinguishing these entities. Middle meningeal artery embolization warrants caution in SCD patients, given the risk of moyamoya vasculopathy. This case underscores the importance of a broad differential when evaluating SCD patients with periorbital swelling and intracranial collections. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26291.

title: Hemorrhagic lumbar synovial cyst mimicking a neoplastic process: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Synovial cysts with extensive hemorrhage, marked mass effect, and tumor-like appearance are rare and may mimic neoplastic processes. Observations A 56-year-old man presented with progressive mechanical low back pain, neurogenic claudication, gait instability, and bilateral weakness. MRI revealed a 2.0-cm lesion arising from the right L3 facet joint, causing severe central canal and right foraminal stenosis with displacement of the cauda equina. Imaging features suggested pigmented villonodular synovitis. Intraoperatively, however, the lesion appeared fleshy, partially encapsulated, and dural adherent, resembling a nerve sheath tumor, with necrotic regions suggesting malignancy. Frozen-section analysis demonstrated benign fibroconnective tissue with marked reactive and degenerative changes, including necrosis and hemosiderin deposition, without evidence of neoplasia. Intraoperative confirmation of benign pathology shifted operative priorities toward anatomical preservation rather than extent of resection; gross-total removal was nevertheless achieved and the patient had complete neurological recovery. Permanent pathology was most consistent with a degenerative synovial cyst with hemorrhage. Lessons This case highlights the importance of integrating imaging findings, intraoperative appearance, and histopathological evaluation rather than relying on a single diagnostic modality. The combination of a focused differential and confirmation of benign pathology guided the extent of resection, balancing maximal lesion removal with preservation of adjacent structural elements. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26317.

title: Spindle cell oncocytoma: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Spindle cell oncocytoma (SCO) is a rare, nonadenomatous sellar tumor that often mimics pituitary adenomas both radiographically and clinically, making diagnosis and treatment difficult. Observations A 67-year-old male presented with fatigue and weakness, with MRI revealing an enhancing sellar mass with suprasellar extension and laboratory findings consistent with panhypopituitarism. He underwent endoscopic endonasal resection, which revealed a fibrous, highly vascular tumor adherent to surrounding tissue, consistent with SCO on final pathological analysis. Gross-total resection (GTR) was achieved, and the patient has been monitored regularly with no signs of recurrence at 9 months postoperatively. Lessons SCOs are an exceedingly rare entity often indistinguishable from pituitary adenomas preoperatively, yet their intraoperative hypervascularity and fibrous texture can complicate resection and predispose patients to recurrence. Accurate identification of these tumors and GTR when possible are essential to appropriate treatment. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26333.

title: Delayed intraparenchymal pneumocephalus causing internal capsule injury after endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery for recurrent Rathke's cleft cyst: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Pneumocephalus is a rare but serious complication after endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery (ETSS), usually associated with CSF leakage and occasionally progressing to tension pneumocephalus. Delayed intraparenchymal pneumocephalus causing focal brain injury after ETSS for recurrent Rathke's cleft cyst (RCC) is exceptionally rare. Observations A 74-year-old woman underwent ETSS for recurrent RCC and was discharged on postoperative day (POD) 10 after an uneventful early course. On POD 37, she developed sudden left hemiparesis and mild dysarthria. Head CT demonstrated pneumocephalus extending from the sella toward the right internal capsule without rhinorrhea. With conservative management, the pneumocephalus gradually resolved, revealing parenchymal injury involving the posterior limb of the right internal capsule on CT and MRI. She later reported repeated nose blowing after discharge, including on the morning of symptom onset. Intraoperative endoscopic review revealed a depression in the anterior perforated substance, anatomically corresponding to the ruptured RCC and subsequent injury site. Lessons In recurrent or ruptured RCCs, occult communication between the sellar region and adjacent brain may permit air entry after postoperative Valsalva maneuvers. Strict counseling, recognition of high-risk parenchymal findings, and airtight multilayer reconstruction with a vascularized mucosal flap may reduce this risk. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26647.

title: Quantitative, longitudinal measurements of response to immunotherapy for glioblastoma using multiparametric MRI in a long-term survivor treated with autologous tumor lysate-loaded dendritic cell vaccine: an illustrative case.
abstract: Background Neurosurgeons are in the forefront of developing clinical trials that harness the immune system to combat glioblastoma. Autologous tumor lysate-loaded dendritic cell vaccine (DCVax-L) is a novel immunotherapy for glioblastoma. An unmet need is to develop a sensitive, specific, feasible, clinically relevant, neuroimaging biomarker that accurately reflects response to immunotherapy. Observations This illustrative case involves a 63-year-old female who survived for 64 months following near-total resection of a glioblastoma and enrollment in a clinical trial (NCT00045968) using DCVax-L. A multivariate logistic regression model was used to assess treatment response longitudinally at 11 time points measuring predictive probability (PP) of tumor progression based on diffusion tensor imaging- and perfusion-weighted imaging-derived parameters within the contrast-enhancing region. Lesions were considered true progression (TP) if the PP was ≥ 50% and pseudoprogression (PsP; predominant treatment effects) if the PP was < 50 %. These findings were subsequently validated by histopathological analysis during resection for tumor recurrence. Lessons These findings support the use of multiparametric MRI to monitor the effects of immunotherapy in patients with glioblastoma. Such multiparametric prediction models using noninvasive, advanced neuroimaging may be helpful to differentiate TP from PsP in longitudinal assessment of treatment response. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26655.

title: Spinal subependymoma mimicking an intradural extramedullary tumor: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Spinal subependymomas are rare, benign tumors that typically arise within the spinal cord and usually appear as intramedullary lesions on MRI. The authors report a rare case of cervical spinal subependymoma with exophytic growth that mimicked an intradural extramedullary tumor on MRI. Observations A 53-year-old man presented with right-sided paresthesia. MRI revealed a spinal tumor causing marked spinal cord compression. The lesion was isointense on T1-weighted images, slightly hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and showed no gadolinium enhancement. A focal CSF cleft between the tumor and spinal cord led to a preoperative diagnosis of an intradural extramedullary tumor, and schwannoma was suspected. However, intraoperative pathological examination suggested a low-grade glioma, prompting a change in the surgical strategy. Subtotal resection was therefore performed to preserve neurological function. Histological examination subsequently confirmed the diagnosis of subependymoma. Lessons Spinal subependymoma may rarely present with an apparent intradural extramedullary appearance on MRI. The presence of a CSF cleft and exophytic growth should not exclude an intramedullary origin. Awareness of this atypical presentation and avoidance of anchoring bias are essential for appropriate intraoperative decision-making. When subependymoma is suspected, maximal safe resection should be prioritized over aggressive tumor removal to preserve neurological function. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26728.

title: Endoscopic transorbital approach for resection of Meckel's cave aspergillosis: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Aspergillosis involving Meckel's cave (MC) is rare. Only 5 previous case reports exist in the literature. The primary treatment for this disease is surgical debridement combined with antifungal therapy. The authors present a minimally invasive technique using an endoscopic transorbital approach (ETOA) to manage this condition. Observations A 26-year-old male corn farmer presented with progressive right-sided facial pain and numbness for 1 month. MRI demonstrated a markedly hypointense T2 signal lesion in the right MC with gadolinium enhancement. CT revealed sphenoid sinus opacification with bony erosion. Nasal endoscopy with sphenoidotomy and mucosal biopsy were noncontributory. He underwent an ETOA via lateral canthotomy. Irregular yellowish rubbery tissue adherent to all divisions of the trigeminal nerve was resected. Histopathological analysis confirmed septate fungal hyphae. The fungal culture identified Aspergillus flavus. After 6 months of voriconazole, the facial pain resolved despite persistent numbness, and MRI demonstrated radiological resolution of the lesion. The patient remained free of recurrence at 1 year. Lessons MC aspergillosis can present as trigeminal neuropathy in immunocompetent patients. The ETOA provides direct extradural access permitting tissue diagnosis and debridement without temporal lobe retraction. Combined with antifungal therapy, this approach may be a feasible strategy for this disease. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26736.

title: Postoperative epidural fluid collection mimicking epidural abscess: illustrative cases.
abstract: Background After craniotomy, fluid may accumulate in the surgical bed, raising suspicion for hemorrhage, abscess, or postoperative pseudomeningocele. Typically, peripheral contrast enhancement, internal restricted diffusion, and adjacent edema are consistent with infection. Observations The authors present 4 cases with postoperative epidural fluid collections mimicking epidural abscesses on MRI with restricted diffusion on diffusion-weighted imaging. Three of these cases were associated with adjacent brain edema. The fluid appeared 1-3 months after the surgery on routine follow-up MRI in the absence of clinical symptoms, and nearly resolved, either spontaneously without treatment or with conservative therapy alone. Given imaging findings concerning for infection in the absence of symptoms, diagnosis and management were challenging. Lessons When there is increased epidural fluid collection after craniotomy, radiographic findings may mimic abscess, but they are not always clinically significant. Clinical assessment is a crucial component of the diagnosis to avoid unnecessary intervention, and follow-up imaging is recommended. The pathogenesis of this restricting, enhancing fluid collection remains unclear. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26757.

title: Robust foreign body giant cell reaction after polymethyl methacrylate cranioplasty: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Foreign body giant cell reaction to a cranioplasty implant is a rare complication of this common neurosurgical procedure, and it may cause clinically significant symptoms. Here, the presentation, imaging, management, and pathology of a patient who developed a robust fibroinflammatory reaction to a polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) cranioplasty implant are reviewed to aid with future timely diagnosis and management of this complication. Observations A 38-year-old male who previously underwent decompressive craniectomy after a gunshot wound to the head with subsequent PMMA cranioplasty presented 1 month postoperatively with surgical site swelling and fevers. MRI demonstrated a subgaleal fluid collection and an epidural mass. The patient was initially treated empirically with antibiotics but remained febrile and developed worsening headache. The patient underwent surgical removal of the implant with excision of fibrovascular tissue after interval MRI demonstrated enlargement of the epidural mass. Intraoperative cultures were negative, and pathological evaluation confirmed the diagnosis of fibrovascular granulation tissue with foreign body giant cell reaction. Postoperatively, the patient's symptoms resolved. Lessons Fibroinflammatory reactions to synthetic cranioplasty materials can mimic surgical site infections, but key imaging, laboratory, and clinical findings can support the diagnosis. Timely treatment with surgical removal of the implant may be curative. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE26817.

title: Awake craniotomy with functional mapping for recurrent high-grade IDH-mutant glioma during pregnancy: illustrative case.
abstract: Background Although gliomas during pregnancy are rare, they present significant clinical and ethical challenges due to the potential effects of pregnancy on tumor behavior and the risks associated with the standard of care. Given the peak incidence of IDH-mutant glioma in the 3rd and 4th decades of life, clinicians face a challenge in balancing maternal oncological outcomes with fetal safety, while navigating the uncertainty surrounding the effects of standard treatment modalities on fetal development. Observations A 31-year-old woman at 23 weeks of gestation with a history of IDH-mutant glioma presented to the authors' institution with worsening neurological symptoms. MRI indicated tumor progression, and re-resection was performed via awake craniotomy with functional mapping. The maternal-fetal medicine team was consulted to guide the selection of anesthesia and optimize intraoperative positioning, ensuring the safety of both the patient and fetus. Postoperative recovery was uneventful, with stable maternal and fetal outcomes. Pathological analysis confirmed progression to a grade 4 astrocytoma. Lessons This case highlights the feasibility of awake craniotomy with functional mapping during pregnancy. Management of gliomas in pregnancy requires a multidisciplinary approach, balancing maternal health and fetal safety, with careful consideration of treatment timing and anesthetic strategies. https://thejns.org/doi/10.3171/CASE2696.

title: Decoding MRI Presentation of Primary Central Nervous System Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma: A Novel Subgroup Perspective.
abstract: Background and purpose Primary central nervous system Epstein-Barr virus-negative diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PCNSL) of immunocompetent patients is an aggressive extranodal lymphoma with challenging imaging features. In a large histopathologically confirmed cohort, we aimed to update conventional MRI characteristics of PCNSL, identify radiologic subtypes, and explore early survival differences across subgroups. Materials and methods We retrospectively evaluated the consecutive cohort of immunocompetent patients diagnosed with PCNSL who presented to our lymphoma unit between 2010 and 2023, enrolling patients with available prebiopsy 1.5T or 3T brain MRI including T1-weighted, T2-weighted, FLAIR, DWI, and postcontrast T1 sequences. Two neuroradiologists independently assessed lesion characteristics (number, location, morphology, volume, signal). Unsupervised hierarchical clustering was applied to identify radiologically homogeneous subgroups. Associations between subgroup and progression-free/overall survival were assessed using Cox regression in prespecified models adjusted for age, sex, International Extranodal Lymphoma Study Group score, and induction regimen. Results We enrolled 100 patients (median age 63.9 years, 51% women). Lesions were multifocal in 55% and involved only supratentorial brain in 66%, both supratentorial and infratentorial compartments in 28%, and only infratentorial in 6%. Morphology was predominantly mass-like (75%). Median volume was 5.5 mL (interquartile range 2.0-14.9). Relative to brain cortex, T2 signal was hypointense in 63%, isointense in 21%, and hyperintense in 16%; T1 was isointense in 50%, hypointense in 44%, and hyperintense in 6%. Enhancement was solid in 74%, patchy in 7%, closed-ring in 4%, and mixed solid-patchy in 15%. Hierarchical clustering identified 4 subgroups according to radiologic characteristics: 1) classic mass-forming (40%): supratentorial, T2-hypointense, solidly enhancing masses; 2) CSF surface-predominant (22%): ependymal, intraventricular, or cortical-pial locations with homogeneous enhancement; 3) infiltrative (20%): small enhancing foci with extensive T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and perivascular enhancement; and 4) atypical mass-forming (18%): large, heterogeneous lesions enriched in necrosis and hemorrhage. Adjusted overall survival differed across subgroups in exploratory analyses ( P = .02), with higher mortality in CSF surface-predominant and infiltrative patterns and lower mortality in the atypical mass-forming group compared with classic mass-forming. Conclusions This study updates MRI features of PCNSL and identifies 4 radiologic subgroups, offering a basis for future molecular correlations and prognostic stratification.

title: Microcephaly with Simplified Gyral Pattern in Children: Quantitative Morphometric Assessment on Brain MRI and Correlation with Clinical Outcome.
abstract: Background and purpose Microcephaly with simplified gyral pattern (SGP) represents an often subtle subtype of malformation of cortical development that is commonly accompanied by epilepsy and neurodevelopmental delay. However, whether gyral simplification scales to reduced brain volume and whether MRI features predict clinical outcome still remain unclear. The aims of this study are therefore to apply a quantitative morphometric approach to distinguish a simplified gyral pattern from microcephaly-related effects and to correlate quantitative MRI-derived features with clinical outcome. Materials and methods From a single-center cohort of 34 patients with microcephaly and visually confirmed SGP (shallow sulci, normal cortical thickness), 18 subjects (mean age 7.1 ± 6.5 years) who fulfilled the eligibility criteria were retrospectively included for final analysis. Twenty-six age- and sex-matched healthy controls were included. GM/WM volumes (GMVs/WMVs) and surface-based measures were derived using FreeSurfer. Scaling corrections based on log-log robust regression and cortical folding analyses were subsequently analyzed. Principal component analyses clustered along morphometric phenotypes. ANCOVA, Kendall τ correlations, and logistic regression were applied to evaluate group differences and clinical outcome predictors. Results Compared with healthy controls, patients showed significantly reduced WMV, cortical surface area, local gyrification index (LGI) (all Q < 0.003), and mildly increased cortical thickness. Allometric modeling indicated that, although WMV and LGI scaled proportionally to total brain volume, cortical surface area was disproportionately reduced, suggesting deviation beyond microcephalic scaling. Spectral folding analysis showed loss of specifically macroscale (primary) folding power. Morphometric clustering separated 4 subtypes differing in cortical thickness and area, of which the cluster with the lowest surface area and LGI exhibited universal developmental delay and included both early deaths. Across the cohort, neurodevelopmental delay correlated negatively with surface area. Logistic regression suggested lower surface area, WMV, and LGI as predictors of adverse clinical outcome ( Q < 0.02). Conclusions The presence of SGP may reflect additional disturbance of primary sulcation and tangential cortical expansion beyond scaling to microcephaly alone. Our results suggest reduced cortical surface area as a key morphometric marker and a strong MRI feature predictive of neurodevelopmental delay, underscoring the clinical value of quantitative morphometry for stratifying disease severity in microcephaly with an SGP.

title: The Superficial Subplate as an In Vivo Imaging Biomarker of Normal Cortical Development in Humans: A 3T MRI Feasibility Study.
abstract: Background and purpose The superficial subplate (sSP) forms the interface between the cortical plate and the deeper subplate, as a transient sublamina prominent during mid-fetal development of the human brains when many cortical malformations originate and prenatal counseling is needed. Our aim was to assess the visibility of the sSP throughout development using in vivo 3T fetal MR images in the human brain. Materials and methods In this retrospective observational study, 51 human fetuses (19-36 gestational weeks [GWs]) medically assessed as neurotypical were imaged on a 3T MR scanner in vivo, using single-shot, fast spin echo T2-weighted sequences, and images in 3 planes were selected. Three readers twice assessed the visibility of the sSP on the selected images in the region of the frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes. To explore the relationship between the visibility of the sSP and gestational age, we used regression analysis. A quadratic model was applied to investigate the nonlinear association between visibility scores and fetal age. The interobserver agreement on the visibility of the sSP was scrutinized both pair-wise and among all 3 raters. Weighted κ statistics determined inter- and intrarater agreement. Results The visualization of the sSP on in vivo fetal 3T MRI was possible between 19 and 27 GWs, in 1 or more lobes, (the frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital), with optimal visibility between 20 and 27 GWs, coinciding with the peaks in glycosaminoglycan expression in the sSP. Interrater agreement ranged from moderate to excellent (weighted κ = 0.57-0.93), with a mean κ of 0.81 (SD, 0.10 on first assessment, improving to κ of 0.88 with SD, 0.03 on second assessment). Intrarater agreement was good to excellent (κ = 0.75-0.90). Conclusions The sSP is visible on T2WI on in vivo fetal MRI at 3T. A deeper understanding of the in vivo appearance of the laminar organization of the human fetal brain, including the sSP, is required to accurately interpret altered fetal brain development, thereby improving early diagnostic accuracy, reducing false-positive assessments, and supporting prenatal counseling in cases of suspected cortical malformations.

title: Volumetric Postcontrast T1 Turbo Spin-Echo vs Gradient-Recalled Echo MR Sequences for Detecting Brain Metastases: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background Contrast-enhanced 3D T1-weighted MRI is the imaging reference for detection and follow-up of brain metastases. Volumetric GRE-based sequences, such as MPRAGE, are widely used but remain prone to susceptibility and lower lesion conspicuity. 3D black-blood TSE-based sequences, such as sampling perfection with application-optimized contrasts by using different flip angle evolutions (SPACE), have been increasingly embedded into routine workflow and are thought to improve lesion detection in part through vessel signal suppression. Purpose We aimed to investigate the comparative diagnostic performance of 3D T1 TSE vs GRE sequences for the detection of brain metastases. Data sources Studies comparing the diagnostic performance of postcontrast 3D T1 TSE and GRE sequences in adults with brain metastases were searched on MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Central, Google Scholar, and PROSPERO, from inception through April 2025. Study selection Fifteen studies encompassing 544 patients with 4338 metastases were included. Data analysis Data on diagnostic accuracy parameters, image quality, and interrater agreement were extracted. Random-effects models were applied to compute pooled sensitivity and comparative OR for lesion detection. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 and QUADAS-C tools. Data synthesis Pooled sensitivities for detection of brain metastases were 97.4% (95% CI, 93.2%-99.0%) for TSE- and 76.1% (95% CI, 69.3-81.9) for GRE-based sequences, with a comparative OR of 12.0 (95% CI, 5.45-26.6; P < .0001). Detectability of small lesions (<5 mm) was significantly better on TSE (96.1%; 95% CI, 87.7-98.8) than GRE (58.4%; 95% CI, 47.9-68.2), although both techniques performed comparably for larger (≥5 mm) lesions (98.2% for TSE, 94.4% for GRE). OR estimates were 17.2 (95% CI, 4.50-66.1) for small and 2.81 (95% CI, 0.92-8.56) for large lesions. Contrast-to-noise ratio and interrater agreements were slightly higher on TSE than GRE. False-positives (FPs) were more common with TSE, mostly related to incomplete vessel suppression (49 FP counts in TSE, 35 in GRE). Limitations Our meta-analysis is limited by high heterogeneity, case-only studies, possible small-study effects, and high risk of bias for the reference standard domain. Conclusions Postcontrast 3D T1 TSE sequences provide higher sensitivity and improved lesion conspicuity compared with GRE sequences, particularly for small metastases, although at the cost of slightly higher FPs.

title: Sacral Dural Tears in Spontaneous Intracranial Hypotension: Imaging Phenotype and Treatment Outcomes in a Multicenter Cohort.
abstract: Background and purpose Sacral dural tears are an underrecognized cause of spontaneous intracranial hypotension, and their clinical behavior and response to treatment remain incompletely defined. We hypothesized that outcomes following epidural patching in sacral dural tears are driven primarily by disease chronicity and baseline imaging features, mirroring patterns observed in other spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH) leak subtypes, and are less dependent on procedural variables. Materials and methods We performed a multicenter retrospective cohort study of patients with SIH attributed to sacral dural tears who underwent epidural patching and had clinical and/or imaging follow-up. Of 61 identified patients, 54 met inclusion criteria. Clinical outcomes, brain and spine imaging findings, and procedural variables were analyzed. Univariate and multivariable logistic regression models were used to identify predictors of clinical and imaging outcomes. Myelographic techniques were compared for rates of precise leak localization. Results The mean age was 37.8 years, and 85% of patients were women. Complete clinical improvement after patching occurred in 28 of 50 patients (56%), and complete resolution of sacral extradural CSF on follow-up spine MRI occurred in 17 of 37 patients (46%). Greater improvement in Bern score was independently associated with complete clinical improvement (OR 0.73; 95% CI, 0.54-0.99; P = .04) and showed a pattern toward imaging resolution. Unorganized baseline extradural CSF morphology predicted better clinical ( P = .03) and imaging ( P = .03) outcomes. Procedural variables, including injectate type, volume, and needle approach, were not associated with outcome. Dynamic CT myelography precisely localized the leak more frequently than digital subtraction myelography (75% vs 31%; P = .02). Eight patients underwent surgery, with mixed clinical and imaging outcomes. Conclusions Epidural patching outcomes in sacral dural tears causing SIH are driven primarily by baseline imaging phenotype, disease stage, and intracranial imaging response rather than procedural technique. These findings support a morphology- and chronicity-aware approach to diagnosis and treatment and suggest that sacral dural tears represent a distinct SIH subtype with outcome patterns similar to other leak mechanisms.

title: Deep Learning-Based Noncontrast CT Imaging Markers Enhance Posttransfer DWI Core Volume Prediction.
abstract: Background and purpose Deep learning enables the extraction of ischemic lesion size and hypodensity imaging markers from deep learning-based NCCT (DLNCCT) assessment in patients with acute ischemic stroke, but it remains unclear whether those markers can predict posttransfer core volume. Materials and methods We performed a post hoc analysis of prospectively enrolled patients transferred from a primary stroke center (PSC) to a comprehensive stroke center (CSC) for endovascular treatment (EVT). Using a validated DLNCCT segmentation method, we quantified total lesion volume (per 10 mL), modified net water uptake (mNWU %), and severely hypodense volume (≤26 Hounsfield units [HU] per 10 mL) and compared these markers with core lab rated ASPECTS (per point decrease) and CTP-based evaluation for their association with (adjusted regression coefficient [95% CI]) and predictive performance in addition to baseline variables ( R 2 ± SEs) for posttransfer CSC admission DWI core volume. Results We included 420 patients (239 [57%] men) with a median age of 72 years (interquartile range: 61-80). We observed 11.2 mL (95% CI, 8.3-14.1] larger posttransfer core volumes per point decrease in ASPECTS, and 10.0 mL (95% CI, 6.8-13.3), and 20.0 mL (95% CI, 12.7-27.2) larger posttransfer core volumes per 10-mL increase in total and severely hypodense DLNCCT volume, respectively. mNWU was not associated with posttransfer core volume ( P = .63). In addition to clinical baseline and CTA variables, posttransfer core volume prediction with ASPECTS ( R 2 : 0.49 ± 0.02) and DLNCCT ( R 2 : 0.50 ± 0.02) did not differ significantly ( P = .58). Compared with using CTP imaging markers ( R 2 : 0.56 ± 0.02), adding ASPECTS ( R 2 : 0.63 ± 0.02; P < .01) and DLNCCT ( R 2 : 0.65 ± 0.01; P < .01) improved performance for posttransfer core volume prediction. Conclusions Total and severely hypodense DLNCCT volumes are independent predictors for posttransfer core volume. These DLNCCT markers improved CTP-based posttransfer core volume prediction.

title: Dynamic Brain [ 18 F] Fluoroestradiol PET Protocol Optimization for Improved Detection of Breast Cancer Brain Metastases.
abstract: Background and purpose Brain [ 18 F] fluoroestradiol (FES) PET enables noninvasive assessment of estrogen receptor (ER) expression and may improve the detection of ER-positive (ER + ) breast cancer brain metastases (BC-BM), with pilot studies demonstrating clinical utility. Our aim was to leverage our dynamic brain [ 18 F] FES PET acquisition protocol to characterize BC-BM uptake kinetics across different postinjection intervals, with the goal of improving lesion detectability. Materials and methods Patients with ER + primary disease and BC-BM were enrolled prospectively and underwent dynamic [ 18 F] FES PET/CT and contemporaneous standard-of-care contrast-enhanced brain MRI. PET was acquired during 90 minutes using a dynamic protocol (34 frames). Four 15-minute static time windows were reconstructed, including 30-45, 45-60, 60-75, and 75-90 minutes after injection, respectively. MRI was used as the criterion standard for clinical lesion characterization and segmentation, with subsequent [ 18 F] FES PET co-registration. The time window-specific PET MRI lesion matching rate (LMR) and mean standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR, normalized to cerebellar cortex) were calculated. Results Eleven patients with a total of 92 MRI-confirmed lesions were included (73 parenchymal, 8 leptomeningeal, 6 calvarial, 4 dural-based, and 1 pituitary stalk). Time window-3 yielded the highest LMR at 68% (63/92 lesions), followed by time window-2 (62%), time window-4 (60%), and time window-1 (57%). The mean SUVR increased across time, with means of 1.83 (standard deviation [SD], 1.46), 2.08 (SD, 1.88), 2.29 (SD, 2.37), and 2.38 (SD, 2.50) for time window-1, -2, -3, and -4, respectively. Despite a higher SUVR at later time points, 8 lesions (6 parenchymal, 1 leptomeningeal, and 1 calvarial) that were visible at 60-75 minutes were undetectable at 75-90 minutes. Conclusions Time window-3 at 60-75 minutes after injection provided optimal LMR for brain [ 18 F] FES PET in ER + BC and suspected BM. Imaging beyond this interval may not further improve diagnostic yield and may reduce visibility. Limitations of this study include the small cohort size, population heterogeneity regarding prior treatment, and lack of pathologic confirmation. Our findings suggest that 60-75 minutes after injection may represent the optimal acquisition time window and highlight the importance of timing standardization for neuro-oncologic applications of brain [ 18 F] FES PET.

title: Fibrin-Heparin-Coated Intracranial Stents as Salvage Therapy in Pediatric Focal Cerebral Arteriopathy-Inflammatory Type.
abstract: Arterial ischemic stroke (AIS) in children is frequently associated with underlying arteriopathy. We report a 13-year-old boy with progressive AIS due to focal cerebral arteriopathy inflammatory type (FCA-i). Despite initial medical therapy, including antiplatelet agents, immunosuppressive therapy, antimicrobial treatment, and intra-arterial spasmolysis, he experienced clinical and radiographic deterioration. Endovascular therapy with balloon angioplasty and fibrin-heparin-coated intracranial stents achieved successful revascularization and stabilization. Vessel wall MRI and elevated Mycoplasma pneumoniae antibodies supported the diagnosis of FCA-i. Follow-up demonstrated sustained stent patency and vascular improvement, with persistent distal upper extremity-predominant hemiparesis.

title: Radiologic Phenotyping in Patients with SOX10 Pathogenic Variants: Insights into Neck, Brain, and Temporal Bone Abnormalities.
abstract: Background and purpose The SOX10 gene is essential for developing neural crest-derived tissues, including the temporal bone, peripheral and central nervous systems, and melanocytes. Pathogenic SOX10 variants are linked to a broad clinical spectrum, including Waardenburg syndrome (WS) in isolation, Kallmann syndrome (KS), as well as an entity characterized by the combination of peripheral demyelinating neuropathy, central dysmyelinating leukodystrophy, Waardenburg syndrome, and Hirschsprung disease (PCWH). This study aims to characterize the full spectrum of abnormalities in the brain, temporal bone, and neck regions, and their syndromic associations. Materials and methods Fifteen pediatric patients with genetically confirmed SOX10 germline pathogenic variants were included. All underwent MRI, and 9 also had CT of the temporal bone. Imaging and clinical data were systematically analyzed by 2 pediatric neuroradiologists. Results Phenotypic analysis revealed bilateral temporal bone abnormalities in all patients, mainly characterized by a specific combination of semicircular canal dysplasia/hypoplasia (with high prevalence of severely hypoplastic or absent posterior semicircular canal) and a very reproducible form of cochlear hypoplasia called flattened cochlea. Olfactory bulb agenesis or hypoplasia was identified in all but 2 patients. Other abnormalities include white matter changes suggestive of a hypomyelination pattern or deficient myelination in 4 patients and neck findings typically characterized by parotid gland aplasia/hypoplasia (15/15, 100%) or lacrimal gland aplasia/hypoplasia (13/15, 86%). Clinical phenotypes ranged from sensorineural hearing loss to WS type II or IV and PCWH. Conclusions These results confirm the strong correlation between pathogenic SOX10 variants and characteristic temporal bone malformations, which, in association with other radiologic abnormalities, represent highly specific diagnostic markers. The constellation of findings reflects the shared neural crest origin of the affected tissues and should always be investigated to support appropriate genetic testing. Early identification of these features via MRI can aid diagnosis, especially in children without classic syndromic signs, and support the patients' management.

title: Novel Neuroimaging Biomarker of Cortical Gray/White Border Integrity in Blast-Related Mild Traumatic Brain Injury.
abstract: Background and purpose Recent studies suggest that blast or mid-impact neurotrauma are characterized by scar-border forming astrogliosis at the gray-white matter junction. Individuals with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) and blast trauma have increased neuroinflammation and impairment of axonal remyelination on postmortem histopathology. However, there are currently only limited methodologies to use in the assessment of the cortical gray/white interface using in vivo neuroimaging. The purpose was to investigate the gray-white matter contrast (GWC) at the gray-white matter junction that may be linked to neuroinflammation/astrogliosis in the setting of blast exposure and/or mTBI, through 3D T1-weighted MPRAGE images. Materials and methods Post-9/11 veterans ( n =723) from the Translational Research Center for TBI and Stress Disorders completed MRI. Participants were grouped into 4 categories: participants with a history of blast-related mTBI (blast-mTBI), participants with a history of mTBI due to other mechanical forces (blunt-mTBI), participants with a history of close blast exposure but no mTBI, and those without a history of lifetime mTBI or close blast exposure. MRI data processing for morphometry and cortical surface mapping was done using FreeSurfer image analysis. Signal intensities in gray and white matter along the cortical and white matter interface were used to calculate mean GWC value. Results Veterans in the blast-mTBI group showed diffuse patterns of increased GWC relative to the other groups, particularly in the frontotemporal lobes. This effect was driven primarily by a greater number of high GWC regions in the blast-mTBI group compared with the no-neurotrauma and blunt-mTBI groups. Conclusions There was diffuse increased GWC on MR in the blast-mTBI group compared with the no-neurotrauma, close blast exposure, and blunt-mTBI groups. These findings may be linked to astrogliosis and neuroinflammation in patients with blast-mTBI. Histopathologic correlation with imaging findings will be necessary to better understand these effects.

title: Structured Vascular Segment Analysis for Giant Cell Arteritis: A Proposed Scoring System for CTA-Based Diagnosis.
abstract: Background and purpose Imaging for giant cell arteritis (GCA) has traditionally relied on ultrasound, MRI, and, more recently, nuclear medicine. CTA has not been systematically evaluated, despite near-universal availability, rapid acquisition, and comprehensive neck vessel assessment. We evaluated the ability of CTA to discriminate between patients with biopsy-proved GCA and age- and sex-matched controls by assessing cervical arterial abnormalities across multiple cervical arterial segments. Materials and methods This retrospective single-center study included 20 biopsy-proved GCA cases (with CTA performed within 4 weeks before or 2 weeks after biopsy) and 20 age- and sex-matched controls. Two neuroradiologists independently assessed 21 predefined arterial segments for abnormalities (absent/present). Segment-level positivity was defined by circumferential wall thickening, >50% stenosis/occlusion, or perivascular inflammatory fat stranding. Vessel-group-level involvement was through consensus positivity (both readers positive; either side). Per-patient total scores were evaluated with receiver operating characteristic analysis (DeLong area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC]), prespecified thresholds with secondary exploratory analysis through McNemar testing, and interreader agreement by percent agreement and Cohen κ. Results Median age was 76 years (interquartile range, 70-84 years); 60% were women in both groups. Across 806 evaluable segments, consensus involvement in GCA cases was most frequent along the maxillary (80%; 16/20), facial (75%; 15/20), and superficial temporal (70%; 14/20) arteries. Total-score discrimination was excellent (AUROC 0.971 for both readers). At total score ≥3, sensitivity/specificity were 0.90/1.00 for both readers, with paired differences favoring cases (exact McNemar P < .001). Pooled segment-level agreement was high (agreement 0.978; κ 0.924). Conclusions Structured multisegment CTA scoring of craniocervical arterial segments showed excellent discrimination of biopsy-proved GCA from matched controls, supporting CTA as a useful diagnostic tool in patients with GCA.

title: Clinical Presentation, Misdiagnosis, and Imaging Findings of Anterior Disc Herniations.
abstract: Anterior and anterolateral lumbar disc herniations are uncommon and usually do not present with classic radicular symptoms. This contributes to a broader and sometimes misleading differential diagnosis based on the initial presentation. When identified on cross-sectional imaging performed for nonspinal indications, displaced disc material can be mistaken for a retroperitoneal mass, potentially prompting additional imaging or invasive evaluation. We report 6 cases of anterior and anterolateral disc herniations identified on CT and MRI, including some patients presenting with abdominal or flank pain. Imaging demonstrated anterior disc extrusion, some with marked inflammatory changes. In some cases, the initial diagnosis included retroperitoneal neoplasm or an inflammatory process. Recognizing this imaging pattern and its clinical context may help accurate diagnosis, avoid unnecessary procedures, and guide appropriate management.

title: Whole-brain cortical morphometry and structural covariance network disruption in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis.
abstract: Background Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a progressive, fatal encephalitis caused by persistent measles virus infection. Quantitative cortical imaging in SSPE remains poorly characterised, and the topology of the cortical structural covariance network (SCN) has not been examined. Objective To characterise whole-brain cortical structural alterations in SSPE using surface-based morphometry (SBM) and voxel-based morphometry (VBM), evaluate their clinical correlates, and describe the topology of the cortical SCN. Methods Twenty-eight patients with SSPE and 48 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent 3.0 T volumetric T1-weighted MRI. SBM was performed in FreeSurfer using the Desikan-Killiany (DK) atlas, adjusted for age and sex; VBM used the FSL-VBM pipeline with threshold-free cluster enhancement, adjusted for age, sex and total intracranial volume. Clinical associations used Pearson correlation with false discovery rate (FDR) correction and Spearman sensitivity analyses; severity was quantified with the Neurological Disability Index. Group-level SCNs were constructed from age- and sex-adjusted regional thickness correlations; graph metrics were computed across 16 network densities and summarised as the area under the metric-versus-density curve, so that findings do not depend on a single arbitrary threshold. Group differences were assessed by subject-label permutation testing with bootstrap confidence intervals. Results VBM identified widespread bilateral grey matter volume reduction extending from cortex into deep grey matter and cerebellum, with additional right-lateralised clusters in the planum temporale and frontal pole. Vertex-wise SBM demonstrated 35 bilateral cortical thickness clusters and 21 cortical volume clusters; in the covariate-adjusted regional analysis, 38 of 68 DK regions showed significant thinning after FDR correction, and 18 of 68 regions showed significant volume reduction, most prominently the bilateral frontal pole and posterior cortices. Cortical thickness and volume correlated negatively with disease duration across most regions, but not with clinical severity. SCN metrics differed consistently in direction across all densities - longer characteristic path length, higher modularity and local efficiency, and loss of degree assortativity in patients - but no metric difference survived subject-label permutation testing after FDR correction (smallest adjusted p = 0.24); SCN findings are therefore reported as descriptive. Conclusions SSPE produces widespread, duration-dependent cortical thinning and grey matter volume loss involving association, limbic and primary cortices. Group-level SCN topology showed a consistent directional pattern of network reorganisation that did not reach corrected statistical significance at this sample size. Prospective, longitudinal and multi-centre studies are required before any clinical application of these measures can be considered.

title: Prompt volumetric responses following preoperative embolization of skull base meningiomas: association with intratumoral contrast enhancement loss.
abstract: Objective The role of preoperative embolization for skull base meningiomas remains controversial because potential surgical benefits must be balanced against endovascular procedural risks. Although embolization may induce early tumor volume reduction, evidence in skull base meningiomas remains limited. This study evaluated prompt volumetric responses after preoperative embolization and their association with intratumoral contrast enhancement loss on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Methods This retrospective study included 82 consecutive patients with skull base meningiomas who underwent preoperative endovascular embolization followed by surgical resection at a single institution between September 2013 and March 2025. Tumor volumes were measured on contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI obtained pre- and post-embolization. Individual volumetric responses were evaluated, and patients were categorized into four groups according to the degree of intratumoral contrast enhancement loss. Neurological complications were assessed. Results Tumor volume was significantly reduced after embolization (18.9 ± 14.2 mL vs 17.3 ± 13.7 mL, P < .001), with a mean reduction rate of 10.5 ± 12.4%, within a mean interval of 4.1 ± 1.8 days after embolization. Tumor volume decreased in 74 of 82 patients (90.2%). Volumetric responses exhibited substantial heterogeneity, ranging from -34.5% to 41.1%. Greater intratumoral contrast enhancement loss was associated with larger volume reduction rates (P = .04). Transient neurological complications occurred in 4 patients (4.9%), and permanent deficits occurred in 2 patients (2.4%). Conclusions Preoperative embolization of skull base meningiomas was associated with early tumor volume reduction within days, although the magnitude of response varied substantially among tumors. Intratumoral contrast enhancement loss on post-embolization MRI was associated with greater tumor volume reduction and may serve as a semiquantitative imaging correlate of reduced tumor vascularity/perfusion after embolization.

title: Third Ventricular Volume as an Adjunct Imaging Marker for CSF-Venous Fistulas Causing Spontaneous Intracranial Hypotension.
abstract: Background CSF-venous fistulas (CVFs) are an increasingly recognized cause of spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH); however, brain MRI findings may be normal in approximately 20% of patients, underscoring the need for additional imaging markers. This study aimed to evaluate third ventricular volume as an adjunct imaging biomarker for patients with CVF causing SIH, particularly in patients with low-risk conventional MRI findings. Methods A total of 32 patients with myelographically confirmed CVF who underwent pre-treatment brain MRI were included. Third ventricular volume and total ventricular CSF volume were measured and converted to age- and sex-adjusted normative percentiles (Combinostics, Tampere, Finland). Small third ventricular volume and low total ventricular CSF volume were defined as values below the 25th normative percentile. Findings were evaluated in the overall cohort and stratified by Bern score, with low-probability Bern score defined as 0-2. Results The mean age was 55.7 years, and 21/32 patients were female. Mean third ventricular percentile was 21.9 ± 27.2 and mean total ventricular CSF percentile was 35.4 ± 23.7. In the overall cohort, 22/32 patients (68.8%) had small third ventricular volume, whereas 10/32 patients (31.3%) had low total ventricular CSF volume. Among patients with Bern scores of 0-2, 5/10 patients (50.0%) had small third ventricular volume, compared with 1/10 patients (10.0%) with low total ventricular CSF volume. Third ventricular percentile showed a weak to moderate positive correlation with total ventricular CSF percentile (ρ = 0.45, p = 0.0097); however, among the 22 patients with small third ventricular volume, 14 (63.6%) had preserved total ventricular CSF volume, representing 43.8% of the overall cohort (14/32). Exploratory symptom-based analyses did not identify statistically significant associations with small third ventricular volume. Conclusion Reduced third ventricular volume was common in patients with CVF-related SIH and was more frequently observed than low total ventricular CSF volume, including among patients with low-probability Bern scores. Third ventricular volumetry may provide a useful adjunct imaging marker for CVF-related SIH, particularly when brain MRI findings are nondiagnostic.

title: The importance of CSF distribution for target values and risk profiling for idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus shunt surgery.
abstract: Background and purpose Idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus is characterized by gait disturbance, cognitive impairment, and urinary incontinence. Symptom improvement can be achieved by shunt surgery, especially regarding gait difficulties. This study investigated whether CSF volumetry can define postoperative target values associated with clinical improvement and, secondly, predict potential non-response or overdrainage complications. Materials and methods Forty-seven patients with iNPH were prospectively followed for three years after shunt surgery. Quantitative MRI was performed at baseline and at 3, 12, and 36 months postoperatively. Automatic segmentation yielded ventricular volume, subarachnoid CSF volume, ratio of ventricular and total CSF volume and ratio of total brain volume and intracranial volume. Clinical outcome was assessed using the Hellström iNPH scale. Patients were classified as responders and non-responders and further subdivided with and without overdrainage complications. Results Eighty-seven percent of patients were classified as responders. Responders demonstrated a 26% reduction in ventricular volume(139 ml at baseline and 102 ml at three years) accompanied by a >60% improvement in iNPH score. The ventricular/total CSF ratio decreased from 0.34 to 0.25. Non-responders exhibited low ratios already at baseline, due to a significantly higher subarachnoid CSF volume. Overdrainage-related postural headaches were associated withlow subarachnoid CSF volume, younger age, higher baseline iNPH score, and higher BPV/ICV ratio. Aggregate z-scores combining multiple baseline metrics improved discrimination between responders, non-responders, and patients at risk for overdrainage. Conclusions Baseline volumetry may provide target values and risk stratification for shunt surgery in iNPH. Responders showed a reduction of ventricular volume to ∼100 ml and ventricle/total CSF ratio to ∼0.25. High subarachnoid CSF volumes at baseline, however, was associated with poor response, while low subarachnoid CSF volume indicated an increased risk of postural headache. Quantitative CSF segmentation may improve patient selection and postoperative management in iNPH.

title: Transcranial Focused Ultrasound: Established and Emerging Applications in Neurosciences.
abstract: Transcranial MR-guided high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) thermoablation is an established incisionless image-guided treatment for movement disorders; however, neuroradiologist involvement in clinical decision-making and procedural workflows is highly variable and site-specific. Transcranial low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) is a rapidly evolving non-invasive, image-guided technology for neuromodulation and blood-brain barrier disruption. Compared with HIFU, the optimal protocol, therapeutic mechanism, and safety limits remain uncertain for LIFU. Despite these gaps, LIFU has significant potential for neuropsychiatric and neuro-oncologic diseases. Familiarity with transcranial ultrasound principles and the pivotal role of CT and MR imaging for targeting and evaluating outcomes is increasingly important for neuroradiologists. This review uses HIFU as a clinical model to illustrate the integration of imaging into focused ultrasound workflows. We then discuss LIFU with respect to technical factors, imaging considerations, safety, and limitations. We highlight its emerging applications, including neuromodulation, targeted drug delivery, and liquid biopsy. Finally, we conclude by summarizing key knowledge gaps, outlining future directions, and proposing strategies to more actively engage neuroradiologists in this emerging field.

title: The unknown face of Sturge-Weber Syndrome type 3 - a hybrid scoping review of the literature.
abstract: Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS) type 3 is a rare neurocutaneous disorder characterised by isolated leptomeningeal angiomatosis without facial capillary malformation or ocular involvement. Existing literature is limited to case reports and small series, resulting in incomplete characterisation of its clinical and radiological phenotype and frequent diagnostic delay. The increased prevalence of contrast-enhanced MRI has improved detection of pial angiomatosis and associated parenchymal abnormalities. This scoping review aimed to map the available evidence and define current knowledge gaps. Our aim is to synthesise published data on SWS type 3, describe demographic, clinical, and imaging features, and contribute a 15-patient institutional cohort.PubMed and EMBASE were systematically searched (31 March-4 April 2025), with additional studies identified through reference screening. Eligible studies reported isolated leptomeningeal angiomatosis without port-wine birthmark and included contrast-enhanced MRI. Seventy-five published cases were identified. Heterogeneity in study design and reporting precluded quantitative pooling; data were synthesised descriptively. SWS type 3 demonstrates a consistent pattern of unilateral, predominantly occipitoparietal leptomeningeal angiomatosis, most commonly presenting with focal-onset seizures. Despite improved MRI-based recognition, substantial gaps remain regarding natural history, pathophysiology, and optimal management. Prospective, standardised studies are required to refine diagnostic criteria and guide evidence-based care.

title: ASFNR Clinical State of Practice Statement on Imaging of Chronic Subdural Hematoma.
abstract: Background The efficacy of middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAE) for chronic subdural hematoma (cSDH) has heightened interest in imaging biomarkers that may reflect neomembrane activity, predict recurrence, and identify patients most likely to benefit from treatment. Characterization of hematoma internal architecture, referred to as the imaging phenotype, may provide indirect information regarding the biological activity and maturation of the neomembrane. However, imaging phenotype has not been incorporated into randomized trials or validated treatment-selection algorithms, and standardized definitions and reporting remain lacking. Methods The American Society of Functional Neuroradiology Clinical Practice Committee developed this State of Practice statement through expert consensus and review of the available literature. Key message Noncontrast CT (NCCT) remains the primary imaging modality for cSDH assessment. Hematoma burden should be characterized by maximum thickness measured perpendicular to the inner table, midline shift, and, when appropriate, volume. Volume may be estimated using the ABC/2 formula, whereas segmentation is more accurate for irregular, crescentic, or multiloculated collections when available. Internal architecture should be described using the Nakaguchi framework of homogeneous, laminar, separated, and trabecular phenotypes, with mixed or transitional features explicitly reported. Advanced techniques, including dual-energy CT, photon-counting CT, MRI, and arterial spin labeling, may provide information regarding membrane activity but are supported by limited, largely single-center evidence and currently have a problem-solving rather than routine role. Standardized reporting and prospective validation are needed before imaging phenotype or advanced-imaging biomarkers can guide treatment selection.

title: Clinical Impact of Vertebral Artery Injury Detected by Computed Tomography Angiography in Cervical Trauma : A Neurosurgical Perspective.
abstract: Objectıve To evaluate the incidence, radiological features, and clinical impact of vertebral artery injury (VAI) detected by computed tomography angiography in patients with cervical trauma, and to assess its association with neurological deficit and mortality. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 71 cervical trauma patients managed in our neurosurgery clinic between June 2024 to October 2025. After exclusions (age <18 years, malignancy, inadequate imaging, comorbid systemic pathology), 30 patients were included. Demographics, trauma mechanism, computed tomography angiography (CTA) findings, Biffl grading, neurological status and outcomes were compared. Statistical analysis was performed using non-parametric tests with p<0.05 as significance threshold. Results VAI was detected in 13 patients (43.3%), predominantly Biffl grade 4 (23.3%) and grade 2 (13.3%). Neurological deficit was present in 43.3%, more common in VAI-positive cases, though not statistically significant (p=0.519). Mortality occurred exclusively in the VAI-positive group, demonstrating a significant association (p=0.026). Foramen transversum involvement (p=0.002) and facet joint injury (p=0.038) were significantly associated with vascular injury. No significant correlation was found with age, sex, trauma mechanism or other osseous structures. Conclusıon The high VAI incidence detected via CTA highlights the importance of early vascular screening in cervical trauma. Biffl grade distribution and significant association with mortality underline the prognostic weight of high-grade lesions. Foramen transversum and facet involvement may serve as predictors of VAI, guiding clinicians on which patients require urgent CTA. Larger prospective studies are warranted. Early CTA screening may improve neurosurgical risk stratification and prevent missed vascular injuries in high-risk cervical trauma patients.

title: Long-term Clinical Outcomes of Acute Zonal Occult Outer Retinopathy in a Tertiary Referral Center.
abstract: Purpose To characterize the clinical features, multimodal imaging findings, and long-term visual outcomes of patients with acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR) in a single-center cohort. Methods This retrospective cohort study included 34 eyes of 26 patients with AZOOR who were referred to a tertiary referral center between January 2015 and December 2023. Best-corrected visual acuity, fundus photography, fundus autofluorescence, optical coherence tomography (OCT), Humphrey 24-2 visual field examinations were conducted during the initial and final follow-up visits. Results The mean follow-up duration was 50.8 ± 37.9 months (range, 14-138 months). Of these 26 patients, 24 (92.3%) underwent systemic treatment. Disruption of the outer nuclear layer and ellipsoid zone (EZ) was commonly noted at baseline. In contrast, the retinal pigment epithelium was relatively preserved. During follow-up, the proportion of eyes with intact EZ increased from 26.5% to 41.2%, although this change was not statistically significant (p = 0.065). EZ restoration was observed in five eyes. Visual acuity and visual field indices remained largely unchanged during follow-up. Conclusion In this cohort, patients diagnosed with AZOOR demonstrated heterogeneous long-term structural and functional outcomes. Although partial recovery of outer retinal structures was observed in some patients, visual impairment often persisted despite structural improvement. Long-term multimodal follow-up may therefore be important for evaluating disease progression and prognosis.

title: Evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for pediatric hepatoblastoma: a systematic review and expert recommendations from Korea.
abstract: Hepatoblastoma (HB) is the most common primary liver malignancy in children, predominantly affecting those younger than 3 years of age. Although the overall survival rate has improved significantly over the past few decades, standardized clinical practice guidelines for HB in Korea have been lacking. This clinical practice guideline was developed to provide evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis and treatment of HB in children. A multidisciplinary working group comprising pediatric hematologists/oncologists, radiologists, surgeons, pathologists, and methodologists systematically reviewed the literature published up to May 2023. For pretreatment imaging, both abdominal computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are useful for PRE-Treatment EXTent of disease (PRETEXT) staging, with each modality offering distinct advantages. PRETEXT staging at diagnosis is recommended as it provides valuable prognostic information. For standard-risk HB (PRETEXT I-III without metastasis and alpha-fetoprotein ≥100 ng/mL), cisplatinbased chemotherapy without doxorubicin is recommended over cisplatin-doxorubicin combination therapy, as it demonstrates equivalent survival outcomes with fewer adverse effects. In carefully selected patients who are eligible for complete resection at diagnosis, upfront surgery without neoadjuvant chemotherapy should be considered to spare unnecessary chemotherapy and its toxicities. For patients with residual pulmonary metastases after chemotherapy, pulmonary metastasectomy should be considered. Sodium thiosulfate administration following cisplatin should be considered to reduce ototoxicity, although the supporting evidence is derived predominantly from standard-risk patients and its availability in Korea remains limited. Regarding histological subtypes, well-differentiated fetal HB is associated with favorable outcomes and may be treated with surgery alone, whereas the small cell undifferentiated pattern is no longer classified as a HB subtype and requires immunohistochemical and molecular testing to distinguish it from malignant rhabdoid tumor and other small round cell tumors. This guideline represents the first evidence-based clinical practice guideline for pediatric HB in Korea. It aims to standardize the diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, ultimately improving outcomes for Korean children with HB. Given the rarity of this tumor, international collaboration and prospective data collection remain essential for future guideline updates.

title: Imaging-Enhanced Prediction of Upper Limb Motor Function After Stroke Using Automated Segmentation and Cluster Analysis.
abstract: Background Stroke is a leading cause of long-term disability, and early prediction of motor outcomes is critical for guiding individualized rehabilitation strategies. Although neuroimaging offers prognostic insights, its clinical integration remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate whether explainable imaging-derived features can improve the prediction of upper limb motor impairment and to identify distinct recovery profiles through cluster analysis. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 242 patients with acute ischemic stroke who underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging and motor function assessment. Clinical and imaging variables-including infarct volume, motor tract involvement, and subtype classification-were extracted using automated software. Predictive models for Fugl-Meyer Assessment upper extremity (FMA-UE) scores were developed using hierarchical regression, and K-means clustering was applied to standardized baseline data. Cluster characteristics were compared, and recovery profiles were visualized. Results Incorporating imaging variables improved prediction of FMA-UE scores (adjusted R²: 0.595), with motor tract lesion volume emerging as a key predictor. Cluster analysis revealed three distinct patient subgroups: Cluster 1 (mild impairments, younger age), Cluster 2 (older patients with multiple comorbidities), and Cluster 3 (severe neurological deficits, large infarcts). Functional outcomes differed significantly across clusters, with Cluster 3 showing the greatest disability (76% with follow-up modified Rankin Scale 4-6, P < 0.001). Conclusion Imaging-derived features from early magnetic resonance imaging improve the prediction of upper limb motor outcomes after stroke. Cluster-based stratification identifies clinically meaningful subgroups, supporting precision rehabilitation through personalized care planning and targeted secondary prevention.

title: Hepatic Cysts in Korea: Prevalence, Incidence, and Risk Factors Based on a 5.8-Year Follow-up Health Screening Cohort.
abstract: Background Hepatic cysts are fluid-filled liver lesions that are mostly asymptomatic, but fewer than 15% of patients present clinically significant symptoms. Reported prevalence ranges from 2.5% to 71%, yet prior studies have been limited by small populations and incomplete assessment of risk factors. This study aimed to determine the prevalence, incidence, and risk factors using data from a large health screening cohort in Korea. Methods We performed a retrospective cohort analysis of 78,676 participants in the Health and Prevention Enhancement cohort who underwent abdominal ultrasound at the Seoul National University Hospital Healthcare System Gangnam Center from 2003 and 2014. Hepatic cysts were identified using a validated rule-based text-mining algorithm applied to ultrasound reports. Prevalence was estimated from baseline data. Incidence was assessed in 41,179 participants initially negative for hepatic cysts. Risk factors were determined through Cox proportional hazards modeling. Results The prevalence of hepatic cysts at baseline was 8.54% (95% confidence interval [95% CI], 8.34-8.73). The incidence was 23.4 per 1,000 person-years at risk (95% CI, 22.8-24.0). Cox regression identified hepatitis B virus surface antigen (HBs-Ag) positivity (hazard ratio [HR], 1.20; 95% CI, 1.00-1.45) and renal cyst presence (HR, 1.46; 95% CI, 1.31-1.64) as independent risk factors, whereas diabetes mellitus (HR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.54-0.77) and high physical activity (HR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.81-0.97) appeared protective. Conclusion This study provides the prevalence of 8.54%, incidence, and risk factors of hepatic cysts. Renal cyst presence and HBs-Ag positivity are significant risk factors, whereas high physical activity and diabetic status are protective.

The prevalence of hepatic cysts at baseline was 8.54% (95% confidence interval [95% CI], 8.34-8.73). The incidence was 23.4 per 1,000 person-years at risk (95% CI, 22.8-24.0). Cox regression identified hepatitis B virus surface antigen (HBs-Ag) positivity (hazard ratio [HR], 1.20; 95% CI, 1.00-1.45) and renal cyst presence (HR, 1.46; 95% CI, 1.31-1.64) as independent risk factors, whereas diabetes mellitus (HR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.54-0.77) and high physical activity (HR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.81-0.97) appeared protective.

Conclusion

This study provides the prevalence of 8.54%, incidence, and risk factors of hepatic cysts. Renal cyst presence and HBs-Ag positivity are significant risk factors, whereas high physical activity and diabetic status are protective.

title: Radiofrequency Ablation for Low-Risk T1N0M0 Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Objective To evaluate the efficacy and safety of ultrasound (US)-guided radiofrequency ablation (RFA) for low-risk T1N0M0 papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), with emphasis on T1a versus T1b outcomes and longitudinal volume regression. Materials and methods MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and KoreaMed databases were searched for studies published between January 2000 and March 2025. Both single-arm and comparative studies were eligible when RFA outcome data could be extracted independently. Thirty-five studies (9,787 tumors) were included in the analysis. Pooled estimates for complete disappearance, persistent tumors, disease progression, and complication rates were calculated using random-effects models. The volume-reduction ratio (VRR) was assessed at sequential follow-up intervals. Subgroup analyses were used to compare the outcomes for T1a and T1b PTCs. Results Among the 9,787 RFA-treated tumors, the pooled complete disappearance rate was 87.2% (I² = 97.9%). The pooled persistent-tumor rate was 0.1% (I² = 57.6%), and the pooled disease-progression rate, which reflected newly developed tumors (0.8%; I² = 63.9%) and lymph node metastasis (0.2%; I² = 19.8%), was 1.3% (I² = 70.0%). The VRR increased from 63.4% at 6 months to 88.7% at 12 months and reached 97.9% at 24 months. The pooled complication rate was 2.7% (I² = 93.0%), and the major complication rate was 0.02% (I² = 0%). Subgroup analyses showed lower complete disappearance rates (89.2% vs. 58.8%; P < 0.001) and higher persistent-tumor rates (0.02% vs. 2.2%; P < 0.001) in T1b tumors than in T1a tumors; disease progression ( P = 0.234) and total complication rates ( P = 0.794) were comparable. Conclusion US-guided RFA may provide effective tumor control with favorable safety in low-risk T1N0M0 PTC. However, heterogeneity across several efficacy outcomes limits the interpretability of these estimates. T1b PTCs showed lower complete disappearance and higher persistent-tumor rates than T1a PTCs, supporting the need for heightened surveillance of T1b disease.

title: Quantification of Aortic Cusp Parameters Using Computed Tomography in Valve-Sparing Aortic Root Replacement Surgery: A Prospective Study.
abstract: Purpose Determining the feasibility of valve-sparing aortic root replacement (VSRR) requires accurate preoperative assessment of aortic valve cusp geometry. However, the reliability of computed tomography (CT) for measuring cusp parameters remains unclear. This study evaluated the agreement between CT-derived cusp measurements and intraoperative measurements and explored the potential of CT-based cusp asymmetry to predict intraoperative cusp plication. Materials and methods In this prospective study, 32 consecutive patients undergoing VSRR with the reimplantation technique were enrolled. Preoperative CT was used to measure cusp free margin length and geometric height. Agreement between CT-derived and intraoperative measurements was assessed using Bland-Altman analysis and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). An exploratory analysis evaluated whether CT-derived cusp asymmetry predicted the need for intraoperative cusp plication. Results CT measurements demonstrated good agreement with intraoperative measurements for cusp free margin length (ICC 0.80-0.87). In contrast, geometric height showed only moderate agreement (ICC 0.44-0.69). Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated moderate discriminative ability of CT-derived cusp asymmetry for predicting intraoperative cusp plication (area under the curve, 0.71; 95% confidence interval, 0.49-0.91), although the association did not reach statistical significance ( p =0.06). Postoperative echocardiography demonstrated none-to-mild aortic insufficiency in 96.9% of patients. Conclusion Preoperative CT demonstrated good agreement with intraoperative measurements for cusp free margin length in tricuspid valves, although the absolute limits of agreement were wide. CT-based quantification of cusp asymmetry may provide additional information for preoperative surgical planning; however, its association with intraoperative cusp plication remains exploratory and requires validation in larger studies. Clinical research information service (cris) registration number KCT0006180.
